articles.title: How big is Russia's threat against Germany?
articles.summary: Experts believe that, so far, Germany has been ill-prepared — both militarily and mentally — for Russian provocations. They also warn against the idea that ending support for Ukraine would make…

image.caption: Germans have been protesting both for and against supporting Ukraine in its war with RussiaImage: DW

blocks.text: Warnings keep mounting about Russia's threat to Germany. On October 12, Sinan Selen, president of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, said that Russia's covert attacks and destabilization efforts against Germany and other European countries are "not a temporary development but a long-term hybrid attack."

Even if the war in Ukraine were to end, said Selen, the Russian threat would not disappear. "For Russia, this is about completely redrawing the map of Europe and redefining its own role within Europe and in global politics."
He added that Russia's aggression would continue to be felt not only in Ukraine, but also in the Baltic states, in Poland and in Germany.
Russia is tied down in Ukraine — for now

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the threat situation as one in which "our country is not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare." Russia's goal, he said, is not to defeat Germany militarily "but to subdue us politically and socially."

Security experts, however, are not so sure that Russia is only interested in exercising political and social influence. Last year, political scientist Carlo Masala told the political talk show Maischberger that "Russia is preparing for a major war." And he didn't mean just a cyberwar. Inspector General Carsten Breuer, the Bundeswehr's highest-ranking officer, agreed.

For now, though, Russia remains tied up in its war against Ukraine. According to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, there is no immediate military threat to NATO territory. But according to military experts, European intelligence agencies, and the German Defense Ministry, Russia will have the personnel and equipment to wage a conventional war against NATO by 2029. The Russian defense industry is running at full speed, and Moscow plans to expand its armed forces to 1.5 million soldiers.

At the moment, Russia has other objectives, believes Stefan Meister, an expert on Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP): "I don't think Russia has any interest in a direct military conflict with NATO right now. It wants to test NATO and also display its capabilities," he tells DW.
If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared?
An accidental military confrontation?

An example of Russia's hybrid war might be the failed attack with an explosive-laden drone against a Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport in August. Soon after, the German government stated that it was certain Russia was behind the attack.
Security expert Nico Lange told DW at the time that Germany was very lucky the explosives did not detonate: "Honestly, it was pure coincidence and not the result of German defensive measures."

As for why Germany was targeted specifically, Lange said: "I believe that Germany has always been a primary target of Russian influence and hybrid warfare. Russia believes that Germany is the key to European decision-making. Germany is now leading the way in supporting Ukraine."

Moscow swiftly responded to the German government's accusation with an angry denial. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was "the beginning of a real war," though there was no immediate further escalation.

Nevertheless, there is always the risk that things could spiral out of control following a Russian provocation and subsequent response, according to Stefan Meister: "Accidentally shooting down an aircraft that they were trying to intimidate would trigger a counter-reaction. But I don't believe that Russia is currently aiming for a direct war but rather for provocations, polarization, and sowing uncertainty among the population."
AfD says less money for Ukraine means more for Germany
Not everyone shares the assessment that Russia poses a threat to Germany — some believe that the threat can be averted.

Despite the war in Ukraine, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the populist left-wing Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Russia, resume Russian energy supplies and end support for Ukraine.

AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said in early September, "People are fed up with this escalation against Russia, with the billions being squandered there on a system that is actually funded by German taxpayers' money."

The message appears to have resonated among the population, especially in eastern Germany. The AfD saw strong gains in all three state elections in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, it became the strongest party by far and may even run the government there soon, which would be the first time that a far-right party has held power in Germany since the end of WWII.

The CDU's security policy expert Roderich Kiesewetter disputed the claim made by the AfD and BSW that ending aid to Ukraine would mean greater security and more money for German schools and infrastructure: "Spending on education, social policy, and infrastructure is only possible if we live in freedom and democracy — and, above all, in peace and security. Anyone who believes that we'll have more money for social programs if we stop supporting Ukraine and let Russia have its way is either gravely mistaken or is making themselves a tool of Russian propaganda."

blocks.caption: German high school students have gone on strike to protest plans to reintroduce military conscriptionImage: Snowfield Photography/picture alliance

blocks.text: A decades-long pacifist mindset

The perceived security threat has led the German military, the Bundeswehr, to fast-track significant modernization through substantial investment. But it is struggling to find enough recruits for its planned expansion. Many young Germans have taken to the streets to protest against plans to reintroduce conscription. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius faced criticism from inside his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), for saying that Germany must become "capable of waging war." Many found the statement to be too militaristic.

Is Germany prepared for a military threat? "Not at all. Germany is not well prepared militarily or in the civilian sector, and the population isn't mentally prepared for it either," said Meister. "Just look at the demonstrations against conscription and the military that continue to take place, even though Germany needs a draft. For decades, we've grown up in this culture of pacifism, in a comfort zone. I believe there is very limited societal resilience, but above all, we are not at all mentally prepared for war."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are under increasing political pressure — especially from the far right — to scale back support for Ukraine. But Merz never tires of emphasizing that Ukraine will continue to receive support under his chancellorship, calling it a matter of Germany's security. He recently visited Kyiv once again and, together with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, surveyed the destruction caused by Russia.

But this also means that the threat from Russia will continue and even intensify, says Stefan Meister: "I believe we will see a massive increase in attacks such as the one in Leipzig, of provocations involving drones. We will see attacks on infrastructures and possibly also on specific individuals within the military-industrial complex. I believe this is the real, concrete danger facing Germany in the coming months."
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Chinese envoy's remarks seen as 'wolf warrior diplomacy'
articles.summary: Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan"s controversial remarks are an example of “wolf warrior diplomacy,” according to defense analyst Renato Castro.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 10:58pm
Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan’s controversial remarks are an example of “wolf warrior diplomacy,” according to defense analyst Renato Castro.

In a report by JP Soriano on "24 Oras" Weekend on Saturday, Jing claimed that China would "easily win" if it resorted to force in the West Philippine Sea. Several Filipino officials and government agencies have described the remarks as a threat.

“Dito sa wolf warrior diplomacy, talagang ginagamit mo ang lahat para takutin and, to a certain degree, bastusin mo yung host government, na nakikita natin ngayon, ‘no? So, in a way, talagang ginagawa niya yung trabaho niya,” Castro said.
(In wolf warrior diplomacy, you use everything to intimidate and, to a certain degree, disrespect the host government, as we are seeing now. So, in a way, he is doing his job.)
Sen. Risa Hontiveros called on Jing to apologize, warning that he should be declared persona non grata if he refused.
Jing’s remarks prompted President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to summon the Chinese envoy.

“Hindi naman sasabihin niya na isang diplomat, kung wala po talagang ibig sabihin po ‘yan. Kung baga, talagang veiled threat na ho sa atin ‘yan. Let's expect the worst. Kasi talagang gigil na gigil na sa atin ang mga Tsino ho, dahil ho talaga, hindi tayo nagpapatinag sa kanila,” Castro said.

(A diplomat would not say something like that if it did not mean anything. In other words, it is really a veiled threat against us. Let’s expect the worst because the Chinese are extremely frustrated with us for refusing to back down.)
Tensions between the Philippines and China have continued to rise amid their territorial dispute in the West Philippine Sea.

China continues to claim most of the disputed waters despite a 2016 arbitral ruling that invalidated the legal basis of its expansive maritime claims under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The ruling, issued under the arbitration proceedings at the Permanent Court of Arbitration, was in favor of the Philippines.—Jean Mangaluz/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: China's influence in the gaming industry is growing
articles.summary: Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the…

image.caption: The Chinese game 'The Defiant' is set during the Second Sino-Japanese WarImage: 4Divinity

blocks.text: In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

blocks.caption: Game developer Connor Xu wants to tell stories from Chinese historyImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: "The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.
Gaming is part of everyday life in China

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

blocks.caption: 'Honor of Kings' is largely unknown outside China, but it's one of the country's most popular gamesImage: Tencent/Level Infinite/TiMi Studio Group

blocks.text: People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.
Limits on gaming time and extensive controls

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

blocks.caption: The Chinese role-playing game "Genshin Impact" bears visual and gameplay similarities to "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild"Image: Cognosphere/miHoYo/HoYoverse

blocks.text: Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.
No license? No sales in China

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

blocks.caption: The strategy game 'Heroes of Might and Magic III Remake' is currently being developed by Ubisoft's studios in Chengdu and ShanghaiImage: Ubisoft

blocks.text: The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.
Strict criteria for video games

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.
Chinese culture is an international hit

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

blocks.caption: The video game 'Black Myth: Wukong' became an international hitImage: Game Science Interactive Technology Co

blocks.text: Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.
The problem of self-censorship

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.
History from a Chinese perspective

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."
Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.
This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar’s attorneys say federal search of her home was ‘neither justified nor lawful’
articles.summary:
Minnesota lawmaker’s attorneys asked for return of seized items and the preservation of any recordings of search

Ilhan Omar’s…

blocks.text: Ilhan Omar’s attorneys have asked the US Department of Justice to return property that federal agents removed days earlier from her home during a search.
The lawyers for the Minnesota Democrat contended that the seizure as “neither justified nor lawful”, according to a letter that the Associated Press reported on Friday.

The federal investigation into Omar was launched just weeks ahead of the 3 November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot. Democrats accused Donald Trump, a Republican, of abusing his power as president to target a political opponent.

Omar’s attorneys wrote that there is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, according to the Wall Street Journal, which first reported on the lawyers’ letter.

“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the president’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers,” the congresswoman’s attorneys wrote.
The federal government has issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives, and seized her phone in its investigation of the congresswoman.
A justice department spokesperson said the letter from Omar’s defense team was “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”, according to the AP.
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” the spokesperson, Emily Covington, wrote in a text message on Friday evening.

The letter from Omar’s lawyers also accused the justice department of violating the agency’s longstanding policy aimed at avoiding potentially influencing an election. And they raised concerns about whether the investigators followed instructions from the magistrate judge who approved the search.
The attorneys demanded in the letter that the justice department preserve any audio and video taken during the search on Monday.

The justice department launched the investigation after years of Trump and conservative media figures promoting unsubstantiated rumors that Omar’s ex-husband is actually her brother – and that she married him so that he could obtain immigration status.
Omar, the most prominent Somali American in the US, has denied that allegation.

Citing sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News reported that the search on Monday was related to a criminal fraud investigation concerning Omar’s immigration paperwork. Omar’s father filled out that paperwork when she was a child.
“I’m ok,” Omar posted on X after the raid. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
Omar also said the search was “just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation”.
The president has consistently launched racist attacks against Omar and other Somali Americans in Minnesota.
In December, he described them as “garbage” who “come from hell, and they complain, and do nothing but bitch”.
He said Omar “should be thrown the hell out of our country”.
After Monday’s search, Trump denied being involved in the investigation.
“I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me,” Trump said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Selma Blair ‘did not intend to harm anyone’ during airplane incident, representatives say
articles.summary:
Actor experienced a ‘medical emergency’ on flight during which she allegedly injured crew members, statement says

Actor Selma Blair…

blocks.text: Actor Selma Blair did not mean to hurt anyone during the recent flight which led to her arrest on allegations that she assaulted a pair of cabin crew members, a police officer and a nurse, her representatives said on Friday in a statement that characterized the episode as a medical emergency.

The lengthy statement also dismissed prior media coverage of Blair’s arrest after a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York as unsympathetic and inaccurate, singling out reporting from several outlets alleging that she tried to open the door of the airplane that she and her fellow passengers were on.
“Selma Blair experienced a medical emergency on the flight,” her representatives’ statement contended. “There was no attempt to open the door of the aircraft. Selma did not intend to harm anyone.”

Friday’s statement from Blair’s camp added some contours to brief remarks made in the days since her arrest by her publicist and lawyer which maintained that there had been a medical emergency but did not elaborate much.

Without specifying who may have done so, the statement on Friday called it “outrageous” for anyone to suggest Blair does not have multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic neurological disorder which she went public about being diagnosed with in 2018.

“What Selma has been able to do physically in the years since is nothing short of a miracle,” said the statement, which was reported by the Associated Press and People. “She still has bad days, and she lives with pain daily.”
The statement said Blair has a condition secondary to her MS known as pseudobulbar affect, “which bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her”.
Blair therefore “travels with a service dog who doesn’t leave her side”.
“And the authorities took her dog from her,” said the statement, which described Blair as a disability rights and MS community advocate.

Blair’s statement faulted media outlets which – in covering her arrest on Sunday – referred to a 2016 incident in which she reportedly began screaming uncontrollably while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico, before being removed on a stretcher.
The actor apologized after that earlier incident, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”, blacking out as a result while saying and doing things that “I deeply regret”.
Blair’s representatives expressed gratitude to the “handful of journalists [who] have taken the time to report on Selma as a human being rather than a headline”.
“Fair reporting has been the exception,” said their statement on Friday, which accused the media of building a narrative around Blair almost solely on police allegations “and a decade-old headline”.

“There is much more to this than has been reported,” the statement continued, without offering specifics. “And we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion.”

Authorities accused Blair of injuring two flight attendants while traveling from LA to the John F Kennedy airport (JFK) in New York on Sunday night. She also was alleged to have kicked a police officer taking her to the hospital and kicking a nurse once she arrived at the facility, said a statement from the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates JFK.

She pleaded not guilty on Monday to state assault charges involving the officer and the nurse, with a judge ordering Blair to stay away from them. Blair was freed on bail and tentatively scheduled to return to court in January.

Meanwhile, the AP reported that Blair had gotten a notice from the FBI charging her with assault for alleged actions on Delta flight 938. The outlet cited a federal law enforcement official who spoke on the condition of anonymity for not being authorized to speak publicly about the case.

Details of exactly what happened in the moments leading up to Blair’s arrest haven’t been disclosed by Delta, state authorities or the FBI. An air traffic control audio recording from the flight Blair was on captured the pilot saying: “One flight attendant and one passenger … sustained some minor injuries – a bloody nose as well as some bite marks.”

“I don’t think we need an ambulance or anything like that – but we just want to get some medical personnel at the gate to look at their injuries,” the pilot said, according to the recording, a copy of which was published by NBC Los Angeles.
Beside that case and the incident in 2016, Blair grappled with controversy when she apologized in February 2024 for an Islamophobic comment on social media.
Blair’s major film credits include Cruel Intentions in 1999, Legally Blonde in 2001 and Hellboy in 2004.

She earned a 2011 Grammy award nomination for best spoken word album for children for her work on Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl – The Definitive Edition. And she also starred in the acclaimed 2021 documentary Introducing, Selma Blair, which explores her life after her MS diagnosis.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after cancer operation
articles.summary: Doctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lung

blocks.text: Pope Leo has been discharged from hospital in Rome after undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.
Leo, 71, was deemed “fit for discharge”, his doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritoria, said in a statement published by the Vatican.
He walked unaided from the hospital on Saturday afternoon, to cheers from well-wishers.

Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, has been in the Gemelli hospital since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung in order to extract the tumour.
“Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge,” the statement said.

Doctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They are waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.
Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma.
The pontiff celebrated mass in his room on the 10th-floor of the Gemelli hospital in the north-west of the Italian capital before being discharged.

blocks.caption: Leo celebrating Mass at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome. Photograph: Vatican Media/AP

blocks.text: The Vatican said he would recite the Angelus prayer on Sunday “from the window of the papal apartment”. It was during his angelus last week, in a rare moment of Vatican transparency, that Leo made the shock announcement to the crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square that a small nodule on his lung had been detected during a check-up.

The pope has worked from hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital. The pope’s appointments had been cancelled until 20 October.
It is uncertain if he’ll make an intense 12-day trip to South America planned in November.
Cardinal ​Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s secretary of state, told reporters on Friday that Leo may need to readjust his trip schedule, at least with regard to South America, depending on his health.
Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.

blocks.caption: The Gemelli hospital in Rome. Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/AP

blocks.text: The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russia will intensify war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukrainian president calls the move a ‘reward’ for Vladimir Putin as Russia strikes country’s power plants

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Donald Trump’s decision to roll back sanctions on Russia will intensify the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, as Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine’s power plants in an attempt to black out the country’s cities before winter.

The Ukrainian president also said he expected the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin.

“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”
In a social media message earlier, Zelenskyy described Trump’s latest actions as a “reward” that would embolden the Russian president.

“A US ⁠sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground,” said Zelenskyy. “We must keep trying to end the ‌war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.”

In its latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, Trump announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.

The act, named for the late senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the legislation, would have introduced tough new sanctions on Russia including a 100% tariff on major importers of Russian oil such as China and India, as well as sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, financial institutions and shadow fleet of oil tankers.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said the decision to waive the sanctions would encourage Vladimir Putin to intensify the war in Ukraine and called for support in the US to resurrect the bill.

“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he wrote in a statement. “This law could have – and still can! – help a great deal. But the law needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”

The move was greeted by the Russian presidential envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”
The legislation, which sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps the country’s energy supplies moving, was due to be implemented in two days.

It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.

Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1m tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
after newsletter promotion

The Trump administration’s decision to waive the sanctions is the latest consequence of a brutal quarrel between Trump and Zelenskyy. Several times this week, the US did not provide intelligence of impending ballistic missile attacks to Ukraine, and the White House reportedly ordered the Pentagon to throttle the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet network used by Ukraine’s armed forces to run its drone operations on the frontline.

“We very much hope – and I personally hope – that the president of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops the strikes on our energy infrastructure, and stops this war,” Zelenskyy said on Saturday. “But once again, you cannot achieve this by restricting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And even less so by lifting sanctions.”

Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he has blamed the war in Ukraine, rather than the closure of the strait of Hormuz, for the worldwide spike in diesel prices. Ukraine unilaterally halted the strikes after Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, but resumed them when it became clear that Russia was stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian power plants and substations.

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had launched one of its worst strikes yet against the country’s energy infrastructure, hitting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities and causing “severe consequences”.

He also indicated that Ukraine’s dwindling stock of anti-air weapons made it difficult to shoot down many of the loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles being launched each night at Ukraine.

“Although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them,” he said, the “sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences.”

articles.title: Isabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonym
articles.summary:
Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits

The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio…

blocks.text: The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.

Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday with La hora antes del alba, which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired by Chile.

The new story follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.
Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.
“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”

She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.
“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.

Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional title Los que faltan.

However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”

The prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded to La bestia, a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Mola was in fact three male writers – Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.

The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.

Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.

Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”
The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.

articles.title: ‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off
articles.summary:
School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments

On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the…

blocks.text: On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.
But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town.

The local comprehensive, King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC), has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field – and it is likely houses will be built on it.

School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.

“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.
“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”

Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealing almost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.

Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”

Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign group Friends of Lower Field, said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”

Lewis Winks, a leading member of the Right to Roam group, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known for progressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate, about a century ago.

blocks.caption: Campaigner Lewis Winks said Lower Field had been shared by the school and community for about a century. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian

blocks.text: A key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.
Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”
after newsletter promotion

The Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”

But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to them are unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.
Matthew Shanks, chief executive of Education South West, said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.

He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.

School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.
Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for six years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.

“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”

articles.title: Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California
articles.summary:
A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistance

Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late…

blocks.text: Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California.

The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor.
But for Rucci, a 66-year-old lawyer with a complicated past, none of these obstacles seemed insurmountable.

Rucci is among the new class of middlemen who inhabit the burgeoning world of datacenter development. The rapid rise of artificial intelligence – galvanized by Silicon Valley companies worth trillions of dollars – has fueled one of the biggest industrial construction booms in history. The technology requires far more computing power than traditional internet services, and that means building enormous new structures to house millions of servers.

blocks.caption: A portrait of Sebastian Rucci at the location of his proposed AI data center, Imperial, California, on 1 July 2026. Photograph:  John Francis Peters

blocks.text: This proliferation of datacenters is now attracting modern-day prospectors seeking land in hopes of cashing in on one of the fastest-growing and most lucrative industries on Earth. Set in their sights are areas like Imperial county: rural, underdeveloped and desperate for an economic boost.

“I didn’t know much about datacenters,” Rucci said, recalling a couple of years back. “I made calls to people I knew in Silicon Valley. And within a short period, I realized: holy shit, this stuff is huge.”

Rucci, a self-described expert at doing the tedious legwork of packaging permits and plans, proved adept at selling a bright future of economic development to county lawmakers. He said his sales skills also nabbed him a direct line to Google, which floated interest in being the tenant of the datacenter, according to emails between Rucci and county agencies.

With the promise of these potential partnerships and support from construction unions, Rucci moved into high gear last year and began plotting his nearly 1m-square-foot datacenter – a facility the size of 16 football fields combined. He said he had invested about $5m already, and, if it gets approved and passed off to a builder, he expects “big multipliers of that” in return.
What Rucci didn’t expect, however, was the firestorm of resistance his project set off in the community.

Over the past year, more than half a dozen lawsuits have been filed, along with recall efforts for local officials who supported the project. Even a temporary 45-day datacenter moratorium was approved. Echoing similar battles against such development across the US, Imperial county residents told the Guardian they fear increased emissions, harm to the region’s rare desert wildlife, constraints on the power grid and rapidly dwindling water supply, along with noise issues. Rucci denies the project will have such effects.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators wave signs during a nationwide protest against AI datacenter expansion in Imperial. Photograph: Sandy Huffaker/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: It seems the backlash succeeded – for now. Rucci’s developments are on pause after a county judge ruled last month that his project cannot move forward until it clears an extensive environmental review. Despite a bold start, Rucci could end up a cautionary tale of what can go wrong when a businessman moves too fast without community buy-in.

“This project was presented as a Noah’s Ark that’s going to come save everybody,” said Francisco Leal, who lives in a residential neighborhood across the street from Rucci’s proposed datacenter. “But the community sees this project as a Trojan horse.”
From strip club owner to datacenter developer

When Rucci landed on that vast plot of land in Imperial county in late 2024, only two things really mattered: finding a location that could be exempted from California’s strict environmental building requirements, and getting his hands on a lot of electricity. In unincorporated Imperial county, he had both.

Because the land was zoned for industrial use, he was able to apply for an exemption from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which would fast-track the project by avoiding the environmental permitting process. And for electricity, Rucci was able to work with the local energy provider to eventually get 330 megawatts of electricity – enough to power a city the size of Tallahassee.

Rucci is based in Huntington Beach, but has started several businesses throughout southern California, St Louis and Ohio. In early 2025, he said one of his connections introduced him to a longtime Google employee who helped guide him through the process. In a July email to Imperial county’s planning and development services, Rucci wrote that the datacenter would “enable Google to conduct artificial intelligence and large language model training for its Gemini system”, Google’s suite of AI models.

“We have secured interest from Google for this project, which we are confident will transform the area through increased tax revenues, new employment opportunities, and expanded energy production,” Rucci wrote in another email in August to the county’s air pollution control district.

“We are not involved in a datacenter project in Imperial county,” said a Google spokesperson. She did not respond to questions about the company’s relationship with Rucci. He said Google’s response made sense considering they do not have a formal agreement.

While California has dozens of datacenters capable of cloud computing, streaming and internet searches, the state has scant facilities dedicated to AI. That’s because California is one of the most rigorous states when it comes to environmental permitting for energy and water-intensive facilities such as AI datacenters.

blocks.caption: No Data Center signs are posted in the front yard of a home which is right behind the proposed site for a 950,000 sq ft data center on 12 March in Imperial. Photograph: Gina Ferazzi/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images

blocks.text: Major projects in California take an average of seven years to get completed, said Michael Thomas, the founder of Cleanview, which tracks datacenter development. For comparison, the average in Texas is about three years. Thomas said he had seen a surge of new players, like Rucci, get into AI datacenter development nationwide. These people, he said, were willing to take on the risk and find ways to speed up the process.

“Land and power have become so scarce at the scale that these big tech companies need,” Thomas said. So, if a developer can shorten the timeline, “a company like Google or Microsoft or Meta may be willing to pay you a huge premium … It’s potentially a way to make millions of dollars very quickly.”

Rucci is no stranger to taking on risk. He has owned a strip club, addiction treatment centers and dozens of accounting and real estate endeavors. In 2010, while operating the strip club, Go Go Cabaret, he was convicted on four counts of illegal liquor sales for which he had to serve a 30-day jail sentence. He was also charged with engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity, money laundering and promoting prostitution, but those charges were later dismissed. In 2019, California suspended his license to practice law for nearly three years.

He has also filed for corporate bankruptcy at least twice. The most recent time, in 2023, took place after the Department of Justice investigated one of his addiction treatment centers for alleged fraud, ending with a government seizure of $600,000 of assets. No criminal charges were filed, however, and that money was later returned with interest after Rucci sued the government to reclaim the seized funds.

Since zeroing in on Imperial county in 2024, Rucci has registered several new businesses related to the vast datacenter campus, from construction and energy supply to ongoing operations. The umbrella company for his project is an LLC called Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing (IVCM). Rucci says the facility will bring in more than 1,600 construction jobs and nearly $30m in annual tax revenue. It will also include an electrical substation, on-site battery energy storage and more than 130 methane-gas-fueled generators, according to an application submitted to the county planning department.

Rucci said his diverse experience was well-suited for such a complicated project. “That doesn’t mean that my background isn’t colorful,” he said. “I’ve challenged cities. I fought the federal government. I’ve done a lot of stuff. But that doesn’t mean that I don’t know how to process this and get it through.”
Battle lines

At first, Leal had no clue that the dusty 75 acres of land across the street from his house had been bought by a developer. It wasn’t until the day before Thanksgiving last year when he found a colorful flyer hanging from his door that his world began to swirl around him. The flyer mapped out the huge project and warned that construction was moving forward without requiring the state’s usual environmental review.

Leal began scanning the internet, and what he found shocked him. His back fence was all that separated his home from Rucci’s property. While Leal lived in Imperial city, the datacenter would fall just outside city limits on unincorporated county land. It was clear that living next to this facility would permanently change the quiet life he and his wife had envisioned when they moved there some 20 years earlier.

“When we bought that house, we planned for it to be the house where we would retire, where our kids would grow up and return when they visit,” Leal said. “The quality of life of anybody living half a mile from the datacenter will be affected.”

He started texting his neighbors that same day. As word spread, people began to organize, holding meetings and rallies against the datacenter proposal. Within months, close to 3,500 people would sign a petition opposing the facility, and state senator Steve Padilla, who represents the district, would sound the alarm, introducing a series of bills aimed at datacenters.

blocks.caption: Residents protest against the plans for a new datacenter. Photograph: Courtesy of Valle Imperial Resiste

blocks.text: As AI datacenters have popped up around the world, they’ve come under scrutiny for being extremely resource-intensive. A query through chatbots such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini needs nearly 10 times as much electricity as a typical internet search, and that number can increase for more complicated prompts. Because supercomputers run hot, they typically need extensive water-cooling systems.

Imperial county is a critical habitat for wildlife like the desert pupfish, which is listed as an endangered species under the California Endangered Species Act and swims through agricultural drains and canals, much like one that crosses Rucci’s property. Other desert animals of concern include the flat-tailed horned lizard, yellow-breasted chat and burrowing owls.

As Leal got more involved in the datacenter fight, he met other concerned residents, like Christopher Scurries. Scurries lives nearby and is a music teacher at Imperial high school. He said he was worried about datacenter noise, what’s known as a constant low hum. “I’ll definitely hear when I’m here in my house,” he said. Scurries and his wife moved to the area in 2017 so they could afford a home. Now with a two-year-old daughter, his previously pleasant life feels uncertain in the shadow of the datacenter.

It’s testament to a long-simmering sentiment in this corner of the Sonoran desert, where pollutants from agriculture and industry, along with poverty, have long taken an undue toll. One in five adults is unemployed in the region and the poverty rate, at close to 20%, is the highest in California.

“The benefits these structures may bring into a community – the jobs, tax revenue, even the infrastructure improvements – may feel uncertain or uneven compared to the scale of the impact,” said Carla Walker, the US director of environmental justice and equity at the research organization World Resources Institute. “Communities are asking these questions of who benefits and who pays the price.”

For Jacob Rodriguez, who was born and raised in the area, who pays the price has been top of mind. “It’s an existential threat,” he said of the datacenter project, noting that residents had long dealt with pollution and dwindling water supplies. “The respiratory problems and the air quality here are already abysmal … eventually, indirectly, this will cost lives.”
‘I’m not here to run for Miss America’

By March, tensions between Rucci and the community had reached a boiling point. At an Imperial county board of supervisors meeting, dozens of residents, including Leal and Scurries, packed into the chambers for a public feedback session. As Rucci stood at the lectern, trying to present his more than 100 slides on the project, the crowd steadily chanted “no datacenters” and waved “not in my backyard” signs. It got so raucous that Rucci, the main speaker on the schedule, left the meeting early.

As he walked out of the building, protesters yelled “Fuera, Rucci, fuera” (“leave” in Spanish). Visibly fed up, Rucci unexpectedly approached a person screaming through a bullhorn and roared in their face.

blocks.caption: Tensions grew heated between Rucci and community members during a meeting in March.

blocks.text: By this point, the project was at the center of a heated legal battle. The city of Imperial had sued the county for bypassing public input and environmental reviews when it approved the datacenter (the environmental nonprofit Sierra Club later joined on). Rucci, in turn, counter-sued in federal court on behalf of his company IVCM, alleging the city carried out a “bad-faith campaign of administrative obstruction and targeted retaliation”.

He then went on to sue an anti-datacenter activist named Jake Tison, the Comité Cívico del Valle non-profit, and its executive director, Luis Olmedo, and the local public-media news station KPBS and one of its reporters, Kori Suzuki, for defamation. Those three defamation suits were dismissed. Rucci has appealed in the cases against KPBS and Comité Cívico del Valle and is working to reverse the ruling on Tison.
“Look, I’m not here to run for Miss America or Mr America,” Rucci said. “I’m here to do a datacenter.”

Rucci, on behalf of IVCM, also sued the local utility, the Imperial irrigation district, for rejecting an application for water to cool the datacenter. The utility’s sole source of water is the drought-stricken Colorado River. The AI facility would need about 750,000 gallons of water a day, according to Rucci.

He says the water the datacenter would use is equivalent to a 160-acre farm, of which there are several in the area. The utility’s officials, however, voiced concerns about how the project would affect residents. Karin Euenio, one of the utility’s directors, wrote in an op-ed: “I believe it is my duty to speak up when a proposal raises serious concerns about ratepayers, reliability, and community wellbeing.”

blocks.caption: The proposed site of the 950,00 sq ft datacenter is on a dusty parcel next to the Victoria Ranch housing community. Photograph: Gina Ferazzi/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images

blocks.text: The tumult continued through the spring and summer, with Rucci’s IVCM spending $30,000 in a campaign to back his company spokesperson, Carlos Duran, to fill the seat of one of the utility district’s directors. He lost.

For its part, the community instigated its own political organizing efforts with a recall campaign of Peggy Price, the chair of Imperial county’s board of supervisors who has been supportive of the datacenter. That campaign is ongoing.

While things had been looking good for Rucci after he got county approval for the project in April, it took a drastic turn over the last month. The judge presiding over the city’s lawsuit ruled Rucci must go back to square one for the entire approval process. That means before breaking ground, the datacenter must clear lengthy environmental reviews to assess its impact on the power grid, water supply and emissions.

Alene Taber, a lawyer representing Imperial, said these reviews could take a year or more and that alternative locations for the datacenter would have to be taken into consideration. She said it was meaningful “that there [will be] a transparent, public, environmental process”.
Rucci, however, said he was not deterred and is going to challenge the judge’s ruling. “It’ll be just a matter of time,” he said. “I’m not going away.”

articles.title: India news: CJP founder released a day after detention

image.caption: Abhijeet Dipke waved to the media as he was released from the police stationImage: Arun Sankar/AFP

blocks.text: October 17, 2026
CJP founder released a day after detention
Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released by an Indian court on Saturday, one day after his detention for attempting to lead a protest rally in New Delhi.
The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man."
The CJP's head of legal affairs, Ratna Singh, said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms.

Neha Bora, a prominent student activist and the face of the protests, was also detained on Friday while attempting to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters. She was released earlier on Saturday.
Dipke called Friday's protest a show of support for the two CJP leaders detained and jailed for five days this week for demonstrating at an unauthorized protest site.
Opposition parties and CJP activists defied a security crackdown and rallied to demand the resignation of India's chief election commissioner.
They accuse the election commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party.

articles.title: Widespread protests taking place across France over cost of living concerns

image.caption: Protesters march from Place de la République during the latest student protests in Paris on Saturday. (Getty Images)

blocks.text: Why French students are trashing the streets in protest

For weeks, high school students in France have forced a chaotic confrontation about the government’s priorities, but as CBC’s Chris Brown explains, their demands for more funding come as the country faces a precarious debt crisis.

items: October 17Why are students protesting?Protesters march from Place de la République during the latest student protests in Paris on Saturday. (Getty Images)Many high school students say the state of their learning environment is poor, from decaying infrastructure to a lack of teachers. More than half of all schools in France are short-staffed this year, according to a survey conducted by a secondary school teachers' union.The shortage has affected public education in France for close to a decade. The chronic failure to replace absent teachers or hire substitutes means students can miss hundreds of hours of instruction.The students say they are also fed up with overcrowded classrooms, with an average of 25-30 students a class.They also describe dilapidated buildings, pest infestations — including cockroaches and rats — and uninsulated classrooms severely affected by temperature shifts, particularly during recent heat waves.Students and their supporters have taken to the streets for weeks because they feel the government is doing too little, too late. The Education Ministry will receive an additional 1.2 billion euros ($1.9 billion Cdn.) in funding next year — but that won't be enough, according to opposition parties, who say the amount barely keeps up with inflation.

Wave of protests across France over cost of livingSarah PetzProtesters face police officers during a demonstration to protest against the high cost of living, in Paris on Saturday as part of a nationwide call for mobilization bringing together various groups expressing their anger: former 'yellow vests,' secondary school and university students, climate activists and even farmers. (Kiran Ridley/AFP/Getty Images)Hundreds of demonstrations over the cost of living are taking place across France today as high school students, who have been holding protests over school conditions, band together with the country's gilets jaunes (yellow vest) movement. A website set up by the organizers of Saturday's protests shows more than 800 rallies spanning all corners of the country were planned. In Paris, posters announcing the return of the yellow-vest movement have appeared on the streets as organizers seek to bring together grievances ranging from education and working conditions to purchasing power and the cost of living.The prospect of yellow-vest demonstrators returning to the streets will evoke memories of the 2018 protests over high fuel prices that developed into one of the biggest challenges to Emmanuel Macron's presidency. Some protests descended into clashes with police, including on Dec. 1, 2018, when there was rioting around the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.Macron appealed for "calm and respect" on the eve of the protests, adding that the right to protest must go hand in hand with "respect for people and property," Le Monde reported Friday. -With files from Reuters

articles.title: Pope to be discharged days after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: The pontiff will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing in St Peter's Square on Sunday.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.
The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.
On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff.
A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.

The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.
The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".
It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.

The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.
The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.
Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.
It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges support for new U.S. sanctions on Russia hours after Trump paused them
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters on Saturday to speak out in defence of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing…

image.caption: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, shown in Brussels on Friday, urged his supporters on Saturday to speak up in support of U.S. sanctions against Russia, which U.S. President Donald Trump has put on hold. (Omar Havana/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters on Saturday to speak out in defence of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.
Ukraine's leader also said Moscow carried out massive strike on energy infrastructure

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters on Saturday to speak out in defence of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.
The White House’s decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults with winter approaching.
Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but he did not directly criticize the U.S. leader. Tensions between Ukraine and Washington have deepened in recent days.
Zelenskyy blasts U.S.-Russia diesel deal after Trump calls Ukraine strikes on refineries 'a disgrace'

"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote on social media platform X.

He also expressed hope that the new sanctions could be revived. "This Act could have helped enormously — and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters," he said.
'Severe consequences' from strikes: Zelenskyy
Zelenskyy also said on Saturday that Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.
"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.

items: Trump pauses sanctions package targeted at Russian economy

blocks.text: Ukraine's air force said that Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight. All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.

Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the nearly five-year-old war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.
Russia claims it has taken control of another town

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Saturday its forces had taken control of eight more Ukrainian settlements, including the town of Dobropillia in eastern Donetsk region, news agency Interfax reported.

The town, southwest of the key centres of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, has been under sustained Russian attack for some time. But Ukraine's General Staff denied Russia's claim and said on Saturday that Ukrainian forces remained in control of the eastern town of Dobropillia.
Escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports is making shipping risky

In an emailed statement, General Staff spokesperson Andriy Kovaliov said Ukraine also rejected Russia's claim that Russian forces had captured more than 1,800 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory and 92 settlements since Sept. 1.
Russia's Defence Ministry also said it had struck Ukrainian drone storage sites and transport infrastructure used by Ukraine's armed forces over the past 24 hours.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Sara Duterte denies Jollibee franchise ownership
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte denied claims that she owns a Jollibee franchise, accusing online news platform Rappler of publishing misleading reports about her business interests.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 8:19pm
Vice President Sara Duterte denied claims that she owns a Jollibee franchise, accusing online news platform Rappler of publishing misleading reports about her business interests.

“I do not own a Jollibee franchise or any other franchise. I previously invested in a company that is part of a legitimate business organization owned and operated by individuals with an established reputation for integrity and good standing,” Duterte said in a statement on Saturday.

“A basic level of research and due diligence should make this clear. Rappler should understand that investing in a company does not automatically equate to owning the company itself, much less owning, managing or operating its individual businesses or franchises,” she added.
She also raised concerns over the “apparent targeting of legitimate businesses, which inevitably causes unwarranted reputational and commercial damage.”
Jollibee was previously linked to Duterte in a forensic financial report presented by analyst Alexander Cabrera during her impeachment trial.
According to Cabrera, GenCorp, a company listed in Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), reportedly owned five Jollibee restaurants.
GMA News has reached out to Rappler for comment and will update this story once a response is received. —VBL, GMA News
