articles.title: Bank of England governor walks out of IMF summit in protest against Russia
articles.summary:
Andrew Bailey among finance leaders to leave session in Bangkok when Russian finance minister addressed group

The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has taken part in a walkout of…

blocks.text: The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has taken part in a walkout of finance leaders who left an International Monetary Fund meeting in protest against Russian involvement.

Bailey joined counterparts from France, Germany and a number of Scandinavian and Baltic countries who left the session in Bangkok when the Russian finance minister, Anton Siluanov, addressed the group in Russian.
The Bank of England confirmed that Bailey took part.
The president of the German Bundesbank, Joachim Nagel, said nearly half of all delegates took part in the joint departure when Siluanov started speaking.
“The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe,” one European diplomat told the Reuters news agency.
“We cannot normalise relations with Russia.”
The walkout was acknowledged by the chair of the IMF’s steering committee, the Saudi finance minister, Mohammed al-Jadaan.
Al-Jadaan said: “We came here for a reason, and we achieved ⁠it. Look at this chair statement, it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that’s what matters.”
Germany had warned against efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage. Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers this year.
The US has been supportive, with the treasury undersecretary Erin Browne telling Reuters that Washington supported Russia’s presence despite concerns from European countries.

The meeting in the Thai capital heard that the global economy was showing remarkable resilience despite the war between Russia and Ukraine, and in spite of the issues around the strait of Hormuz caused by the US’s bombing campaign.
However, al-Jadaan added that there was no room for complacency, amid public debt levels and high bond market rates.

A statement from al-Jadaan after the IMF meeting said: “The global economy has weathered the latest in a series of shocks better than expected, but buffers have been eroded, and resilience cannot be taken for granted.”

He added: “Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security.”

articles.title: Nursery owner in China jailed for life after hundreds of children poisoned
articles.summary: She and five staff members were found to have used the inedible paint in meals to make them look more appealing.

blocks.text: A nursery owner and five members of her staff have been jailed after they were found to have poisoned more than 200 children with lead-tainted food.

Li Huifang, who operated the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui, in the Gansu province, was sentenced to life in prison for producing and selling toxic and harmful food, according to Chinese state media.
In July 2025, 247 pupils and staff at the nursery were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels after children began falling ill.
A report into the incident found that chefs at Heshi Peixin had used inedible paint to "enhance the look" of its meals to attract more students - despite the paint being being clearly marked as such.
In addition to the sentence, the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court also ordered the confiscation of 500,000 yuan (£56,200; $74,700) of Li's personal assets, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Nursery executive principal Zhi Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,00 yuan.
Four other members of staff who worked in the nursery's kitchen received sentences of between six to eight years, according to state media.
The court found the four had been instructed by Li and Zhi to add toxic and harmful ingredients to food served to children and staff.
Food samples were later found to contain lead 2,000 times in excess of China's national safety limit.
The investigation into the poisoning began after 235 children from Heshi Peixin nursery had to be treated for lead poisoning after eating steamed red date cakes and sausage corn buns.

Investigators found that the red date cake and the corn sausage rolls had lead levels of 1052mg/kg and 1340mg/kg respectively, both of which far exceed the national food safety standard limit of 0.5mg/kg.
Lead poisoning is "particularly harmful to young children" and can "severely damage the brain and central nervous system", according to the World Health Organization.
Officials later found that dozens of provincial officials and hospital staff attempted to cover up the incident by tampering with blood tests and accepting bribes from a nursery investor.

China has since published a set of national guidelines for the provision of meals on campuses. Among the measures is the requirement for every new batch of food to be tested, and for flour, rice and cooking oil to be purchased from centralised procurement points only.

articles.title: From little acorns … to his 1,000th article for the Guardian country diary
articles.summary:
As Mark Cocker approaches a landmark for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper, he is still inspired by powerful encounters with nature

In the autumn of 1987, Mark…

blocks.text: In the autumn of 1987, Mark Cocker sat in a field near Norwich and watched a jay burying acorns for the long winter ahead. He described the scene in his first country diary for the Guardian. Thirty-nine years on, some of those jay-planted acorns will be mature oaks now, and Cocker is completing his 1,000th diary for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper.

In his next diary, he will reflect on the changing birdlife around Flint Clough, in the Peak District, where he first marvelled at rare birds aged 12 after devouring bird books in his bedroom. As a boy, he would find cuckoo, golden plover, ring ouzel and twite, a once-common bird which is now virtually extinct in England.

On his latest visit a few weeks ago, he saw raptors he would have only dreamed of as a boy, “a whole slew of buzzards, two peregrines, two marsh harriers – the first I’ve ever seen in Derbyshire – and several red kites”.

blocks.caption: Mark Cocker standing on Flint Clough in Derbyshire. Photograph: Fabio de Paola/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Guardian country diary began in 1904 with the nature-loving dispatches of Thomas Coward, a retired textile bleacher from Cheshire. Today there is a diverse roster of about 30 diarists spread from Cornwall to the Cairngorms who include farmers, scientists, conservationists, a vicar, a thatcher and a forager, as well as writer-naturalists such as Cocker, who pens a fortnightly dispatch, usually from his local patch in Derbyshire.

Despite honing his skills by working as a warden at Holkham national nature reserve in north Norfolk, while also becoming the first member of his family to attend university, where he studied English, Cocker says it took him 10 years to master the deceptively difficult craft of the diary – a compelling story about rural life in just 360 words.

“You need quite a long apprenticeship to get it right because it’s so short,” he said. “It’s like a haiku. You’ve got to awaken the subject from its dormancy and get straight into the theme. And then the best diaries link it to something else.

“You have a single shaft of light and, if you can, you excavate its relationship to the other parts. You have to often imply or adumbrate rather than specify. And it’s that connection between the part and the whole, the moment and the universal, which is the trick of the diary.”

For Cocker, who earlier this month published The Nature of Seeing, a collection of recent diaries alongside new essays exploring how we might experience nature more fully, the close observation required for appreciating nature is a discipline that benefits all writing. He points to the surprising number of literary greats who have also kindled a passion for wildlife, from Margaret Atwood to Vladimir Nabokov.

blocks.caption: Cocker is convinced that, for all its modesty, the country diary’s time has come. Photograph: Fabio de Paola/The Guardian

blocks.text: Before he began writing, Cocker worked as a refuse collector, a road sweeper, a potato picker and, as a penniless student, posed nude for the local art college.

His big break came after a conservationist friend wrote to the Guardian to complain about the surfeit of inconsequential diaries about cricket matches. “She said: ‘The Guardian needs to get its boots and hat and coat on, and get out into the wild,’” remembered Cocker.

Cocker did that, writing early columns on chiffchaffs, silver-studded blue butterflies and sparrowhawks, before becoming a regular when the legendary Lakeland diarist Enid Wilson fell ill. Between them, Wilson and Cocker have covered a span of 76 years.

blocks.caption: The country diary of 21 March 1904. Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: Cocker shrugs off his own skills as a naturalist, which he says would be completely normal in another culture or era. In The Nature of Seeing, he writes about Inuit fishers who navigated home through the fog by recognising the subtly different patterns of snow bunting songs which corresponded to particular sections of the (invisible) coastline. “That is the level of attention to the living world which we’ve lost and need to recapture,” he said.

He never steps outside with a preordained list of subjects to write about but seeks powerful encounters. “I have to feel the article viscerally. I have to feel that it moved me. That’s really where the experience begins and ends. If it doesn’t engage you personally, if you aren’t affected by it, the diary is a cheat.”
After Phil Gates retired recently following nearly 40 years on the diary, Cocker is now the longest-serving diarist.

The country diary editor, Paul Fleckney, said: “Mark is a gift to the diary. What you get from him is hyper-detailed knowledge with one eye on the bigger picture, and all written with such persuasion. Beneath it is a deep, deep love for the natural world, but also a rare kind of indefatigability. It’s as if all he wants to do is open people’s eyes and ears to the wonders around us, and it is infectious.”
In a time of climate and biodiversity crises, as overconsumption imperils humanity, Cocker is convinced that, for all its modesty, the country diary’s time has come.

“Meaning has been poured on to the diary because it is a repository now for a sense of the impending crisis which assails all life,” he said. “We’re now recognising that the intensifying nature of capitalism, the rise of the right, migration, climate change, drought, starvation, overpopulation – everything is to do with one meta-story, and that is our relationship with the rest of life. The diary’s become a valuable philosophical place for big ideas to be shared.”

articles.title: CDC to send ‘disease detective’ to help tackle Pennsylvania measles outbreak
articles.summary:
State has confirmed six measles-related deaths and county at center of outbreak lacks its own health department

The county at the center of Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is at a clear…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: The county at the center of Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is at a clear disadvantage because, local officials say, it lacks its own health department and it will now get special assistance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
As of Wednesday, Pennsylvania had confirmed 1,222 measles cases, up from 86 the week before. Six measles-associated deaths have also been confirmed by the state.
The CDC announced on Thursday it would send a scientist – specifically, a “disease detective” – from the agency’s epidemic intelligence service to help tackle Pennsylvania’s growing outbreak.

“CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” a CDC spokesperson told NBC News on Thursday.
The spokesperson also added that the CDC director, Dr Erica Schwartz, recommends the MMR vaccine “as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection”.
The network also reported that in addition to the deployment of the “disease detective,” the CDC was releasing nearly $4m to aid the measles response efforts in Pennsylvania.

Lancaster county, the focus of the state’s outbreak with more than 415 confirmed cases as of 9 October, is the largest county in the state to not have its own health department. The plain community, or Amish, who have historically had lower rates of vaccination, make up about 8% of the county’s population.

The Guardian reported earlier this month that the state was bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials sharing concern that it was “only a matter of time” until the disease spread beyond the outbreak’s center.

blocks.caption: A sign reading ‘measles testing’ is seen during an outbreak in Gaines county, Texas, in February 2025. Photograph: Sebastian Rocandio/Reuters

blocks.text: The outbreak also comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by growing vaccine skepticism, particularly because of the influence of the controversial health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr. Kennedy has also notably had a public dispute with the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, who has lambasted the administration and Kennedy for spreading vaccine misinformation.

“I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said in August during a briefing to report two measles deaths in his state, their first in three decades.
He continued: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation. There’s real-life consequences to scaring people.”

Alice Yoder, who was elected to the Lancaster county board of commissioners in 2023 and previously worked as a critical care nurse, told the Guardian that county officials were “very concerned” about the outbreak and that, without its own health department, the county was at a clear disadvantage.

“It’s a lot for our state to handle from a communication standpoint,” Yoder said. “They’re perhaps doing the best that they can, knowing that Pennsylvania has 67 counties, with 60 being under the auspices of the centralized state system rather than having their own health departments.”

She added: “By having a local health department, particularly one of our size, I believe it would mean we would have local data, it would be in real time, and we would have that information quickly. And most importantly, we would have an established staff, which has established relationships with a variety of partners within our community, which means that once we find a sign of an outbreak we would be able to respond to it really quickly.”

Yoder, who is now advocating for the county to establish its own health department, added that because the county doesn’t have one, she and her colleagues find out about measles cases and deaths only through media announcements at the same time as the general public.

blocks.caption: A medical assistant gives a measles, mumps and rubella vaccination to a young person in Coral Gables, Florida, in August. Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I never thought I would see measles again in my lifetime, but once it occurred I thought that we probably should have been prepared for it,” she said.

An advantage for counties in Pennsylvania that do have their own health departments, such as Montgomery, is their ability to work with local community health initiatives, like coalitions aimed at promoting immunity.

Susan Wenrick, vice-chair of the Montgomery County Immunization Coalition, which is made up of members of county government, healthcare professionals and other community members, said one of the coalition’s main goals was to improve access to vaccines.

“The biggest challenges to vaccinating people in Montgomery county have been access and availability, but one positive thing that came out of the pandemic was the public-private partnerships that were created to bring vaccines to communities, along with addressing the uninsured and underinsured barrier,” Wenrick said.

She added: “These are challenging times due to the amount of misinformation that is available, along with the average person turning to Google or social media for their health information instead of consulting their healthcare professional. A big part of MCIC’s efforts is to provide trusted resources for all.”

As of Friday, the CDC reported 4,410 measles cases nationwide, marking an ​increase of 330 from its update last week. As noted by Reuters, ​the CDC “shifted to using mortality data from ​the National Center for Health Statistics for measles-related deaths, rather than ‌relying ⁠on state health departments, a change that has drawn scrutiny”.

articles.title: UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains
articles.summary: United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers

blocks.text: The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.

The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible signs that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.
Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.

Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations inside Yemen in January, cutting off its funding supply line.

Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.

blocks.caption: Yemeni Southern Giants Brigades fighters celebrate and wave their weapons. Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.

Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.

There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.
The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen, and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.

UAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, the Houthis are determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.
On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.
The missiles landed about 500 meters from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 meters from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.
The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fattah el Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.

In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging closer with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.

The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.

Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.

No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.

articles.title: Ombudsman, Customs to formalize data-sharing deal in November
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman will sign a memorandum of agreement (MOA) with the Bureau of Customs (BOC) in November to facilitate data sharing, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Saturday.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 7:56pm
The Office of the Ombudsman will sign a memorandum of agreement (MOA) with the Bureau of Customs (BOC) in November to facilitate data sharing, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Saturday.
“Itong November, we’ll be signing a MOA (memorandum of agreement) na with Customs, data sharing na. Customs, first time ‘yan mangyayari,” Remulla said in his radio program.
(This November, we’ll be signing a MOA with Customs on data sharing. It will be the first time this will happen with the BOC.)
In a statement, BOC Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno confirmed the planned agreement.

“Ombudsman Boying Remulla and myself have a common objective. To fight corruption in government. This is why the Ombudsman and BOC will formally sign an agreement to institutionalize the automatic sharing of data and other information so that cases will be strong and offenders will be held accountable. This is an effective deterrence against smuggling,” Nepomuceno said.
Remulla previously said the lack of data sharing with the BOC had hampered efforts to build strong anti-smuggling cases.
He also said the bureau had failed to provide complete documentation needed for the filing or investigation of cases.
The Department of Justice (DOJ), National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), and the BOC had previously signed a separate MOA aimed at combating economic sabotage. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says Russia is trying to cut electricity and heating to civilians ahead of winter. He also called the US president's waiver of new sanctions on Moscow a boost for…

image.caption: Zaporizhzia in eastern Ukraine came under renewed attack overnightImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.
His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.

blocks.caption: Overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia killed a 64-year-old man Image: Daria Nazarova/AFP

blocks.text: What did Zelenskyy say?

In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.
"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.
Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.

"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.
He said Russia had "expanded ‌its campaign ​against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch ⁠Ukraine's ​reserves ​and repair ​capacity as ‌thinly as possible." ​
Russia claims multiple infrastructure attacks
The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.
Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.
However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.
It said another steel plant in ​Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front ​line, had also been struck.
Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed ​and ‌19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Russian state news ​agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.

blocks.caption: Russia's overnight attacks hit numerous civilian sitesImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Trump's sanctions waiver a boost for Putin: Zelenskyy
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.
On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.
The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."
"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."
Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.

articles.title: It's over: Canada ends England's 41-match unbeaten streak in women's rugby
articles.summary: England's unprecedented 41-game unbeaten run was broken by Canada 24-21 and witnessed by the biggest crowd in North American women’s rugby on Friday in Toronto.

image.caption: Team Canada celebrates their win over England in women's rugby action in Toronto on Friday. It was the first loss suffered by the Red Roses in 41 matches. (Arlyn McAdorey/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Rugby
England's unprecedented 41-game unbeaten run was broken by Canada 24-21 and witnessed by the biggest crowd in North American women’s rugby on Friday in Toronto.
Top-ranked Red Roses fall to Canadians 24-21 in Toronto
Canada, unable to handle England's scrum, trailed 14-5 at halftime and 21-12 after more than an hour and didn't settle a compelling WXV contest until a 78th-minute try by Shoshanah Seumanutafa.
“We really had to grind it out and find a way,” Canada captain Sophie de Goede said. “That's kind of the DNA of our team.”
England suffered its first loss since the 2022 Women's Rugby World Cup final, its only previous defeat in 72 matches since 2019.

items: Canadian women's rugby aims to deal England its 1st loss in 41 matches during upcoming double-header

blocks.text: “Sometimes the flipped coin doesn't go on the side you want it to go,” England captain Meg Jones said. "It's just the nature of the beast."

England showed vulnerability last month at home where it drew with Canada 26-26, ending its 39-match winning streak. That effort gave Canada confidence for the return match at home, including the availability of world player of the year De Goede, rested from its last match, a loss in France, and wings Asia Hogan-Rochester and Alysha Corrigan after injuries.

The hope drew 18,621 spectators, 7,000 more than the previous biggest crowd for a standalone women’s match in North America. England should have scored first but Claudia Moloney-MacDonald dropped the ball over the tryline.
Then Canada used numbers after a Zoe Harrison yellow card for fullback Savannah Bauder to score in a three-on-one.

England stumbles continued with three turnovers in the Canada 22, two on the tryline. But after Canada lock Laetitia Royer was sin-binned, England powered ahead with tries by Maddie Feaunati and Harrison before halftime.

items: Canada halts England's record 39-match win streak in a gripping 26-26 rugby draw

blocks.text: Canada closed to 14-12 in the second half when Corrigan collected her own grubber kick and celebrated before scoring. But England moved further ahead 21-12 after 12 phases when prop Sarah Bern smashed over.

Canada was plagued by forward passes but stayed calm. A missed penalty touch-finder by England was countered and prop DaLeaka Menin, one of three Canada survivors from its last win over England 10 years ago, plowed over to cut the gap to two again. Another England clearance was returned by Canada from its half and De Goede and Gabrielle Senft lined up Seumanutafa to beat the cover to the left corner flag and cap a milestone night in Canadian rugby.
They go again in Ottawa next Friday.

articles.title: Plaque telling story of African-Caribbean prisoners in Britain stolen within days
articles.summary:
Descendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects spirit of racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’

The theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of…

blocks.text: The theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of African-Caribbean prisoners in 18th-century Britain reflects the enduring racism that has fuelled centuries of atrocities against Black and Indigenous Caribbean people, their descendants say.

Drummer Ronald Raymond McDonald was part of a delegation that travelled from Belize and elsewhere to Portchester Castle last week to honour their ancestors: 2,500 men, women and children transported to Britain as prisoners of war in 1796.

McDonald, whose Garifuna ancestors from St Vincent and the Grenadines were among the prisoners, said he was heartbroken to learn that the plaque had been stolen and a nearby bench vandalised with hateful graffiti.
“Why would somebody do something like that when people are simply honouring their ancestors … It’s very sad,” he said.

The plaque, installed at the castle, commemorated the more than 2,000 prisoners held there, marking an extraordinary chapter of Black British history: one of the largest known arrivals of African-Caribbean people in Britain before the Windrush era.

The unveiling was part of a ceremony organised by the St Vincent and the Grenadines 2nd Generation (SV2G), in partnership with the University of Warwick and English Heritage, and was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations.

blocks.caption: The unveiling was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations. Photograph: English Heritage

blocks.text: But days later, English Heritage staff discovered the plaque was missing. They said a padlock to one of the castle gates had been removed and the incident had been reported to police.

Garifuna advocate Princess Eulogia said the theft reflected “a spirit of racism that haunts generation after generation and hides in plain sight”. It was time, she said, to recognise that “we are all connected” and to end the hate.
Queen Mother Chief Freda Paulino-Sideroff, who is Garifuna and had travelled to the UK for the ceremony, was returning home to the US when she learned of the theft.

“Hate will never define who we are as a people. We are resilient survivors of our ancestors who have endured,” she said. In the 1700s, her Garifuna ancestors were expelled from St Vincent by British forces and left to perish on the barren island of Baliceaux as Britain sought to crush decades of resistance to colonisation.

Emilio ‘Sásamu’ Thomas, a Garifuna cultural ambassador who also travelled from Belize for the ceremony, echoed Paulino-Sideroff’s defiance, saying Garifuna people would not allow themselves to be victimised. His message to the perpetrators, he said, was: “Whatever pain that they are experiencing, we’re here to help them to relieve that pain.”

The missing plaque was meant to honour the prisoners, whose story, researchers say, had been largely lost to history. They came from a coalition that included formerly enslaved Africans, Caribbean-born people, Indigenous people and French soldiers who fought against British control of St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines and Grenada. Their defeat and removal helped strengthen British rule in the region.
It was unveiled on 9 October, exactly 230 years after one of the ships carrying the prisoners was wrecked at Rapparee Cove in Devon, with many of those on board losing their lives.

Iona Keen of English Heritage called the removal an act of vandalism, while University of Warwick professor Katherine Astbury said the plaque was intended to provide a visible memorial of the prisoners, and a reminder of “an important, forgotten part of Caribbean history”.

The incident comes during Black History Month and amid renewed debate over slavery reparations. Campaigner and author Sir Patrick Vernon said vandalism of memorials representing Black British history had occurred repeatedly over decades, citing damage to other memorials.
He described the theft as symbolic of an “ongoing battle and the legacy of enslavement”.

Jacqueline Roberts, SV2G chief executive, said the theft could not erase history, and stressed the importance of continuing research to uncover more hidden stories. “Our history is intertwined with British history,” she said. “It’s important to understand that part of our journey, because it is part of the complexity of our identity, and affects our sense of belonging.”

Anthony Severin, St Lucia’s high commissioner and chair of the Caribbean community diplomatic caucus in the UK, described the theft as a “desecration of the memory and spirit of our commemorated ancestors”. He pledged that the plaque “whether returned or replaced, will remain affixed to the walls of Portchester Castle”.

articles.title: ‘We are in hiding’: Briton with severe health issues fears deportation from Sweden
articles.summary:
Mark Smith, who is married to a Swedish woman, says he was told three times he needed to do nothing in order to remain after Brexit

A seriously ill British man living in Sweden has been…

blocks.text: A seriously ill British man living in Sweden has been forced into hiding amid fears he will be deported as a result of what he says is a government Brexit residency error.

Mark Smith, 60, who has had hearts attacks, strokes, severe headaches and chronically high blood pressure that has been difficult to treat, was told on the phone he should leave Sweden by 17 October as he was an “alien” without permission to stay.

Terrified of deportation, he and his wife have moved out of their home in Falkenberg, in south-west Sweden, to a caravan park. “We are in hiding, we daren’t go back to our apartment. We are scared to go out as we don’t know if the police will come and take us,” Smith said.

A court ruled on 12 October that a decision on deportation would not be suspended but gave him until 20 October to “submit his application for a retrial” in relation to “the grounds for the decision on indefinite deportation”.

Smith has been in Sweden since 2017 and says he was told by authorities he did not need to do anything to stay after Brexit in 2020. He worked, had private health insurance, supported his wife and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority, as required under Swedish rules.

He was unaware, however, that Sweden was among 13 of the 27 EU member states that required Britons living in the country before Brexit to make a formal application to remain. Other countries, such as Spain, did not opt for that system and just required Britons to declare they were a resident.

Smith said: “I asked the tax authorities three times on different occasions if I had to do anything because of Brexit and they said no, telling me I had to wait for five years to apply for permanent residency.
“Because it was the tax authority, a government body, I took it for granted that what they told me was correct,” he added.
David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights activist working through the Brits in Sweden group, said Smith’s case was typical of many Britons living in Sweden.

blocks.caption: Smith has been in Sweden since 2017. He worked, had private health insurance, and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority.

blocks.text: Milstead said: “Mark’s experience is far from unusual. I have encountered many British citizens who actively sought information from the Swedish authorities about their residence rights after Brexit, only to receive vague, unhelpful answers, sometimes being told that they needed to do nothing.”

They include the 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas, whose husband also inquired about Brexit residency and was told by the tax authorities there was nothing to do, and who is now fighting a removal order.

Smith had a minor heart attack on Wednesday night but wanted his situation publicised because he said the British government needed to know what was happening to expats in Sweden, “not just to me but others”.
His wife, Petra, said his health conditions had left him so vulnerable she was not sure “if he will last until Christmas”.
She said: “He has been told he can’t drive, he can’t fly – what do they expect him to do? Get up and walk to England? Come on, Sweden, we need to step back from all of this and be better.”

After 12 years together, she said deportation would be devastating for her and her 15-year-old son who has special needs, who Smith co-parents. “It is wrong what they are doing, I feel ashamed to be Swedish. What they are doing is racist to British people,” Petra said.

blocks.caption: Smith’s troubles began in 2021 when he applied for sickness benefit and was told by officials he should have applied for post-Brexit residency.

blocks.text: Milstead said Smith’s case was “depressingly familiar” and should warrant the urgent attention of the European Commission, which has previously said Sweden was not breaking any laws.

“A gentleman with Mark’s serious health conditions should not be having to fight deportation. It is difficult to understand how the European Commission has concluded that Sweden’s treatment of late applications under the [Brexit] withdrawal agreement does not warrant a challenge,” he said.

“Sweden stands out so starkly from other EU countries, and there are serious questions that remain unanswered, particularly about proportionality and the treatment of vulnerable people. These are precisely the kinds of cases where the protections of the withdrawal agreement ought to matter most.”

The Scandinavian country has found itself under mounting pressure over its approach to the withdrawal agreements having deported 458 Britons, including one man who had been in the country since he was 10 years old, and a 65-year-old man married to a Swede with no family or property in the UK.
after newsletter promotion
Sweden has also issued removal orders to a man with dementia who is in 24-hour care and who has been in the country for 25 years.

Under the legally binding treaty, it was agreed governments would communicate the Brexit residency rules, consider late applications on reasonable grounds, and exercise “proportionate” decisions including in the case of vulnerable people.

Smith’s troubles began in 2021 when he started to get ill and applied for sickness benefit. He was told by officials that he should have applied for post-Brexit residency. The couple immediately did so; they recall making the application at the end of 2021, in time for Sweden’s 31 December 2021 deadline.

They waited more than two years to hear back and when they did it was a rejection on the grounds that they were not married and therefore did not have a family connection to merit his residency in Sweden.

blocks.caption: Mark Smith and Petra on their wedding day in Sweden in 2023. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: They were married in 2023 and had been living together since 2017.

It is not clear if Smith applied for the specific Brexit residency or through the usual immigration route, an important difference and one that may not have been made clear to British protected by the withdrawal agreement. Family connections are not a criteria under free movement rights, which apply to any individual regardless of marital status, so campaigners believe they have a strong case.

Smith said: “We were so much in love, we lived together, we did everything together, even now we hold hands walking down the streets. We wanted to get married, we wanted to do it the right way. I wanted to ask Petra’s father for permission and have him give her away, but two weeks after he gave me permission to marry his daughter, he passed.
“So we were looking into marriage but things just kept happening. But we don’t understand why this matters.”

They also said they had not been given the full court paperwork from the first case appealing against the migration agency’s decision, so they appealed to a higher courtwithout the full arguments against them.

After speaking to a judge this week, Petra has had assurances that all the paperwork will be sent to them by post, but they feel angry that they were not apprised of the information that the migration agency was arguing before the courts.
Sweden’s migration agency has said there is no evidence Sweden has taken an extreme approach to the withdrawal agreement.

The UK Foreign Office has raised concerns about Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement with the European Commission on numerous occasions, but has been told Sweden is not breaching the agreement.

A spokesperson said: “We are in touch with Mr Smith and are providing consular support. We know this is a distressing and challenging time for those concerned and we are urgently raising the situation with both the Swedish authorities and the European Commission.”

The Foreign Office welcomed a statement by Sweden’s former migration minister Johan Forssell in August that Sweden would examine “additional measures” that would address the issue of Brexit deportation, and a similar declaration by Magdalena Andersson, who is on track to form the new government.

articles.title: Voters head to the polls in British Columbia's municipal elections
articles.summary: Voters are set to cast ballots in 162 municipalities and 27 regional districts.

image.caption: A voter heads into Kensington Community Centre in Vancouver in 2022. Saturday is general voting day for B.C. municipalities this year. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Voters are set to cast ballots in 162 municipalities and 27 regional districts.
Voters set to cast ballots in 162 municipalities and 27 regional districts
Saturday is general voting day in British Columbia's municipal elections.
Voters will cast ballots for local elected representatives from among about 3,500 candidates in the province's 162 municipalities and 27 regional districts.
Polling places will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., local time.
To be eligible to cast a ballot, voters must be at least 18 years old, be a Canadian citizen who has resided in B.C. for at least six months and be a resident of the municipality they are voting in.
Many voters will have received a voter information card with details on where they can cast their ballot.
You can also find out where to vote on your municipality or regional district's website.

articles.title: Union decries 'jaw-dropping' increase in violence against Winnipeg School Division staff
articles.summary: The union representing educational support staff in Manitoba's largest school division is sounding the alarm over what its president describes as a shocking increase in violence against its workers.

image.caption: Manitoba Government and General Employees' Union president Kyle Ross says he hopes to see more educational assistants to ensure consistent care for kids who need support. (Prabhjot Singh Lotey/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba
The union representing educational support staff in Manitoba's largest school division is sounding the alarm over what its president describes as a shocking increase in violence against its workers.
118% jump in violent incidents since 2022-23 year, most involving educational assistants, data shows

The union that represents educational support staff in Manitoba's largest school division is sounding the alarm over what its president describes as a shocking increase in violence against its workers.

New Winnipeg School Division data, released Friday by the Manitoba Government and General Employees' Union, shows a roughly 118 per cent increase in student-related aggression incidents in the division's schools, jumping from 884 in the 2022-23 year to 1,925 in 2025-26.
"When we received the numbers, it was really jaw-dropping, honestly," union president Kyle Ross said in an interview.

"Every day, you have to get up in the morning and wonder, 'Am I going to get spit on? Am I going to have my hair pulled? Am I going to get bit, head-butted?' It's not a thing that most people have to think about when they're walking into their job."
According to the data, educational assistants were the staff group most likely to be harmed by student-related aggression, making up nearly all the cases included in the numbers shared by MGEU.
The increase in incidents, which included hits, scratches, kicks and bites, also raise concerns that staffing levels aren't matching needs, the union says.
Ross said while it's hard to pinpoint any single cause for the increase, he hopes to see more educational assistants to ensure consistent care for kids who need support.
The MGEU wants the province to ensure safe staffing levels with the right training to improve safety for workers in schools. (Warren Kay/CBC)

"Our members tell us often, it's much easier to deal with the same student when you build that rapport up — when they have that trust, when you tell them no and they trust you, it makes a big difference," he said.
"I don't have all the answers, but I know we have to find a better way."

The union said it's calling on the province to target support where it's most needed, ensure safe staffing levels with the right training and strengthen enforcement of violence-prevention requirements.

items: Manitoba teachers face rise in students with complex needs, 'erosion' of support staff: union

blocks.text: In a written statement sent by a spokesperson, Education Minister Tracy Schmidt said the province understands that "investing in more staff is essential to providing kids with the supports they need and keeping our schools safe."

She said the NDP government has provided funding in 2026 to hire 830 new EAs, but added the province recognizes "that there is more work to do," and promised to continue working with school divisions and other partners.

Winnipeg School Division superintendent Matt Henderson said the division has added 300 educational assistants over the last three years and reduced class sizes, and is confident it has "the right amount of people and the right people" in its classrooms.
"Now, it's about really supporting those teams," Henderson said in an interview.
"When there's an incident with a child, often it's because they're trying to communicate something to us. We always say behaviour is communication. And so that's part of it."
'Very complex to solve'
Darby Mallory, a doctoral student at the University of Ottawa, said she wasn't surprised by the numbers.

Violent incidents in schools have been on the rise for years, said Mallory, who studies in the department of criminology and works on the university's Violence and Harassment Against Educators project.
"It's not simply an issue that is happening in a few schools, in a few different school boards, in a few different communities," she said.
Violence against Winnipeg School Division staff spiking: union

"I think the numbers make clear that it's a big problem, that it's one that is affecting teachers and education sector workers across this entire country. And I think that that highlights that the issue is very complex to solve."

One contributor is a general decrease in school funding, leading to larger class sizes, staff layoffs and cuts to resources for students, Mallory said. Though some incidents involve students with specialized needs, rates of violence are high across the board, she said.
The disruption caused by an increase in violent incidents in the classroom affects both workers and students, Mallory said.

items: Manitoba announces school funding hike, but divisions say they're still facing significant financial pressure

blocks.text: "That's not only lost instructional time, but it also is very difficult for students to learn in an environment where they feel like they're unsafe, where they feel like they're walking on eggshells, and where they don't know what is going to come next," she said.
"It's not only an issue that's affecting workers. This is something that is affecting the entire school community."

Caitlyn Gowriluk has been writing for CBC Manitoba since 2019. Her work has also appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, and in 2021 she was part of an award-winning team recognized by the Radio Television Digital News Association for its breaking news coverage of COVID-19 vaccines. articles.title: Two people killed in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond
articles.summary:
Police Scotland says boy, 16, and 80-year-old man died in incident north-east of village of Drymen in Stirling

A 16-year-old boy and an 80-year-old man have been killed during a light…

blocks.text: A 16-year-old boy and an 80-year-old man have been killed during a light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond in Scotland.
Emergency services were called to reports of a collision north-east of the village of Drymen, Stirling, at about 4.45pm on Friday.
Police said the next of kin of the boy and the man, who were pronounced dead at the scene, had been informed.
After the crash, temporary airspace restrictions, including drones, were in place around the village.
Police Scotland said its Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) had been informed, and inquiries were taking place to establish the full circumstances of the incident.
Restrictions were likely to be in place for some time, police said, to allow the AAIB to conduct its investigation.
The Piper Tomahawk II aircraft took off from Glasgow airport on Friday afternoon at 4.17pm, according to data from online flight-tracking tools.
The tracking data showed the plane circled before coming down north of Drymen. The plane stopped transmitting at 4.37pm, according to the data.
Earlier in the day, the plane had taken off from Cumbernauld airport at 11.46am, before flying to Glasgow airport.
It stayed there until about 1pm, then embarked on a flight north-east to Newport-on-Tay, opposite Dundee, before turning round and heading back to Glasgow.
It was on the ground at the airport for just over an hour before it took off again and began its final flight.
Gavin Birch-Williams, the managing director of Glasgow airport, said: “We are aware of an incident involving a light aircraft that departed from Glasgow airport.
“This is a deeply tragic event, and the thoughts and heartfelt sympathies from all at Glasgow airport are with the friends and families affected.”
In a statement, the AAIB said: “An investigation has begun into an accident involving a light aircraft which occurred on 16 October 2026.
“A team has travelled to the accident site near Drymen, north of Glasgow, to make inquiries and gather evidence as part of the process of conducting a safety investigation.”
Officers warned it was a criminal offence to fly in restricted airspace.

articles.title: Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
articles.summary: The French royal jewel will be on public display for the first time since it was found hidden in an apple after a 1926 theft.

blocks.text: A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.
The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand Condé" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the Château de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.
The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.
It will once again be on display in the Condé Museum at the Château de Chantilly until 3 January.
The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.

Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.
While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.
The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.

Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.
The exact origins of the Grand Condé remain a mystery.
It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, drawn up following his death, the Château de Chantilly said.
It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-Amélie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of Orléans, the Duke of Aumale.

He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the Château de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the Musée Condé collection.

October 17, 2026
Merz addresses party youth at annual convention

blocks.caption: Merz will seek to convince the party's Young Union members that he is still on the right trackImage: Henning Kaiser/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Bonn Saturday to address an annual national meeting of his Christian Democratic and Christian Social Unions' (CDU/CSU) youth wing, the Young Union (Junge Union/JU).

Things were testy the last time Merz addressed the 90,000-member group — when they fought over pension policy— and he will now face them with dwindling approval numbers and growing dissatisfaction over the way he has led Germany and his party.
Merz will greet a youth wing that is self-confident as he himself reels from disastrous election results in recent state and municipal elections.
On Friday, the JU overwhelmingly re-elected Johannes Winkel as their chairman, with the CDU federal parliamentarian taking 94.3% of the vote.
"Our generation still has big plans," said Winkel as he spoke to JU attendees, "and we will be the ones who successfully continue to write the history of the CDU and CSU as a people's party."

On Friday, North Rhine-Westphalia State Premier Hendrik Wüst, a rising star within the party, addressed attendees. On Sunday, Bavarian State Premier Markus Söder will take the stage. Both represent potential replacements for Merz.

Despite the number of prominent party leaders addressing the JU amid talk of Merz's possible political demise, Johannes Winkel vowed: "We're not some applause meter. This isn't a casting show for the chancellorship."

articles.title: Ministers must be honest about Russian threat to UK, says former Foreign Office head
articles.summary:
Peter Ricketts called for more resilience in protecting banking, energy and water systems from cyber-assaults

Ministers need to be honest with the British public about the immediate threat…

blocks.text: Ministers need to be honest with the British public about the immediate threat posed by Russia, which could soon lead to lives being lost, a former national security adviser has said.
Peter Ricketts, who advised David Cameron when he was prime minister, became the latest figure to warn about the scale of the threat posed by “hybrid attacks” from Vladimir Putin’s forces.

The peer, who is the former top civil servant in the Foreign Office, warned banking systems, energy or water supplies could be targeted by Kremlin cyber-assaults. He called for further investment in resilience for key sectors.
It comes in a week where the heads of MI5 and the British army have warned about the danger posed by Moscow.
Lord Ricketts also dismissed Andy Burnham’s claim he wanted to be a “bridge” between the US and Ukraine.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv deteriorated sharply this week after Donald Trump waived a number of economic sanctions on Russia and suggested Ukraine needed a new leader.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Ricketts said: “I think they’ve really got to start a conversation with the British people about what may be coming, because not only is Putin trying to break morale in Ukraine, he’s also trying to undermine morale in European countries.”
In response to a question over the impact of disruption by Russia, he added: “I’m not saying there’s going to be industrial war with tanks rolling across the north German plain.

“But these hybrid tanks are getting more reckless, more dangerous. One day, people are going to land up being killed somewhere, and so we are going to have to look at responding in that sense and finding the money to do it.”

Speaking about Burnham’s comments at prime minister’s questions this week saying he wanted to be a bridge between Washington and Kyiv, Ricketts said: “I don’t really go on this bridge business. I mean, I don’t think in Trump’s current mood there’s any influence that Britain can have in the short term.”
Ricketts’s comments join those by the director general of MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, and the chief of the general staff, Gen Sir Roly Walker, in the last few days about Russia.
after newsletter promotion
On Tuesday, McCallum said MI5 was devoting more resources to combating threats from hostile states than it did during the cold war and described Russia as the “number one aggressor”.

And on Friday, Walker told 700 troops at Catterick garrison in North Yorkshire that politicians would soon need to have a “frank conversation” about the “sacrifices” that would be needed to prioritise defence and security.
Walker, a former special forces commander, said soldiers would probably need to fight in a war, given the “extreme jeopardy in the world at the moment”.
The warnings come after a difficult week for Kyiv, with the US appearing to withdraw support.
Trump said the decision to pause sanctions was in the US “national interest”, despite previously signing them into law in September.
Last week, he lifted restrictions on Russian diesel amid spiralling fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections.
He also suggested Ukraine needed a new president. Volodymyr Zelenskyy hit back this week during an EU summit, saying it was nice to be among “real leaders”.
There are also concerns that the US has withdrawn intelligence sharing with Ukraine, leaving towns and cities across the country vulnerable to attack.
Ricketts said the government should spend more money on protections for key infrastructure in Britain, including energy, transport, air traffic control and defence.
He said: “They all need better protection, and that’s an argument that needs to be had with the British people because we need to find the money to do it.”

articles.title: From ‘killing the golden goose’ to better than ever: Has Alberta's relationship with Ottawa changed?
articles.summary: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith once said Ottawa "couldn't help" but be fixated on "punishing" the energy sector. Now, she says Canada is working better than it ever has. So what changed? And will it…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney has a beer with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith as he visits supporters of a Vote to Stay event in Red Deer, Alta., on Oct. 16 ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty. (Todd Korol/Reuters)

blocks.text: The relationship between Alberta and the federal government has faced its share of political and economic conflict over the years. Some Albertans would argue more than its fair share.

From the drawing of the province’s boundaries to natural resource control to the creation of the National Energy Program to pipeline cancellations and political representation, generations of Albertans have expressed feelings of alienation.

Last year, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith added to the litany of rebukes of Ottawa from Alberta leaders over the years. (Her predecessor, Jason Kenney, once said the federal government was "killing the golden goose".)

After launching a panel tour to hear citizens' frustrations, Smith said, “You know what Ottawa can't help but be fixated on? ... Punishing our energy sector and layering on policies to keep it in the ground."
She made those remarks nearly two months after the Liberals won a fourth-consecutive election under new leader Mark Carney.
Members of the Alberta Next panel gathered for a public town hall meeting in Red Deer at the Westerner Park grounds on July 25, 2025. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)
Fast forward to this fall, with Albertans poised to go to the polls in a referendum that could ultimately lead to a separation vote, and Smith is expressing a very different view.
“I do think Canada is working better than it ever has,” Smith told CBC News, noting she will be voting for the province to stay put.

The remarks follow months of Smith saying that, in her view, working out the differences between Alberta and Ottawa would be the key to quelling separatist sentiment, a blueprint she said is shared by Carney.
Premier says Alberta and Canada 'walking together' for first time in a long time
So what changed in the relationship between the province and Ottawa? Is Alberta really in a better place than a year ago? And if so, for how long?

For her part, Smith said that Alberta has “finally” found a government willing to move swiftly on major projects, such as the Pacific Link pipeline, while not “standing in the way” of Alberta developing its resources.
Carney, the premier said, is a “different type of leader.”
“I think he understands the Constitution. I think he respects the constitutional division of powers,” she said. “There’s areas that are federal jurisdiction, and areas of provincial jurisdiction.”
That’s why, the premier argued, Albertans should vote to remain in Canada, with a newfound belief that federation can function fairly.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: But those who say the province needs to go its own way to realize its true potential see Carney’s promises as mere window dressing after years of policy that stymied economic growth and personal freedoms.
Constitutional lawyer Keith Wilson argued in favour of Alberta independence at a debate in Calgary held in late May. (New West Video)
“They’re just saying, 'Hey, we’re getting along.' Well, what if they stop getting along?” said Keith Wilson, one of the most prominent leaders in the Alberta separatist movement.
“I am not satisfied to have the future of my children’s success and prosperity hinge upon whether the prime minister and a premier have a good personal relationship.”
No to the nine ('bad laws')

In addition to the proposed Pacific Link pipeline and other federal investments, Smith has praised federal movement around what she calls the “nine bad laws” that she demanded be addressed in order to avoid an “unprecedented national unity crisis.”
As detailed by Smith in March 2025, they were, in brief:

items: the oil and gas emissions cap;
returning oversight of the industrial carbon tax to the provinces;
the net-zero power regulations;
the EV mandate;
repealing Bill C-69, otherwise known as the Impact Assessment Act;
guaranteeing Alberta “full access” to oil and gas corridors;
lifting the B.C. tanker ban;
ending the prohibition on single-use plastics; and
“halting the federal censorship” of energy companies.

blocks.text: A spokesperson in the premiers’ office said it considers seven of the nine “scrapped or reformed.”
“Investment is soaring and major projects are moving forward again. This is proof of progress and a more collaborative relationship,” Ryan Fournier wrote in an email.
Ottawa and Alberta engaged in 'tough collaboration,' says Carney
The federal government revised those policies amid criticism from some that the moves would claw back environmental protections and concern from others surrounding Indigenous consultation.

Wilson isn’t satisfied with progress to date, citing, among other developments, a recent Alberta Court of Appeal ruling that stated the federal government’s Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional.
“I’m sorry, but this is just … political platitudes, absent substantive action. If the prime minister was serious about these things, he would offer to change equalization,” he said.
“He would announce that he’s going to follow the court decision, and repeal Bill C-69 [the Impact Assessment Act]. Surely, people aren’t this gullible. But maybe they are?”
The Alberta Court of Appeal in Calgary is seen in this file photo. Earlier this month, it ruled the federal government's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional. (Google Maps)

Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute in Ottawa, said that Canada had a “terrible reputation” for investment due to policies implemented under former prime minister Justin Trudeau.
“The corrections to the ‘nine bad laws’ … those are all meaningful, in that they have attracted investment,” she said.

“You can always say that things aren’t perfect, or there’s things we can still do to improve competitiveness, but I don’t think anyone would have anticipated two years ago that we could be where we are here today.”

Earlier this month, the federal and Alberta governments announced that the proposed Pacific Link pipeline, which would carry one million barrels of oil a day from Alberta to the B.C. coast, had become the first project designated in the national interest. That classification means that federal approvals and regulatory reviews will be fast-tracked.
Prominent separatists, meanwhile, have argued that the Pacific Link pipeline is not a point in Carney’s favour.
How much money could the new Pacific Link Pipeline cost Canadian taxpayers?

“This is a nationalized pipeline. Is that really the only way to get something done in Canada, is to have the government do it?” said Cory Morgan, who heads the third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence, in a recent video. “That’s not a good sign, guys.”
Exner-Pirot said government de-risking is necessary for West Coast pipelines given challenges tied to past projects.

After Kinder Morgan halted construction on the Trans Mountain pipeline, the federal government under Trudeau took over, buying the troubled project for $4.5 billion in 2018. The project cost eventually spiralled to $34 billion.

items: Trans Mountain pipeline will soon be at full capacity amid global energy crisis

blocks.text: “The particular circumstances of a west coastal pipeline are terrible,” Exner-Pirot said. “I think, [it is] justified for government to de-risk it, and to show that it can be done.”

Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, says changes to laws and regulations under Prime Minister Mark Carney have made Canada more competitive and attractive for investment. (Paula Duhatschek/CBC)
However, Exner-Pirot said many other energy projects, including other pipelines, are moving forward successfully without government subsidies — like LNG Canada's Phase 2 expansion in Kitimat, B.C.

items: Enbridge breaks ground on $4B natural gas pipeline expansion

blocks.text: “So, the idea that we’re not building anything else except for this one project with government funding or backing is simply not true.”
Fault lines
In the eyes of the Alberta government, the “nine bad laws” may be well on their way to a resolution under Canada’s new prime minister.
But Carney’s comments tied to the “No to the Nine” campaign drew prompt opposition from the provincial government on Thursday.

"No to the Nine" is a prominent federalist advertising campaign that urges Albertans to reject the nine referendum ballot questions not concerned with separation. Five of those questions deal with immigration, while four are aimed at constitutional reforms, like abolishing the Senate.

At a Thursday event, Carney suggested Albertans should vote “No to the Nine." The premier then posted on X that despite the two finding common ground on many issues, it appeared Carney “had yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies” of his predecessor were.
Ian Brodie, a political scientist at the University of Calgary who was chief of staff to former prime minister Stephen Harper, called Carney’s comments a “miss.”

“The winning federalist campaign here is to acknowledge that Alberta has had a short shrift from Confederation over the last few years, and that changes are needed if the province is going to get a fair deal,” Brodie said on CBC Radio's Calgary Eyeopener.
Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Friday at a brewery in Red Deer, Alta. (CBC)
For his part, Carney said Thursday that he didn’t “need a referendum” to co-operate more with the provinces on immigration.
“The province is closer to the needs of the industries here, where the shortages are,” Carney told Global News, adding the federal government had already taken “control” on changes to immigration.

items: Alberta referendum pitches more control over immigration. Here's what you need to know

blocks.text: Despite the potential awkwardness, Carney made a campaign stop with Smith at a brewery in Red Deer on Friday, where he made a point of characterizing the relationship between the two as involving “tough collaboration.”
“In our time working together, the premier has consistently put the most difficult issues on the table, with the intention of finding a common way forward,” Carney said.
The conversations to come
“Ottawa may be 2,000 miles away, but destructive federal policy travels on winged feet and strikes like the wrath of God.”

That’s how Monte Solberg, an Alberta MP from 1993 to 2008 for the Reform Party, Canadian Alliance and Conservative Party of Alberta, characterized the relationship between the West and Ottawa in a 2018 column on alienation written for CBC News.

Today, he’s pushing for the federalist side in the referendum, as part of the Vote to Stay campaign. In his view, now is not the time to separate, as Canada is locked in negotiations with the United States.
“That doesn’t mean that, over time, there shouldn’t be a discussion about how we address some of the unfairness in Confederation,” he said.
As to whether the prime minister is the person who will have that conversation?
“Well, I think it’ll be a priority for the premier [of Alberta], and for some other premiers. They’ll have their chance to make their case that this needs to be addressed,” Solberg said.
“I think there is a potential to do so with this prime minister that there wasn’t with, certainly, Justin Trudeau.”
Voters at a downtown Edmonton polling station are pictured on Oct. 13. (Jack Farrell/The Canadian Press)
For Wilson, who believes in an independent Alberta, none of what’s been offered up can be seen as a win.
In his view, there’s been no offer whatsoever to address what he sees as the “structural unfairness” of how Alberta is treated within Confederation.
“None of what [Smith] is doing is addressing those core issues. I don’t know what’s happened to her. I just don’t,” he said.

Some separatists have argued that Albertans should consider Option 2 — to commence the process to hold a future binding referendum on whether Alberta should leave Canada — so as to preserve leverage in negotiations with Ottawa.

items: Alberta independence campaigners go for soft sell, even if they want a hard exit

blocks.text: Others say they’re opposed to both options on the ballot.

“What Canada needs — is a middle-ground path into the future — a set of constitutional reforms that restore the legal primacy of provincial governments for policies in health, education and social services,” wrote Ted Morton, an Ed Stelmach-era cabinet minister and one of the authors of the well-known "Alberta firewall" letter, which advocated for Alberta to exit the Canada Pension Plan, among other ideas.
Competing referendum signs line a boulevard in Calgary on Oct. 15. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
Polling has suggested that Carney is the most popular politician in Alberta, ahead of Smith and federal Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre.

Duane Bratt, a political science professor at Calgary's Mount Royal University who has argued for the federalist side at events during the referendum campaign, said it is inevitable, as political gravity kicks in, that the prime minister won’t be able to hang onto that level of support forever.
“There’s always frictions between the federal and provincial governments,” Bratt said.
“The question is: are we going to see that same friction that we saw in the Trudeau era?”
