articles.title: Rappler’s Gelo Gonzales named 2026 East-West Center Jefferson Fellow
articles.summary: The three-week fellowship will bring journalists to Honolulu, Tokyo, and Seoul to examine artificial intelligence’s impact on societies and economic security in the Asia-Pacific region

blocks.text: FELLOW. Rappler's Gelo Gonzales, senior multimedia reporter for tech, is one of the 12 fellows for the 2026 Jeffersons.
Rappler
The three-week fellowship will bring journalists to Honolulu, Tokyo, and Seoul to examine artificial intelligence’s impact on societies and economic security in the Asia-Pacific region

MANILA, Philippines – Rappler senior multimedia reporter Gelo Gonzales, who covers technology and its impact on society, is among 12 journalists selected for the East-West Center’s 2026 Jefferson Fellowships.

This year’s fellowship, themed “New Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence: Navigating AI’s Impacts on Societies and Economic Security in the Asia-Pacific Region,” will explore the opportunities and challenges posed by artificial intelligence (AI) across the region.
The program, organized by the Honolulu-based East-West Center, will run from October 25 to November 12, 2026, taking fellows to Honolulu, Tokyo, and Seoul for a three-week reporting and study tour.
The Jefferson Fellowships is the East-West Center’s flagship journalism program, aimed at enhancing public understanding of cultures, issues, and trends in the Indo-Pacific region through news media.

This year’s program will examine how AI is transforming economies and societies, from its potential to improve public administration, healthcare, manufacturing, and agriculture to its implications for employment, economic inequality, data privacy, and the environment. It will also explore concerns that developing economies could be left behind in the AI revolution due to limited connectivity, unreliable power grids, and shortages of technological skills.

During the fellowship, journalists will meet with government officials, researchers, business leaders, and civil society representatives. They will also visit healthcare facilities, laboratories, schools, AI-driven manufacturing facilities, chip makers, and farms to see firsthand how the technology is being deployed.

Gonzales served as Rappler’s technology editor from 2016 to 2025, then specialized on covering technology as a senior multimedia reporter in 2026. He also worked as a lifestyle writer and editor for FHM Philippines from 2009 to 2016.
His reporting focuses on technology and its intersections with society, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure, and technology policy.
Gonzales is one of two Filipino journalists among this year’s 12 fellows, along with Purple Romero, digital verification editor, at Agence France-Presse’s Hong Kong bureau.
Here is the full list of fellows for 2026:

items: Anusha BRADLEY, investigative reporter, Radio New Zealand, New Zealand
Ju Min (Amy) CHIEN, freelance reporter and researcher, The New York Times, Taiwan
Chiara EISNER, investigative correspondent, NPR, United States
Diwash GAHATRAJ, freelance journalist, India
Gelo GONZALES, senior multimedia reporter, Rappler, Philippines
Sae Eun (Jen) KWON, digital journalist, CBS News, South Korea
Sufani LUAN, news correspondent, CNN Indonesia, Indonesia
Louise MATSAKIS, senior business editor, WIRED magazine, United States
Purple ROMERO, digital verification editor, Agence France-Presse, Hong Kong
Inwook SONG, producer and writer, CNN, United States
Anshuman TIWARI, editor, The Bonus, Amar Ujala, India
Stephen VINEY, digital editor, Australian Broadcasting Corporation, Australia

articles.title: N.S. growers eye new apple export markets amid U.S. trade tensions
articles.summary: Nova Scotia's apple growers are finding international markets beyond the U.S., in a move to secure a better position amid trade tensions.

image.caption: Nova Scotia is seeing a bumper season for apples, according to the province's fruit growers association. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
Nova Scotia's apple growers are finding international markets beyond the U.S., in a move to secure a better position amid trade tensions.
Apple producers hope to enter Taiwan market this year while targeting Thailand next year, says association
Nova Scotia's apples are poised to reach more overseas tables this year.
The province's fruit growers association said it's taking steps toward the goal of shipping some of this season's apple harvest to Taiwan.
It marks a new move by Nova Scotian growers to diversify their global markets amid Canada-U.S. trade tensions.

The United States currently accounts for 90 per cent of Nova Scotia's apple exports, according to the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association. While the sector remains untouched by direct tariffs, local growers are seizing the moment as an opportunity.
"We've built a great relationship with the consumers in certain American states and cities," said Emily Lutz, the association's executive director.
"But it is important now more than ever to have alternatives available, and just for other markets to be aware of the quality of fruit that we grow in Nova Scotia."
The move will help growers find a stronger position in case there is a future trade disruption.
Data shared by the association show the province's apple exports to the U.S. exceeded $28 million last year. It was followed by Vietnam, which imported nearly $750,000 worth of Nova Scotia apples.
Lutz said Vietnam has become Nova Scotia's second-largest apple market after a foothold was established about seven years ago.
Growers are now targeting the Taiwan market this year, while also looking to enter Thailand. Lutz said many Southeast Asian countries do not grow apples, which creates opportunities for imports.
Although those countries are closer to Australian and New Zealand producers, Nova Scotia will benefit from having the opposite harvest season.
Emily Lutz said some Southeast Asian countries do not grow apples, which creates opportunities for fruit producers like Nova Scotia. (Paul Légère/Radio-Canada)

In February, the federal government launched the Agrimarketing program, providing $75 million over five years to agriculture businesses nationwide to find new markets. Out of that, the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association secured $300,000.
Lutz said the funding can support their various market development activities, such as attending international exhibitions and hiring local marketing experts.

Michael Van Meekeren, vice-president of Van Meekeren Farms Ltd. in Lakeville, N.S, said while this year's apple crop is not the largest on record, it is still a bumper season, and having access to new markets is an exciting opportunity for growers.
Van Meekeren said Nova Scotia will prioritize exporting varieties with a strong global competitive edge, such as honeycrisp and ambrosia.
He believes exports will not strain local supply, as the Atlantic region has a small population and abundant apple resources.

"We just export the ones that really shine from Nova Scotia," Van Meekeren said. "I think it is the right thing to do for Nova Scotia when we have something that is as good or better than any others in the world."

articles.title: EXPLAINER: How PH is preparing for Super El Niño
articles.summary: Amid the threat of Super El Niño, the public was advised to start storing and conserving water due to possible supply shortages once the drought worsens.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 4:23pm
Amid the threat of Super El Niño, the public has been advised to start storing and conserving water due to possible supply shortages once the drought worsens.
Several government agencies have also launched their initiatives, plans, and technology that they plan to use to mitigate the effects of the extreme heat and dry conditions/
What are these measures?
Air-to-water system

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) has adopted an air-to-water technology, which converts moisture from air to create potable water through a process called Atmospheric Water Generation.
With this technology, air flows through the heat exchanger to evaporate and cool so that the water vapor condenses into small droplets of water.

The water will then go through the filtration process and UV light to remove dirt and other contaminants, and then undergo a mineralization process to add minerals to the water before flowing into the built-in reservoir for storage.
The DSWD said the water could be used for drinking or stored for future use.
Rainwater collection
One of the effects of Super El Niño is the decrease in rainfall—some agencies have advised the public to take advantage of passing rains to collect water.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) has constructed a rainwater harvesting system to store water that can be distributed to communities that may experience water shortages.
In this system, the rainwater that the roof catches flows through the gutters, then through filtration to remove debris such as leaves, and finally to the collection system.
The collected water is stored either in a tank, rain barrel, or cistern. Other rainwater collection systems feature an overflow outlet to release excess water when the tank is full.

The DENR noted that water collected with this system is not automatically safe to use as drinking water, but is instead recommended for non-potable uses such as watering plants, cleaning, and flushing toilets.
Farming
One of the most crucial sectors that must prepare is agriculture, as livelihoods and the food supply depend on it.

In preparation, the National Irrigation Administration said that it targets using the groundwater maps of the Mines and Geosciences Bureau to identify potential groundwater sources to use in its solar-powered irrigation pump systems planned for deployment in various areas.

Using this measure, a site assessment is first conducted to study the water source location and the volume of water needed for irrigation. Once assessed and approved, solar power is used to generate electricity that powers the pumps.
Depending on the design, water may flow through pipes into a storage tank or directly into the irrigation network to be distributed to farmlands.

Aside from securing water supply, agencies are also promoting the use of Project SARAi, or Smart Approaches to Reinvigorate Agriculture as an Industry, led by the University of the Philippines Los Baños and funded by DOST-PCAARRD.
Project SARAI provides farmers with location-specific weather advisories to help them plan their farming activities based on the specific conditions of their location.
The agency noted that while the effects of El Niño are widespread, the actual impact and status vary across different areas and famlands. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Mexico sentences killers of US, Australian surfers to 158 years each in prison
articles.summary: Three Mexican men were found guilty last week of murdering foreign surfers in 2024. The case had drawn global condemnation, particularly in Australia, where two of the victims were from.

image.caption: Brothers Callum and Jake Robinson were on a surfing trip when they were murderedImage: AAP/IMAGO

blocks.text: A court in Mexico sentenced three men to more than 158 years each in prison on Friday for murdering two Australian surfers and their American friend in 2024.
The court also ordered the ​defendants to pay compensation to the victims' families, an official said.
The three defendants, Jesus Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were convicted a week ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
What was the case about?
In 2024, the three victims were on a surfing trip to Mexico's Pacific coast.
Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their American friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were shot dead in Baja California state during an attempted robbery.
The three were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on April 27, 2024.

blocks.caption: The murders of the three tourists in Mexico drew global condemnationImage: Karen Castaneda/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Days later, their search, assisted by the FBI, led to their bodies dumped in a cliff-top well, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
Their killings sent shockwaves through Ensenada, the hotspot for surfing that attracts people from around the world.
While Mexico has long struggled with widespread insecurity, the area where the murders were committed was considered safe for tourists.
What did the families of the victims say?
"There will ​never be justice for the loss of a child, but these men will never hurt anyone else again,” said ​Page Rhoad, mother of the slain ‌American, via Zoom after the sentencing.
The Robinsons' parents traveled to Mexico from Australia for the month-long trial and left after the initial guilty verdict.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin Robinson said.
Debra Robinson said what hurt the most was that her sons "were treated with such cruelty" in their final hours.

blocks.caption: Callum and Jake Robinson's parents were in court to hear the guilty verdictImage: Guillermo Arias/AFP

articles.title: OCD: Gov't can tap P7.8-B NDRRM fund for El Niño response

The Philippine government government can tap over P7 billion available National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (NDRRM) Fund for response and relief efforts due to the effects of El Niño phenomenon, the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) said Saturday.

items: Cagayan Valley - 66

articles.title: France: Police and protesters clash in nationwide protests
articles.summary: Students, trade unionists and Yellow Vest activists are taking to French streets to protest high prices and inequality. Police and protesters have already clashed in Paris and Marseille.

image.caption: Saturday's rallies follow weeks of protests by France's youthImage: Thibaud Moritz/AFP

blocks.text: There have been clashes between police and protesters amid mass rallies across France on Saturday, over high prices and social inequalities and the state of the education system.
Police arrest hundreds nationwide
The Interior Ministry said that some 272 people had been arrested by mid-afternoon following violent incidents in Paris, Marseilles, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.

"Such actions include attempted looting, confrontations with law enforcement, the setting of fires to street furniture and the targeting of seats of power and media outlets," the ministry saidand blamed the unrest on what it described ​as the "ultra-left."
In Paris and Marseille, police have fired tear gas at protesters during clashes.
AFP reported that the windows of the offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in western Paris were broken by protesters, and journalists reported seeing several parked cars torched.
In Lyon, situated in central France, the city's tourism office was set alight with flames and black smoke seen billowing from the building.

blocks.caption: Lyon's tourism office was set alight during chaotic scenesImage: Jeff Pachoud/AFP

blocks.text: Meanwhile in Lille, protesters smashed their way into the town hall of France's northern city of Lille and vandalised the premises before leaving, according to an AFP photographer.
Riot police within minutes confirmed that all the protesters had left.

The protests come on the heels of an initial wave of demonstrations that began last month over the situation at schools in the country, with pupils complaining about teacher absences and run-down facilities.
President Emmanuel Macron has called "for calm and respect" ahead of the protests, saying that the right to protest went hand in hand with "respect for people and property."
France students demand better schools
What do we know about the protests in France?
More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to protest organizers.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told France 2 television that "a pretty big turnout" was expected, while a police source told the French AFP news agency that authorities estimate nearly 200,000 people will attend.

blocks.caption: 40,000 people were expected in the capital, Paris, a police source saidImage: Yann Tessier/REUTERS

blocks.text: However, the Paris demonstrators faced restrictions, with police banning rallies around the Elysee presidential palace, the prime minister's office and the Champs-Elysee avenue, along with other key locations.
A march through the center of the city has also been banned.

blocks.caption: French police are out in force near the Place de la Republique in ParisImage: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

blocks.text: The main Paris demonstration began at 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) at the Place de la Republique..

Reports began emerging late on Saturday morning of riot police clashing with protesters in the Saint-Denis area on the outskirts of the capital, as well as near the Gare du Nord train station, among other areas.

blocks.caption: Protesters clash with riot police officers in ParisImage: Kiran Ridley/AFP

blocks.text: Fears of violence at the French protests
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Thursday that authorities fear there could be violence during the protests.
"This is a moment of fatigue in the country," Lecornu said. "We are ​in an atmosphere ‌of perma-crisis: wars, inflation, and issues surrounding purchasing power."
Jordan Bardella, the head of the far-right National Rally, which is leading the polls ahead of next year's presidential election, said he expected clashes.

blocks.caption: Fires were set and protesters also targeted a police station in MarseilleImage: Thibaud Moritz/AFP

blocks.text: "I'm extremely concerned," he said during a visit to the Paris car show. "It will be a ‌day of chaos for France."
The school protests that have rocked France in recent weeks have already seen considerable violence, with several protesters and more than 900 police injured.
In one notable incident, an adolescent school pupil had one hand blown off and several fingers on the other hand injured by a stun grenade.
The internal police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen cases ​of alleged police violence.

blocks.caption: France's students have been complaining of underfunded public schoolsImage: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS

blocks.text: Who is taking part in the protests?

Students are to be joined by trade unionists and remnants of the Yellow Vests ("Gilets jaunes") movement, which staged mass weekly protests from November 2018 to June 2020, initially against rising fuel prices. They later morphed into protests against the high cost of living and economic inequality in general.

The student protests over the past weeks have been backed by Jean-Luc Melanchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed ("La France insoumise", or LFI), who marched in one demonstration on Tuesday.
The government has blamed the LFI for pouring fuel on the fire of widespread public discontent, an allegation the party has denied.
Student protests in France: Schools shut as unrest grows

articles.title: Filipino composer Rom Dongeto and the song we thought we knew
articles.summary: Decades after a TV commercial propelled it into the mainstream, the activist-born anthem ‘Kanlungan’ — popularized by the voice of Noel Cabangon — continues to transcend generations as a bittersweet…

blocks.text: “Kanlungan” remains an enduring staple of Philippine popular music, recognized across generations for its emotional weight and social relevance. And while Noel Cabangon has become synonymous with the song, few know the story of the man who wrote it.
Rom Dongeto, the composer of “Kanlungan,” traces his artistic origins to the 1980s protest movement, recounting the song’s journey from an obscure track in the early 1990s to a timeless anthem.

blocks.caption: Filipino composer Rom Dongeto and the song we thought we knew

blocks.text: Dongeto’s activism began in Tondo, where he joined student organizing efforts at Torres High School.

During those formative years, he attended a concert at the University of the Philippines Diliman featuring prominent protest musicians Jess Santiago, Paul Galang, and Susan Fernandez. Watching them perform made him realize that music was far more than just art.
“Na-inspire ako…sabi ko, ‘Ito ang gusto kong gawin. Ito ang gusto kong maging vocation bilang isang aktibista,’” said Dongeto.
(I was inspired…I said, ‘This is what I want to do. This is what I want my vocation to be as an activist.’)
Later in college at Far Eastern University, Dongeto founded the cultural group Sinaglahi, performing across the University Belt and Sta. Mesa.
During this period, he crossed paths with Rene Boncocan, a Fine Arts student at UP Diliman and founder of the artist collective Lingkod Sining.

In the early ’80s, the artist network gave birth to Bukluran ng Musikero para sa Bayan, an alliance of progressive bands, such as Nuklus Band and UP Sintunado, as part of the growing movement against the dictatorship.

As Dongeto described it, “Nagsama-sama ‘yan para lumikha ng mga progresibong kanta, mag-perform sa rallies, makatulong sa consolidation ng protest movement, at makapag-inspire ng marami pang mamamayan.”
(They came together to create progressive songs, perform at rallies, help consolidate the protest movement, and inspire many more people.)

blocks.caption: Filipino composer Rom Dongeto and the song we thought we knew

blocks.text: The political landscape shifted dramatically following the assassination of Ninoy Aquino in 1983. The tragedy rapidly accelerated mass mobilizations and galvanized artists, students, and workers nationwide.
Around this time, Dongeto was introduced to folk singer Noel Cabangon through the latter’s activist brother.

“Dahil trabaho kong mag-organize, ‘yon ang ginawa ko. Pinuntahan ko siya sa isang tugtugan sa Kamuning. Kinausap ko siya,” said Dongeto, recalling how he recruited Cabangon to join their growing circle of cultural workers, paving the way for their long-term musical partnership.
(Since my job is to organize, that’s what I did. I went to see him at a gig in Kamuning. I spoke with him.)
The 1986 EDSA People Power Revolution brought a wave of political uncertainty to the movement, particularly among student activists. At the time, Cabangon was in Malaysia.
Reflecting on the pivotal night Ferdinand Marcos Sr. fled the country, Dongeto found himself in Morayta alongside student leader Lean Alejandro.
“Magkasama kami ni Lean sa Morayta noon…I can still remember Lean was crying noong gabing ‘yon at sinabi niya, ‘Huwag tayong manlulumo, magpapatuloy ang pagkilos,’” he said.
(Lean and I were together in Morayta back then…I can still remember that Lean was crying that night, and he said, ‘Let us not lose heart, the movement will continue.’)
Returning home that night, Dongeto channeled the lingering tension and uncertainty into the lyrics of “Ang Ating Awit,” a track that would later appear on Buklod’s second album, Tatsulok (1991).

In the aftermath of EDSA, Buklod dissolved as an umbrella organization. Dongeto noted that fatigue had likely set in after years of relentless struggle, and many believed that the fight had ended following the fall of the dictatorship.
Dongeto, Cabangon, and Boncocan, however, made a conscious decision to carry on as a musical trio, retaining the name.
“So ang ginawa namin, minaintain namin ‘yong pangalan ng Buklod bilang isang musical organization,” said Dongeto.
(So what we did was, we maintained the name Buklod as a musical organization.)

The illusion of a democratic transition was shattered in January 1987 when state troops under the Aquino administration opened fire on protesting farmers in Manila — a tragedy now known as the Mendiola Massacre.
This incident, according to Dongeto, partly inspired the creation of Buklod’s debut album, Bukid at Buhay (1988), a purely acoustic album which he fondly refers to as “classic Buklod.”

“Kanlungan” would ultimately become part of Buklod’s third album, Sa Kandungan ng Kalikasan (1992), a project intended to reach a wider mainstream audience while expanding their advocacy toward environmental awareness.

Writing the song was a fluid experience for Dongeto, taking him just two days to compose it. Unlike earlier protest tracks like “Tatsulok” — where he felt the heavy burden of political analysis through an activist lens — the words and melody for “Kanlungan” simply flowed freely and naturally.
Dongeto noted that he did not feel emotionally or intellectually exhausted after completing it because it came straight from what he was feeling.
Though the song’s vivid imagery leads many listeners to assume Dongeto grew up in a rural coastal town, he clarifies that he wrote it in Tondo using pure creative imagination.
For Dongeto, “Kanlungan” is more than a nostalgic love song; it is an ecological lamentation on fragile ecosystems and human responsibility.
“Meron din siyang lamentation na, ‘Tsong, pag pinakawalan mo ‘to, pag nagkamali ka dito, baka hindi ka na makabalik,’” he shared.
(It features a lamentation, ‘Buddy, if you let this go, if you make a mistake here, you might not be able to come back.)

Dongeto emphasized the direct link between human affection and stewardship of nature: “Kasi gaano man ka-romantiko buhay mo, ‘pag tinamaan ka ng bagyo, bumagsak ang lupa, bumagsak ang bundok, patay ka, ‘di ba? Romantiko ka nga, pero patay ka naman…Kasi kaya tayong lipulin ng pagkakamali natin ‘pag pinabayaan natin ‘yan.”

(No matter how romantic your life may be, if a storm hits, if the ground gives way or a mountain collapses, you’re dead, right? You might be romantic, but you’d be dead… Because our own mistakes can wipe us out if we leave them unaddressed.)

Through its poetic metaphor, the song serves as an urgent reminder to safeguard our shared environment. In the end, no one wants to destroy their own sanctuary, only to be left grieving in the ruins and asking, as the song does: “Maibabalik ba ang kahapon? (Can the past be brought back?)”

In 2003, while studying in the United States, Dongeto was surprised to receive a call from the Philippines. It was Cabangon, who wanted to discuss licensing “Kanlungan” for a McDonald’s commercial. After clearing up concerns regarding copyright, Dongeto agreed.
The release of the ad, which reframed the song around familial homecoming, triggered a backlash from national democratic activists.

Critics called the licensing a sellout, given McDonald’s status as a symbol of US imperialism. The friction was further heightened by the ad’s visual narrative, which featured a family member in military uniform — a stark point of contention given the Armed Forces’ long history of human rights violations in the country. Neither Dongeto nor Cabangon knew the commercial’s specific storyline in advance.

Dongeto shared that he understood and respected the sentiments of his fellow activists, but they stood by their decision. They wanted to push the song’s environmental and social themes beyond progressive circles and into the general public, believing that a far wider audience deserved to hear their work.

While the McDonald’s commercial that elevated it to fame has long faded into memory, “Kanlungan” transcended generations to become one of the most beloved Filipino songs. Its mainstream success cemented its status in Philippine culture and sealed Noel Cabangon as its definitive voice.
“Si Noel talaga ang boses ng ‘Kanlungan.’ Kaya nga ang tao ‘pag sinabing ‘Kanlungan,’ si Noel kaagad ang naiisip,” Dongeto acknowledged.
(Noel is truly the voice of ‘Kanlungan.’ That is why, whenever ‘Kanlungan’ is mentioned, people immediately think of Noel.)

“Kanlungan” broke into the mainstream through the commercial world that its creators once stood apart from. Whether that journey represented compromise or cultural victory remains a matter of perspective.

But the song survived the backlash, outgrew the advertisement that made it famous, and acquired a life of its own — continuing to resonate as both a song of longing and a warning against the destruction of our natural sanctuary. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Here's why some people say the 2-day weekend is due for a makeover
articles.summary: In October 1926, Henry Ford announced his factories would close not just on Sundays but Saturdays, too, making his company the first big North American employer to do so. But advocates for a shorter…

image.caption: The erosion of boundaries between work and personal time has not only increased the amount of work that people do, says labour historian David Henkin, it’s also “decreased the amount of insulation, psychic insulation, that people have from work.” (Worawee Meepian/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: LISTEN | How old is the two-day weekend?:
Cost of Living9:14A brief history of the weekend
As the two-day weekend turns 100 years old, some say it's high time for a calendar shakeup.

"Almost nobody alive remembers the time before we had a five-day week and a two-day weekend," said Grace Tallon, co-founder of Work Time Revolution, a Toronto-based consultancy group that helps employers adopt shorter work hours.
Labour historians and advocates for workweek reform point out that much has changed since the two-day weekend became standard about a century ago, depending on where you are in the world.

Tallon notes that only 20 per cent of women were in the workforce at that time. "Now we have mostly dual-income households, yet we still have a situation where we have a five-day workweek that doesn't serve really any family."
Experts also point out that the weekend is a human-made concept that has evolved before and can evolve again.

Grace Tallon, co-founder of Work Time Revolution, a Toronto-based consultancy group that helps employers adopt shorter work hours, says the way we live and work has changed a lot since we last revisited the length of the workweek. (Submitted by Grace Tallon)
How the two-day weekend came about
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, a long workweek was the norm.
"Basically, if you were working for wages, the regular work week was six days of 10 hours a day," said labour historian Craig Heron, a professor emeritus at York University in Toronto.
"The beginning of the weekend was the Sunday that everyone got off for religious reasons," Heron told Cost of Living host Paul Haavardsrud.
Though Henry Ford is widely credited with instituting a two-day weekend, there's quite a bit more to the story, including decades of work by the labour movement.
Prior to Ford's five-day-week, small groups of workers had achieved similar reforms.
"The most famous group were the printers," Heron said. "They managed to get an eight-hour day by about 1910."

An illustration published in the Canadian Illustrated News shows workers taking part in a Nine-Hour Movement march in Hamilton, Ont., in 1872. The movement pushed for shorter working days and helped spur major changes to Canadian labour law. (Canadian Illustrated News/Library and Archives Canada)
When Ford announced in October 1926 that his factories would move to a five-day week, the company became the first major U.S. employer to do so.
That same month, the American Federation of Labor passed a resolution at its annual congress calling for a five-day week, Heron says.
But it would be a while until the two-day weekend was broadly adopted, including in Canada, he says.
Many workplaces in North America and elsewhere first reduced Saturday work to half a day.
The labour movement grew stronger in the 1940s as the Second World War drove demand for workers, giving unions greater leverage to win shorter workdays through major strikes, he says.
Governments began to take note and legislate accordingly.

In workplaces that adopted policies that reduce hours while maintaining pay through pilots run by the non-profit 4-Day Week Global, participants reported an improvement in their ability to combine paid work with their social lives. (Tint Media/Shutterstock)
Work has changed
Since then, the nature of work has changed significantly, in ways that can affect whether a two-day weekend feels adequate.

"We have a much more fluid kind of work schedule for a lot of people who work electronically, who work at all hours, all times of the day or week, and can be on call anytime," said Heron. "Their cell phone could ring whenever their employer wants them."

While working hours steadily decreased from the late 19th century to the middle of the 20th, they began to increase again after that, says David Henkin, a historian at the University of California, Berkeley and author of The Week: A History of the Unnatural Rhythms That Made Us Who We Are.

The erosion of boundaries between work and personal time has not only increased the amount of work that people do, he says, it has also "decreased the amount of insulation, psychic insulation, that people have from work."
When every weekend is a long weekend
A desire to address that erosion is part of what's fuelling momentum for a four-day workweek.

Tallon is also a former executive director of the non-profit 4-Day Week Global, which conducted four-day-week pilots starting in 2022, in which hours were reduced while pay remained the same. She says all 41 participating companies in Canada and the U.S. kept the four-day week after the six-month trials ended.
One of them was Praxis, a public relations firm in Toronto.

Meredith Nebel, an account director for public relations firm Praxis, says that since the company moved to a four-day week she's been able to keep her weekends more free for family time because she can get errands, chores and appointments out of the way on Fridays. (Submitted by Meredith Nebel)

Meredith Nebel, an account director for Praxis, says days off are staggered. Colleagues cover her work while she's off on Fridays, "and then I take on their Monday work just to make sure that there's no pause in the workflow."

items: These Canadian companies switched to a 4-day work week. Here's why
Why experts say it's time to adopt a 4-day work week

blocks.text: Nebel says she doesn't think she could go back to a five-day week.
"I have more time with my kids. I have time within my own community. I have more time for my own life and my own desires and just building myself as a human," she said.
Nebel says she uses Fridays to get appointments, household errands and chores out of the way so weekends are free for family time and kids' activities.
Charles Latimer, who works for Greenpeace, says having Fridays off since the organization adopted a four-day week has given him time to volunteer.
"I just started a little kids' basketball program after daycare on Tuesdays," said Latimer, who works remotely from Lund, B.C., about 200 kilometres north of Vancouver.
On Fridays Latimer takes care of administrative tasks for the program and also keeps his four-year-old home from daycare, he says.

Charles Latimer, seen here with his four-year-old daughter and their dog, works as head of strategic integration for Greenpeace, which reduced hours to a four-day schedule. (Submitted by Charles Latimer)

Consultant Grace Tallon says switching to a four-day schedule takes considerable planning. "That could mean that you need to restructure your meetings; that could mean that you need to ensure that everybody has heads-down time, when that previously wasn't respected."
At Praxis, Nebel says it hasn't been a struggle to get the work done in less time.

"Work just seems to expand to fill the time that you give it," she said, "but with the four days there's a natural urgency so we plan more deliberately and we're sharper about what actually needs to get done."
'The week is unnatural'
We tend to think of the week — with its five days of work and two of rest — as set in stone.
But Henkin says the very idea of the week as a whole, let alone the way we divide it, is considerably more arbitrary than the other units humans use to measure time.

"The week is unnatural because it is not actually rooted in any of either the astronomical phenomena that produce things like days or … hours or years, nor are they rooted in the biological rhythms that produce patterns of day and night."

Tallon says that whether a workplace is looking to adopt a four-day week or just rein in long hours, it's about "how you start to respect your own time and how the company starts to respect your time."
"And many of these people then feel, 'I can turn off my notifications in the evening. I'm not gonna look [because] I feel I have to. Because nothing's going to blow up or burn down.'"

articles.title: Why Canadian Starlink subscribers (probably) shouldn't worry about U.S interference
articles.summary: The potential ability of the U.S government to affect the operation of a Starlink related satellite system may have also raised questions about Washington's power to affect commerical users of the…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump denied he was involved in the decision to restrict Ukraine access to Starlink and said he didn't think Elon Musk was involved either. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Earlier this week, Ukrainian officials said they had lost some access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, the satellite communications system operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX.
Musk, CEO of SpaceX, denied any involvement in restricting Ukraine's access, saying that decision would be up to the U.S. government.
Meanwhile, on Friday, U.S. President Donald Trump denied he was involved in the decision to restrict access and said he didn't think Musk was involved either.
Trump's remarks followed a Reuters report that the White House had ordered the restrictions.

Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink terminals stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance over Ukrainian territory.

items: Starlink restrictions would hamper Ukraine's war effort. But the country can adapt, experts say

blocks.text: Still, the potential ability of the U.S government to affect the operation of a Starlink-related satellite system may also have raised questions about Washington's ability to influence commerical users of the system.
In Canada, for example, Starlink provides internet access in remote areas and has about 500,000 users.
Here's a look at the U.S. government's relationship with Starlink and Starshield, and the role it plays in each.
A Ukrainian drone operator monitors video feeds and satellite imagery on an array of tablets. Ukrainian officials say restrictions on Starshield have disrupted some drone operations. (Neil Hauer/CBC)
What's the difference between Starlink and Starshield?
Starlink is a Space X's commercial satellite internet network, with more than 11,000 satellites and roughly 13 million subscribers. It is available to businesses and individuals.
Its low-Earth-orbit satellites allow it to deliver faster connections than traditional satellite internet systems.
The network gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how its military operates on the battlefield.

But when Musk and SpaceX became concerned about the commercial system being used for military purposes, the company created Starshield, said Mark Hilborne, an associate professor in the defence studies department at King's College London.
Unlike the thousands of satellites used in the Starlink network, Starshield is limited to around 250, Hilborne said.

It's also a more secure network, is not publicly available and is used specifically for government and military purposes. Its secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals.
Ukraine says Starlink restrictions are disrupting military operations

Few countries have access to Starshield, Hillborne said. The U.S. is the main customer, while the United Kingdom and Ukraine also have access. In Ukraine's case, the Pentagon covers the fees and allows the country to use the system.

While Starshield's missions are separate from Starlink's commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield's secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals ‌but rely ⁠on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
What role does the U.S. government have in Starshield?

According to Musk, the Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S government. That means any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and, ultimately, by the president, he said.
"Mostly, it is used by [the U.S.] and it's for them. And so they probably make the ultimate decisions" regarding its use, Hilborne said.

According to a 2024 Reuters report, the Pentagon has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft ​for missile-warning missions and a spy ​constellation for the National Reconnaissance ⁠Office.

But the relationship between Starshield and the U.S. government is "fuzzy," Craig Douglas Albert, a political science professor and graduate director of the Intelligence, Defense and Cybersecurity program at Augusta University in Georgia, said in an email to CBC News.
This image shows Starlink satellites shortly after being launched into space in 2019. (SpaceX)
SpaceX develops and supplies Starshield through government contracts, meaning the system is privately owned but procured by the U.S. government, Albert said.
"There is a lot on this relationship that is classified and thus, the direct relationship is still unclear," he said.
Does the U.S. government have any control over Starlink?
Again, Albert says, it's not entirely clear.
The U.S can regulate Starlink through licensing requirements and the terms of government contracts governing how the company operates, he said.
However, much of the relationship is classified, limiting public understanding of how much influence the U.S. government has over Starlink, Albert said.
But the U.S. has no direct control over Starlink itself, he said.
What major satellite systems does the U.S. government control?

Major examples would include the Global Positioning System (GPS), a space-based radio-navigation system owned by the U.S. government and operated by the United States Space Force. Its satellites provide services to civilian and military users.
The high-stakes race to get Canadian rockets into orbit

The U.S. Space Force also operates Wideband Global SATCOM (WGS) and Advanced Extremely High Frequency (AEHF) system for military communications, as well as the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) for advanced missile warning.
"The relationship between satellite technology and the U.S. government exists from everyday consumer and citizen consumption through advanced national security operations," Albert said.
Should Canadians be concerned about U.S. government control over private commercial systems?
Hilborne said that while the U.S. may technically have the capability to turn off such a system in a region of Canada, for example, such a move would likely be resisted by commercial operators.
However, the U.S. government could likely apply leverage to a company like SpaceX to bend to its wishes, he suggested.
Albert added that citizens "should always force accountability of technology that is dual use and has a relationship between citizen consumer consumption and national security."

articles.title: In Canada's drone-killing 'Sandbox,' companies compete for a $1M prize
articles.summary: As part of Canada's drive to jump-start a domestic defence drone industry, two dozen companies showcased their technologies and competed for a million-dollar prize at a military base in Suffield,…

image.caption: One of the drones at the fourth Counter-Uncrewed Aircraft Sandbox near Suffield, Alta., a contest hosted by the Department of National Defence. (Evan Dyer/CBC)

blocks.text: The Suffield Research Centre is in the heart of Alberta's Big Sky country, and is also blessed with Canada's sunniest skies, making it the perfect testing ground for one of Canada's most critical areas of innovation: drone and counter-drone technology.
Once the main training ground for the tank crews of the British Army, the British gradually withdrew and left entirely by 2024.
But today, the base is buzzing with activity as militaries urgently rearm with new technologies.
Even the British are back, in smaller numbers for now, and not to drive tanks but fly drones — and shoot them down.

Canada's Department of National Defence this month used Suffield to hold its fourth Counter-Uncrewed Aircraft Sandbox, a drone-killing contest with a million-dollar prize for the most promising innovation.

Companies from Canada, Australia, Finland and the U.S. showcased new methods of detecting and intercepting drones, closely watched by members of the Canadian, Dutch, German, British, American and Ukrainian militaries.
New drone-defence technology put to the test at Canadian showcase
All of the armies are there to learn and observe. But the Ukrainians, as the only military at the Sandbox with real-world experience in drone warfare, are also there to teach.

"They're creating the environment that we want to emulate," said Col. Gabriel Doré of the Royal Canadian Air Force. "They're on the battlefield. They're the ones who are innovating the fastest. And they can tell us immediately if something's going to work or not just by looking at it, because they're living it."
Learning from the experts
The conflict in Ukraine has turbocharged the pace of scientific innovation in all forms of drone warfare: aerial, ground-based, marine surface and underwater.
There are now even drones that can transition from underwater to aerial flight.
"We need to be the number one in drones to fight against Russia," said Ukrainian Army Maj. Sergiy Kuzyara.

Kuzyara said those drones include cheap, simple first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones used on the front lines to marine drones to "deep-strike drones which are reaching Russian refineries or military production plants."
A sign at the Suffield Research Centre, about five kilometres north of Suffield, Alta. (Evan Dyer/CBC)

Kuzyara says his mission in Canada is not only to check out the latest designs, but also "help your producers to understand what's needed at the front line, what direction they need to go to be successful."

Radio-frequency jammers that were cutting-edge tech at the 2022 CUAS Sandbox would already be obsolete on Ukraine's front lines, where jamming is so intense that drone operators have given up almost entirely on radio remote control, opting instead to guide their drones through hair-thin fibre-optic wires trailing from spools many kilometres long.
Some of the technology showcased this year at the Sandbox would not be practical in Ukraine's direct combat zones — although useful for other applications.
Signals jamming influences every aspect of the drone war in Ukraine. Ukrainian Army Lt-Col. Maxim Velychenko says satellite-powered navigation (such as GPS) is also jammed on the front lines.
Kamikaze drones go jet-powered

One example of the frenetic pace of innovation in the drone war: the feared Iranian Shahed drones — fixed-wing kamikaze drones that can travel over 2,000 kilometres — have undergone a recent threatening upgrade.

"We know how to shoot down the Shaheds powered by the internal combustion engines," said Kuzyara. "But they switched to jet-powered and so we need to use something new: jet-powered interceptors or missiles."

The new Shaheds are sometimes mixed with the older kind in what Kuzyara calls a "tricky" manoeuvre to deceive air defence crews — flying together at about 180 kilometres per hour before the jet-powered drones more than double their speed to attack.
Firefighters work at the site of Ukraine's Academy of Sciences building hit by a Russian jet-powered drone strike last month. (Sergiy Chalyi/Reuters)
Paul Ziadé thinks he has the solution.
The CEO of Calgary's North Vector Dynamics has been a regular at the Sandbox. He's designed a metre-long, laser-guided missile with the jet-powered Shahed in mind.

"Our missile does not need to achieve a direct hit on the target," he said. "Similar to many other air defence missiles, all we need to do is get to the proximity of the threat and then the warhead takes care of the rest."
Unlike other air defence missiles, however, this prototype is designed to defeat drones — and is both smaller and cheaper.

In the test witnessed by CBC News, North Vector's missile almost brushed a target drone, considered a kill for a weapon that carries a proximity fuse and uses a warhead to blast a forward-conical explosion.
Having shown its ability to connect with the target, the next round of testing will likely include the warhead.
Cost a critical factor
Weapons already exist that can reliably destroy even a jet-powered Shahed. The problem is their cost.

At the start of the U.S. and Israel-Iran war, the United States and Gulf kingdoms were forced to use Patriot PAC-3 missiles ($5 million Cdn each) and other expensive interceptors to defeat much cheaper Iranian drones.
Ukraine has succeeded in inventing lower-cost interceptors, but jet-powered drones such as the new Shahed and the Geran-5 have forced the use of pricier alternatives.
Cost is critical, says Doré.
"Otherwise it's really easy to send a bunch of drones our way that's going to make us, you know, use very exquisite, very expensive systems," he said.
Suspicious drones are stalking NATO skies with impunity
"We're going to empty our magazines very rapidly."

Reducing cost-per-shot and ensuring you don't run out of firepower are key goals of drone developers, with all sides expecting to see more drone "swarms" in the future, and greater use of AI in targeting and guidance.

Armin Strobel of St. John's-based StrobelTEK did a PhD thesis on drone swarms in 2010, when it was still an exotic and little-researched subject. Today he is competing in the Sandbox as the designer of a cheap, portable optically guided kinetic missile meant to defeat those swarms.
He told CBC News that fully autonomous attack drones are on the horizon.
"There might be some steps in between, but you'll basically just send out drones and say, 'Look for those targets and take care of them.'"
Kuzyara says larger, fixed-wing drones will increasingly come to resemble missiles, as they speed up to defeat interceptors.
Extra points for new ideas
The Department of National Defence doesn't tell competitors how to neutralize drones. Those who show the most promise in innovation win the prize, say organizers.
Examples this year include an explosive 12-gauge shotgun round from Colt Canada, fitted with a proximity fuse that allows a shooter to kill FPV drones without a direct hit.

Alabama-based SCI Technology has a long, tubular drone with six rotors that carries a net. Nets have been used for a while to entangle drones and make them crash, but SCI's solution is for situations where it's not safe to knock an explosive drone out of the sky because of the presence of people or sensitive infrastructure on the ground.

items: The growing drone campaign stalking NATO's skies
Ukraine can adapt if Starlink access restricted, experts say
How NATO is prepping in the Baltic skies

blocks.text: SCI's AeroGuard fires a net that captures the enemy drone, but the net stays tethered to the AeroGuard, which then carries the captured drone to a safe location.
Australia's AIM Defence, which won first prize in 2024, brought two laser units to the 2026 event.

Jenelle Frewen, the company's director of strategic initiatives, says AIM used its $1-million prize to set up a Canadian division that now employs 10 people. Its laser system has since become more powerful, more accurate and lighter.
"We've had a lot of fantastic support from Canada," she said. "We were originally an Australian company, we're now a joint Australian-Canadian company."
'Obsolete in a couple of weeks'
The Department of National Defence finds it worthwhile to provide a free testing facility and cash prizes because its mission in Suffield has a double purpose.
The first is to find the best counter-drone technologies for the Canadian Forces, which recognize a need to catch up in the fastest-growing area of modern warfare.

The second, though, is to foster a domestic drone manufacturing industry. The Carney government's Defence Drone Initiative is focused on developing capabilities in marine drones, underwater drones, uncrewed ground vehicles, explosive payloads, long-range precision-strike drones and the counter-drone interceptors being tested at Suffield.

items: Hamilton drone maker isn't bothered by threats from Russia
Military commander vows fast action on AI and robots

blocks.text: That means creating an environment of constant innovation, says Doré.

"Even if we could come up with a perfect solution today, it would probably be obsolete in a couple of weeks," he said. "It's not so much about finding the perfect solution now, it's about finding the right process and having the ability to iterate rapidly."
He expects that Canadian drone companies will soon "be as competitive as any around the world" if the support from the government continues.
Under those conditions, he said "both counter and drone companies should be able to find a market for themselves, and answer the call when it comes to developing a sovereign capability."

articles.title: Waymo is coming to Toronto. Will its self-driving cars be winter-ready?
articles.summary: Snow-covered objects can become hard to detect, while cameras and sensors sometimes struggle in snowy conditions. Experts say they're not insurmountable — but they will take more training data and…

image.caption: People navigate snow drifts near St. Lawrence Market in Toronto amid record snowfall Jan. 25. As Waymo prepares to start testing in Toronto, experts say it will take time for the company's self-driving cars to be ready for the city's wintry conditions. (Andrew Davidson/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

Snow-covered objects can become hard to detect, while cameras and sensors sometimes struggle in snowy conditions. Experts say they're not insurmountable — but they will take more training data and time for Waymo to adjust to.
Experts say seasonal challenges can be overcome, but require time and training
Waymo is coming to Toronto. But the road to get there will be an often snow-covered one — and experts say that will take time and training data to overcome.
The U.S. company said Friday it plans to start testing the streets of Canada's biggest city, with drivers behind the wheel, in the coming days, as part of its "mapping and safety validation work."
The goal is for riders to be able to hail one of their driverless cabs by 2028 in the city, Waymo said.
The tests will take place at all hours of the day and night and across all days of the week, in an effort to make sure the technology can adapt to Toronto's "distinct driving conditions."
The company didn't expand on what those conditions were. But Steven Waslander, professor and director of the University of Toronto's Robotics Institute, says that likely means snow.
"The big differentiator is really our winter," Waslander said of Toronto compared to other North American cities where Waymo is already up and running.
"The winter challenge is one that [Waymo] haven't demonstrated commercially yet."

Waymo first hit the road in warmer cities with little precipitation like Los Angeles and Phoenix, Ariz., and most of the cities it offers ride-hailing services in today are much warmer and dryer than Toronto. That's for good reason, according to Waslander, who says running autonomous cars in the snow comes with all kinds of extra challenges.

Autonomous cars rely on cameras, radar and lidar systems — which map the 3D environment using light — to situate themselves. All of that information is fed into a computer, which makes decisions about where to turn or when to hit the brakes, augmented by lots and lots of training data.
Adverse weather conditions can pose a challenge for all of those systems, says Krzysztof Czarnecki, an engineering professor at the University of Waterloo.

Cameras and other sensors can get covered by snow and ice, making them less effective. Heavy falling rain and snow can also reduce how well the driving system detects objects — as can snow covering cars or street signs.

Cameras, radar panels and lidar sits atop a Waymo all-electric Jaguar I-Pace SUV in San Francisco, on Aug. 20, 2021. The systems help the autonomous vehicles navigate their environment. (Nathan Frandino/Reuters)

Czarnecki says as autonomous vehicles are trained on more data, they get better at detecting obscured objects like snow-covered signs. But he says autonomous systems still struggle to make sense of them more than a human would.
Other drivers also change their behaviour when snow flies, Czarnecki says, making autonomous vehicles more likely to get "confused" by their actions or those of pedestrians.
Adjusting to those kinds of elements takes time, as Czarnecki says the vehicles will need to be tested and fine-tuned in those environments.
"The more challenging the weather, the more challenging the engineering."
That's why some autonomous cars already on the road in Canada don't run in poor weather.

U.S. startup Gatik, for example, which runs 50 self-driving trucks for Loblaws in the Toronto area, can drive day or night and handle complex driving situations. But it draws the line at heavy rain or snow.
Loblaws using self-driving delivery trucks
Is Waymo winter-ready?

Steve Waslander, a researcher at the University of Toronto who's been studying how autonomous vehicles function in wintery conditions, says those hurdles are big, but not insurmountable. What's needed are engineering solutions, including more data gathered by driving cars in poor weather which the Waymo system can be trained on.
"All of the existing techniques for detection, tracking, prediction, for planning, for control — they can all be applied," Waslander said.
"You just have to know that you're in these conditions and include that training information in the way you build the system."

Waymo has been testing its tech in snow-filled regions, like upstate New York and Michigan's Upper Peninsula. The company is also fully operating in Denver, Colo., and is conducting tests in colder, more northern U.S. cities like Minneapolis and Detroit.

According to the Waymo website, the company has logged tens of thousands of hours driving in snowy weather. The data from those blustery trips is used to train its autonomous driver system — the latest iteration of which has more than 100 million miles of autonomous driving experience — to adapt to all kinds of conditions.

"Today, we operate at below-freezing temperatures in the U.S., including with frost and hail, and we’re validating our system to navigate harsher weather conditions," Waymo said in an emailed statement to CBC News.
A resident attempts to unclog a few storm drains on a flooded street as a driverless Waymo taxi passes in the background, on Nov. 22, 2024, in San Francisco. (Associated Press)

Still, more winter driving data is needed. Waymo's product lead for weather told The Verge in 2025 that snowy conditions often made up less than five per cent of total driving data, though the company was using AI methods to augment and make progress on winter driving capabilities despite that.

Waslander says with the expansions into so many other snowy markets will help collect that data. When Waymo arrives in a new city, Waslander says it usually deploys a fleet of 50 to 100 vehicles to map a city in all kinds of conditions.
Waymo robotaxis now way safer than human drivers: report
"If they do that across [multiple] different cities, you know, the percentage of weather conditions that are adverse will continue to grow," Waslander said.

Aside from the data, Waymo uses heaters and mini windshield wipers to keep its cameras clear and sensors ice-free. And while cars are out on the road, they act like "mobile weather stations" according to the company, collecting data about whether the weather is foggy, rainy or something else, and sharing that with the rest of the fleet so other cars can use that up-to-date information.
Still, as of August 2025, Waymo told a tech publication that it hadn't "validated the Waymo driver" to operate completely without a driver in snowy conditions.
But Waymo doesn't plan to deploy its ride-hailing service in Toronto until 2028, which Waslander says he expects will give the company enough time to problem-solve winter-related issues.

items: Waymo to launch first phase of driverless taxi testing in Toronto
Waymo’s driverless cars involved in 68% fewer crashes than human drivers, U.S. study finds

blocks.text: Czarnecki expects a phased approach might also be possible, where autonomous cars operating while conditions are good but shut down in bad conditions at first, and gradually stay functional in poorer and poorer weather as the system improves.
That's not unlike what the company has done during extreme weather events such as heavy rain in other cities where it's already operating, pulling service when road conditions are particularly bad.
"I see this as a process that will take … a number of years," Czarnecki said.

items: Self-driving cars know the rules of the road — but not rules of humanity

blocks.text: ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Can AI be regulated? Why experts say government intervention is needed — but could be tricky
articles.summary: As concerns mount over incidents of AI agents going rogue, the push from experts and stakeholders have been growing for government regulation of AI systems that are becoming increasingly capable. But…

image.caption: A protestor supporting restrictions on artificial intelligence holds up a sign at a rally before a New York City Council hearing on artificial intelligence safety. Experts and stakeholders have been calling for regulation of the rapidly developing technology following a series of incidents of AI age

blocks.text: As concerns mount over incidents of AI agents going rogue, experts and stakeholders are increasingly pushing for government regulation of AI systems that are becoming more capable.
But some experts say the need for global co-operation and the rapid pace of AI development could make that difficult.

While some, like U.S. President Donald Trump, say they have faith that tech giants can police themselves, other industry leaders, like Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, and Canadian-British artificial intelligence pioneer Geoffrey Hinton say AI requires safeguards that go beyond self-regulation.

Given that most other industries, such as food or aviation, have some type of government oversight, it only makes sense that AI would as well, said Jaxson Khan, an expert in AI policy and adoption at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs.
"In no major industry, do we let companies completely police themselves, whether it's in oil and gas or people who want to produce food and candy or nuclear energy," he said.

items: Bill Gates joins call for AI safeguards, wants to discuss concerns with Trump
Is AI evolving too fast? A look at the debate on slowing it down

blocks.text: "Having such a powerful technology be entirely in private hands, at least without supervision, that seems highly strange given the rest of how our economy and regulatory systems work."
In an interview with CBC News Network last month, Hinton suggested that oversight could be handled by an official agency similar to the Food and Drug Administration in the U.S.

"You can't just produce a drug and market it in America. You have to persuade the FDA that your drug is safe, or rather does more good than harm, and the companies are responsible for doing that," he said.
"So we certainly need something at least that strong for AI. We should have independent people evaluating it, and we should force the companies to satisfy those evaluators before they release it."
Trump is 'ill-advised' about artificial intelligence, says 'godfather' of AI
Hard for governments to keep up
A significant challenge to regulating AI is how quickly models change and improve, Khan said.

A recent Anthropic report said its agents' capabilities double roughly every four months. There's also growing evidence that some AI models have the ability to recursively self-improve, meaning they can build and design their own successors, the report says.
"I don't think we've ever had an incredibly powerful technology with this velocity of change," he said.
That makes it difficult for governments to keep up, said Manon Paquet, associate director of policy at McGill's Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy.
"It's very hard to regulate something first that you don't fully understand yet," Paquet said.

"I'm a former public servant. I pity my colleagues — my former colleagues in Ottawa — trying to wrestle with those issues because it's changing so fast that the time it takes to put forward regulations or legislation, then the problem's already evolved to something else."
Why slowing the AI race won't be easy
Global oversight
Some experts and leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have called for a global, non-industry body to oversee and mitigate the technology's risks internationally.

Earlier this week, around 400 scientists, including Hinton and fellow AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio, called for an international body ​to oversee containment standards and incident reporting for advanced cyber-capable ‌AI systems.
The proposed body would maintain a registry of significant security incidents, which the scientists said should eventually be made ​public.

While it might be difficult to get countries to agree on how to govern AI, such a body could help countries work together to "shore up our respective systems" and create safeguards against potential misuse of AI, Khan said.
"I think stability is really important here, even if we don't get to a perfect model of global governance," he said.

items: Why major countries can't agree on how to regulate artificial intelligence

blocks.text: But with most AI development coming out of the United States and China, those countries would have to commit to participating in such a body and adhering to its rules for it to be useful, said Olivier Blais, vice-president of artificial intelligence at Montreal consulting firm Moov AI.
"If we're not able to convince the countries where the AI systems get produced, I think the impact might be limited," he said.
However, such a body could help develop international guidelines for safe AI development, he said.

"It's important to understand the components of a safe AI system or what are the areas that need to be restrained … and a global organization could lead on the work and could build that foundation," he said.

Last month, the U.S. and China agreed to hold a dialog on the technology's risks and benefits, with the next round of discussions set for November, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House said.
In a separate statement, the Chinese ministry said the two sides should step up exchanges and work toward consensus in line with new developments as AI technology continues to advance.
AI regulation in Canada

Currently, there is no overarching federal regulation of AI in Canada, but the Liberal government's proposed Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, sets out criteria for AI chatbots, including the obligation to reduce the risk of their services generating harmful content.
Carney also recently announced a new national council on artificial intelligence meant to provide the government with guidance for its AI strategy and on making the technology safer.
However, it may prove "very, very challenging" for any federal legislation to be effective given that many of the world's largest AI companies aren't based here, Paquet said.

items: Ottawa launches new national AI council to advise on safety, deployment
Canada is investing $150M to make AI safer. Will it work?

blocks.text: But Blais said that even if the federal government can't control how these companies operate, it could establish policies that requiring them to report incidents that affect Canadians and hold them accountable. In extreme cases, the government could even block access in Canada to AI platforms it deems too harmful, he added.
"At least I think if we're able to record the different incidents, report on them, I think it's a major step forward because at least we can educate citizens and we demonstrate leadership," he said.

articles.title: 1 in 4 Ebola deaths are children in Democratic Republic of Congo's worst outbreak
articles.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo is battling its deadliest outbreak of Ebola, caused by a rare strain with no approved treatment. With children losing parents, facing an estimated 60 per cent…

image.caption: Congolese medical workers dressed in personal protective equipment carry children tested for Ebola inside a secured Ebola response zone in Bunia, D.R.C., on June 9. An estimated 1,900 children have been separated from their caregivers because of the disease. (Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters)

blocks.text: Health·New

The Democratic Republic of Congo is battling its deadliest outbreak of Ebola, caused by a rare strain with no approved treatment. With children losing parents, facing an estimated 60 per cent fatality rate and making up more than a quarter of deaths, experts say children are taking the brunt of the disease.
With more than 9,200 confirmed cases and 4,400 deaths, children are vulnerable 'on so many levels'
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 17, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago
Outside of a treatment centre for Ebola in a northeastern corner of the Democratic Republic of Congo, as the country battles its worst outbreak on record, Neema Nyaloka bounces a baby on her lap.
Nyaloka survived Ebola herself. Now, she works with UNICEF to take care of the droves of children isolating from their parents who are being treated for it.

UNICEF is operating 12 other child-care centres next to treatment centres full of Ebola patients. Some kids are waiting for their parents to recover, but others have been left stranded after family members passed away.
"We have children that are completely orphans, so they lost both parents," Lucia Elmi, director of global emergency programs at UNICEF, said last week.
It's estimated that at least 1,900 children have been separated from their caregivers because of Ebola.

It's just one more way that children are bearing the brunt of an outbreak which has spread to at least seven provinces in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and outstripped the 2018-2020 outbreak to become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in Congo's history.
As of Oct. 15, more than 9,200 cases have been confirmed, while deaths have surpassed 4,400, according to the latest numbers from the D.R.C.'s public health institute.

More than a quarter of those deaths are children. Although most cases are among adults, children have a much higher fatality rate, at 60 per cent compared to 40 per cent for adults, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates.
Children walk by posters warning people about Ebola on June 24 in Goma, Democratic Republic of Congo. (Daniel Buuma/Getty Images)
"Children are really impacted by Ebola on so many levels," Amy Mina, a project leader from Canada with Save the Children, told CBC News.
"Sixty-one per cent of the children who died of Ebola are under the age of five."
'Fighting for your life'
Children in the region already face high levels of malnutrition and displacement due to ongoing armed conflict.
The Ituri province in northeastern Congo, where Mina works, is where the outbreak began, and is still the heaviest-hit region, accounting for 73 per cent of cases.

items: Congo's Ebola outbreak surpasses 4,000 deaths amid violence and mistrust
As Congo Ebola deaths pass 3,000, officials seek to track spread via mobile data
Schools reopen despite concerns amid Congo's Ebola outbreak

blocks.text: Save the Children works with schools and communities to provide supplies and training for staff to recognize symptoms among their students. Every morning since schools opened, the temperatures of every teacher and student are checked as part of this work.

But attendance has dropped, Mina says, because many parents worry schools could be transmission sites. They're also avoiding seeking treatment at the hospital for their children for other health issues out of fear of Ebola.

"Children aren't only dying of Ebola," Mina said. "We are seeing a drop in the number of families and children visiting health centres … and children die of malaria, and dysentery and respiratory diseases."
Cholera is also seeing a rise in the west of the country, with more than 51,000 suspected cases reported since the beginning of 2026.

A 13-year-old student washes her hands outside her school in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Save the Children is working with schools during the Ebola outbreak, supplying infection-prevention kits and training teachers to counter misinformation about the disease. (Submitted/Save the Children)

When children contract Ebola, they have to be entirely isolated to combat the disease just like adults are, interacting only with caretakers dressed head to toe in fully protective gear, which can be terrifying for kids, experts say.

Children are already vulnerable to viruses, with fewer reserves to fight off loss of fluids from illness, says Dr. Joanne Liu, director of the Pandemic and Emergency Readiness Lab at the School of Population and Global Health at McGill University. Liu, a pediatric emergency physician, led emergency responses during the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak in west Africa.
"Can you imagine fighting for your life on your own without your parents?" she said. "We know that that kind of isolation … creates emotional stress, agitation and irritability in the children."
Fractured response
Amid the surge in Ebola, pregnant women are also avoiding clinics, missing prenatal care and choosing to deliver their babies at home.
The UN says, compared to last year, maternal deaths in the region have nearly doubled.
And most deaths from Ebola are happening outside of treatment centres, meaning medical workers can't fully track the chains of transmission to stop them.

"They're dying at home, which represents a huge opportunity for more transmission because they're being cared for by their family, their community members," said Stephanie Hoffmann, a project co-ordinator with Doctors Without Borders in North Kivu, D.R.C.

items: Canada extends Ebola travel restrictions for another 30 days
Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo: What's going on and why is the outbreak so alarming?

blocks.text: Part of the reason this has gotten so "out of control," she said, is because of the gutting of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), a foreign aid program dismantled in 2025 due to alleged inefficiency and wasteful spending, according to the Trump administration. Researchers have estimated that the shuttering of services has already caused the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people worldwide.
Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo’s history

When USAID was operating in the region, cases of Ebola were detected earlier on, Hoffman said, allowing for tracking and isolating. But with less funding and support, cases had already spread dangerously far by the time the outbreak was official.
"I can't say that with the current response, there's going to be an end in sight."
The U.S. announced Friday that it had struck a new deal to supply some of the world's poorest nations with maternal and child health supplies, including Congo, through UNICEF.
Rare strain has no treatment
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain — a rare strain of Ebola for which there is no approved treatment or vaccine, although clinical trials are underway.
Congo's deadly Ebola surge is second only to the 2014-2016 outbreak in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, which killed more than 11,000 people.

Two volunteers wearing personal protective equipment carry the coffin of a three-year-old child, presumed to have died of Ebola virus disease, in Bunia, D.R.C., on June 11. (Benediction Murhabazi/AFP/Getty Images)
And it's affecting other regions as well. So far, two people have died of the virus in neighbouring Uganda, which declared itself Ebola free in August.

Three cases in Kenya are linked to Congo's outbreak — authorities confirmed the third patient on Friday, adding that she is a close relative of the first and second cases. The first case was a Kenyan man who died in early October in Kenya after returning from travelling in Congo.

items: Kenya confirms 2nd case of Ebola in relative of patient who died earlier this month
Kenya confirms 1st Ebola case imported from Congo

blocks.text: Aid groups say while more treatment centres and funding are badly needed to address the health needs in the Democratic Republic of Congo, so is building trust and education.

"There's a lot of mistrust about the response in general," Hoffmann said. "People have a lot of mistrust and a lot of fear about how they'll be treated in a treatment centre. There is a lack of education and awareness about what happens to the body when you have Ebola, what happens in a treatment centre."
It's another battle health-care workers on the ground are fighting, as they desperately try to save lives.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Tashauna Reid is a senior reporter and covers the latest in health for CBC News. Her focus is on stories that impact the lives of Canadians and delivering the information they need to lead healthier and better lives. Tashauna is a regular contributor to CBC's The National, CBC News Network and CBC Radio. Since 2009, she has been working on-camera and behind the scenes at Canada’s public broadcaster.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: This West Bank teen feared he wouldn't survive the year. Now, he's dead
articles.summary: Omar Nassan was a student at a West Bank school where a gunman, later identified as an Israeli military reservist, opened fire this spring, killing two Palestinians. Half a year later, Omar himself…

image.caption: CBC News interviewed 17-year-old West Bank resident Omar Nassan in the village of Al Mughayyir in April, after an Israeli army reservist killed two students at his school. (CBC)

blocks.text: World

Omar Nassan was a student at a West Bank school where a gunman, later identified as an Israeli military reservist, opened fire this spring, killing two Palestinians. Half a year later, Omar himself died in a melee involving the Israeli Defence Forces.
Omar Nassan, 17, spoke to CBC News in April and was killed amid violence in September

The cemetery in the West Bank village of Al Mughayyir is dotted with burial sites draped with the Palestinian flag, marking the graves of local men and boys killed in clashes over the years with Israeli settlers and Israeli security forces.
It was one of the places 17-year-old Omar Nassan insisted that CBC News visit back in April.
