Omar was a student at the local boys' school where a gunman, later identified as an Israeli military reservist, opened fire this spring, killing two Palestinians: 32-year-old Jihad Abu Naim and 14-year-old Aws al-Nassan. Both now lay in that small cemetery overlooking hills, fields and a busy roadway.

items: 2 Palestinians, including 14-year-old, killed in Israeli settler attack in West Bank: health officials

blocks.text: Omar and Aws had been good friends, and he talked about life in Al Mughayyir with a deep sense of frustration and fatalism.
It can’t get more dangerous.Omar Nassan

"To be honest, I didn’t tell this to anyone … but I already accepted death. I’m going to be dead," Omar said. "I lost my friend and he’s not the first first friend I lose, whether it’s getting killed or in prison. He’s not the first or the last friend I lose, so I already accept death. I’m going to be next."
Omar said many young men in the village felt the same way. The stress of life in the Occupied West Bank, combined with the constant threat of violence, had worn them down.
"It can’t get more dangerous," he said. "We’re used to that now. It’s our life."
Omar’s words on that April afternoon proved tragically prescient.

The cemetery in the village of Al Mughayyir is dotted with burial sites draped with the Palestinian flag, marking the graves of local men and boys killed in clashes with Israeli settlers and Israeli security forces. (CBC)
A violent night

On the evening of Sept. 2, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) deployed troops to Al Mughayyir to back up Israeli police responding to a disturbance over missing livestock. Palestinian villagers routinely accuse Israeli settlers of stealing sheep and allowing their own flocks to graze on Palestinian land.

items: Prosecutors charge Israeli settler for killing Palestinian activist in West Bank
Gunman kills 1, wounds 5 in drive-by attacks in Israel near West Bank border

blocks.text: The IDF says it was brought in to retrieve animals owned by Israeli civilians when a violent riot broke out. In a statement, the military says soldiers encountered what it calls "terrorists" hurling cinderblocks and stones. The soldiers fired on what the IDF calls "key instigators" and that "hits were identified."
Two young Palestinians died that night: 16-year-old Khalil Abu Alia and 17-year-old Omar Nassan.

Omar’s family says he was shot just outside their home in Al Mughayyir. His father, Mohammad Nassan, says his son was struck by three bullets and managed to stumble a few steps before crumpling to the ground. He says an ambulance took his son to hospital but medics were unable to save his life.
"My back is broken," Nassan said of his son’s death, in an interview with CBC News. "He helped me in every detail of my life. "
Omar Nassan's parents, Mohammad and Rania, say their son was struck by three bullets during a melee between Israeli Defence Forces and Palestinian protesters in September. (CBC)
Omar’s mother, Rania, says her son loved to eat, did well at school and had a natural talent for working with computers. Omar learned English, she says, at school in her native country, Egypt.

On the night Omar died, Rania Nassan says she heard screaming and chanting outside her home and rushed to lock the door. She says Omar ran after her and begged her to let him go downstairs to see what was happening.
She relented.
"I opened the door and told him to take care of himself," she said. "And that was it."
As the melee in the street continued, Rania says she began receiving text messages from neighours saying Omar had been injured. Women from the village eventually came to tell her that he was dead.
"I felt that my soul was separated," Rania said, describing that moment. "I felt like the mountains would not bear the news."
Before and after Oct. 7

Rania says Omar was deeply affected by the loss of his friend in the school shooting in April. He confided to her his feelings that he could be the next to die. She regrets not talking to him more about it.
Palestinian youth are seen on the streets of Al Mughayyir. (CBC)
The Nassan family believes Omar was shot by an IDF sniper soon after he left his home. The IDF won’t confirm that.

As for the shooting at the school in April, the IDF says the case is currently under review by the Military Advocate General’s Corps, but won’t say whether the review or its ruling will be made public.

Marzouq Abu Naim, whose son Jihad was killed in the school attack, is a member of the Al Mughayyir Village Council. By his count, Israeli settlers and Israeli security forces have killed 11 people in the community, eight of them under the age of 18.
The United Nations Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs lists nine Palestinian deaths in Al Mughayyir since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
Abu Naim says after that attack, in which more than 1,200 Israelis were killed and 251 taken hostage, the IDF began treating people in his village far more harshly.

"Before October 7, the army would keep us apart when there was a problem between the settlers and us," he said. "After October 7, we wished that the army would not come. Because if the army came, the problem would be more difficult. The army sprays tear gas at us and the army shoots."
Abu Naim's son is buried in Al Mughayyir's cemetery. Half a year after showing it to CBC News, Omar Nassan is buried there, too.
Omar's father says the family is planning to install a monument to remember him, but for now, it's just a simple gravesite draped, like others in the cemetery, with a Palestinian flag.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Tom Parry is a senior reporter for CBC News on Parliament Hill. He has been with the CBC since 1990 and has been based in Ottawa, Montreal, Quebec City, Vancouver, Regina, Toronto and London, England.

articles.title: Young people want to know if they're neurodivergent. Here's what doctors say is going on
articles.summary: Mental health experts say they're seeing an increasing number of young patients leaning on advice from social media to connect symptoms to a potential diagnosis, even before consulting with a…

image.caption: Mental health experts say they aren't against patients researching symptoms before a consultation, but say patients may need additional evaluation. (Shutterstock / wavebreakmedia)

blocks.text: White Coat, Black Art·THE DOSE

Mental health experts say they're seeing an increasing number of young patients leaning on advice from social media to connect symptoms to a potential diagnosis, even before consulting with a physician. While, they say they aren’t against patients getting information from online sources, they caution against treating symptoms without professional oversight.
Social media contributing to noticeable spread of patients keen on neurodivergent labels, expert say
LISTEN | Why some people want psychiatric labels:
The Dose20:07Psychiatric labels — why some people want one!
Alberta resident Amy Brandley was diagnosed with ADHD in her youth, but despite receiving treatment, she felt she had symptoms not explained by the diagnosis.
Brandley says she consulted with mental health specialists throughout her childhood for things like not being able to control her emotions, but her concerns were always chalked up to ADHD.

The 27-year-old artist says it wasn't until she saw videos of young women talking about their mental health on social media that she started to make sense of things. Experiences she thought were unique to her — like sensory overload — pointed to a potential explanation: She may be autistic, too.
"It was both a long journey, but also a few sparks here and there of seeing this content and being like, that seems rather familiar, that seems rather relatable," said Brandley.

Alberta artist Amy Brandley was diagnosed with ADHD as a child. It wasn't until her early 20s, after coming across videos on social media, that she considered the root of some of her personal struggles may have been connected to undiagnosed autism. (Submitted by Amy Brandley)
After meeting with an autism expert and undergoing a battery of tests, Brandley was diagnosed with both ADHD and autism spectrum disorder.

Mental health experts say they're seeing an increasing number of young patients, like Brandley, leaning on advice from social media to connect symptoms to a potential diagnosis, even before consulting with a physician.
While, they say they aren’t against patients getting information from online sources, they caution against treating symptoms without professional oversight.
Neurodivergence leading the conversation
Ottawa child psychiatrist Dr. Gail Beck says she's used to patients coming to therapy with concerns about conditions like depression and anxiety.
Over the past decade, however, she's noticed that young people — especially women — are increasingly asking about autism and ADHD.
“One of the things that's … very different, is the number of young people who come to me and tell me that they're neurodiverse," Beck told Dr. Brian Goldman, host of The Dose podcast.
Toronto psychiatrist Dr. Doron Almagor says patients who were never diagnosed as children may see examples of neurodivergence on social media and find that something just clicks.
More than 67,500 Ontario kids waiting for core autism funding as demand grows
Boys are more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD and autism than girls, in part because girls are more likely to mask their symptoms, says Almagor, a former president of the Canadian ADHD Alliance
“They would … try not to cause any trouble, not get in trouble, try to do their work and not get diagnosed with either ADHD or autism.”

People often imagine children with ADHD as class disruptors, unable to sit still or pay attention. While that stereotype can be true, research suggests it’s more often boys who get identified for exhibiting hyperactive symptoms. Girls with ADHD are more often identified for showing the inattentive symptoms associated with the condition.

Likewise, boys with autism may exhibit symptoms like withdrawn social behaviour or blunt, literal communication, whereas research suggests girls might be surrounded by peers but still feel unable to meaningfully connect.
It's OK to look up your symptoms, but be open to being wrong
Beck says she notices her patients typically start to question their mental health around middle and high school, sometimes going to the web for answers.
So when patients come to her having already researched their symptoms — even pitching certain diagnoses — the first thing Beck does is ask them to share their research with her.
"And if they tell me ‘I got it on TikTok, I'm on a group on Instagram,’ whatever they tell me, I will look it up and often with them in the office," she said.
"I want to see where they're getting this information."

items: The mental health of young men is declining. Experts warn it could get worse
Kids and young adults are addicted to screens. New research argues it may be a public health concern

blocks.text: Once Beck knows more about where her patients have researched their condition, she guides them through the consultation, trying her best to correct any misinformation along the way.
Likewise, Montreal psychiatrist Dr. Alexandre Hudon says social media is an everyday part of life, so clinicians can't minimize its influence on how people examine their symptoms.

"It can be really rich because you can open [them] up and really, really try to get a better sense of how they ended up using this information to put labels on their life," said Hudon, who researches how social media and artificial intelligence influence youth mental health.

Not only do these conversations help clinicians learn more about their patients, being open-minded about where patients get their information also helps clinicians guide their patients to more accurate diagnoses, says Hudon.
Nonetheless, Almagor cautions that not all online sources of information are equal.

"One of the talks that I give to the public is trying to guide them to finding social media influencers that are in fact valid, reliable, are able to give good information," said Almagor. He notes that some influencers who present as neutral could be paid content creators capitalizing on the mental health distress of others.
He says patients also need to be open to formal diagnostic evaluations for their conditions, especially if their symptoms point to other reasons for their distress.
Use of AI for health questions also increasing
Of course, people aren't just leaning on social media for mental health guidance.

Some polls suggest almost half of respondents have turned to artificial intelligence chatbots for medical advice, so it's perhaps no surprise that young people are turning to sources like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for mental health help.
Almagor says AI chatbots can be useful, but adds they can often make mistakes because they lack lived human experiences.
Manitoba plans an AI chatbot youth ban. This school already uses them
"Across medicine, you need to be very careful in taking any AI chatbot as medical advice," he said.

Amy Brandley — who sometimes shares about her journey to diagnosis on her own social media channels — says she thinks people rely a little too much on chatbots. She says people are better off learning from each other rather than machines.
"Even if it's just like some person who has like 300 followers on TikTok sharing their experience, I think that's more valuable than what an AI can tell you,” she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sameer Chhabra is an associate producer with CBC's White Coat, Black Art radio show and The Dose podcast. He was previously an associate producer with CBC News: The National's talk team. Drop a line at sameer.chhabra@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Zaldy Co's ex-bodyguards slapped with fresh arrest warrants
articles.summary: A number of former House lawmaker Zaldy Co"s alleged former bodyguards were served new arrest warrants from Zambales and Surigao.

blocks.text: MALETA BOYS
Published October 17, 2026 3:25pm
A number of former House lawmaker Zaldy Co’s alleged former bodyguards were served new arrest warrants from Zambales and Surigao.
In a video report from GMA News Reporter John Consulta, several of the ex-bodyguards were already meant to be released from the San Juan City police station.
Lawyer Levito Baligod and four former bodyguards were already able to post bail after being detained for alleged unjust vexation, leaving 10 other former bodyguards detained.
However, three of those who were released alongside Baligod voluntarily surrendered to police after being served with another warrant from a court in Iba, Zambales.
While the media was awaiting the release of the bodyguards, another arrest warrant reportedly came. This time, the warrant was from the province of Surigao.
The camp of the ex-bodyguards have yet to receive a copy of the arrest warrant.

The men detained in the San Juan police station are part of the 18 former bodyguards who previously claimed that they delivered suitcases filled with cash to several personalities, including President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.
However, four of these former bodyguards have since recanted their allegations.
Meanwhile, Co, who is tagged as the mastermind in the flood control scheme, is believed to be hiding from Philippine authorities in Europe. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Lawmaker seeks Chinese envoy’s expulsion over embassy’s ‘stop bluffing’ taunt
articles.summary: A lawmaker called for the expulsion of Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan after the Chinese Embassy in Manila dared Philippine officials pushing to declare him persona non grata to “STOP…

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 3:21pm

MANILA, Philippines — A lawmaker called for the expulsion of Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan after the Chinese Embassy in Manila dared Philippine officials pushing to declare him persona non grata to “STOP BLUFFING.”
Akbayan party-list Rep. Perci Cendaña criticized the embassy’s remark, calling the Chinese envoy an arrogant and unwelcome visitor.
“NAPAKAYABANG NA BWISITA,” Cendaña said in a post on X on Saturday, October 17.
“Hanggang kailan ba natin ito titiisin? Dapat nang paalisin itong Chinese ambassador,” he added.
(What an arrogant, obnoxious visitor. How long are we going to put up with this? This Chinese ambassador should be sent home.)

The embassy issued the statement after some senators and House representatives proposed declaring Jing persona non grata, a diplomatic measure that would designate him as unwelcome in the Philippines and call for his departure.

“Some senators and house representatives are talking about declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata. Is this threat or coercion? But anyway, just do it. Otherwise, STOP BLUFFING,” the embassy said in a Facebook post.
Marcos wants to discuss envoy’s remarks
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. also said he wanted to discuss Jing’s remarks with the ambassador, saying they sounded like a threat and that he wanted to understand what the envoy meant.

“It sounds very much to me like a threat, and it is not a very diplomatic statement to be made. So we perhaps would like to understand what exactly it is that he means,” Marcos told reporters on Friday.
“I think that deserves a discussion between the ambassador and myself,” he said when asked if he would summon Jing.
China envoy’s remarks draw backlash
The calls to expel Jing came after he drew criticism for saying China could easily win a conflict with the Philippines if it chose to use force, although he said Beijing would not resort to it.
“If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force, and we love peace,” Jing told reporters in Manila on Thursday after delivering a speech at a school.

Jing made the remarks a day after Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro called China a regional “troublemaker.” The ambassador dismissed the characterization as “nonsense” and accused Manila of harassing Chinese workers and teachers, without citing specific examples.

The Department of Foreign Affairs said Jing’s remarks appeared to convey a “thinly veiled threat” of the use of force and were “hardly helpful” given the complicated relations between Manila and Beijing.
Philippine Coast Guard spokesman Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela also called the statement a “direct threat,” citing encounters between Filipino and Chinese personnel in disputed waters.
Hontiveros seeks apology, backs possible expulsion

Sen. Risa Hontiveros also called for accountability over Jing’s remarks, describing them as “gray zone aggression in diplomatic form” intended to intimidate and coerce the Philippines without escalating to open conflict.
“Let it be clear to China that no threat will make us surrender what is rightfully ours,” Hontiveros said in a Facebook statement.
The senator said the Philippines had defended its rights through legal and diplomatic means.
“An ambassador who threatens his host country has crossed a line. Summoning him is not enough,” she said.
Hontiveros urged the government to demand a formal retraction and apology from Beijing, adding that Jing should be declared persona non grata if China refuses.
She also called on the government to raise the matter before the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the United Nations General Assembly.
“When one nation is threatened, every member-state that values international law is threatened too,” Hontiveros said.
“China must be held accountable for these words, as she must be for her actions in our waters,” she added.

China claims most of the South China Sea, including waters within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone. A 2016 arbitral ruling invalidated the legal basis of Beijing’s expansive maritime claims under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

articles.title: Why House prosecutors are betting 'all-in' on Article II in VP Sara impeachment
articles.summary: Following the House prosecution"s decision to drop three out of four Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte, House prosecutor Manila 3rd District Representative Joel Chua said…

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 3:14pm

Following the House prosecution’s decision to drop three out of four Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte, House prosecutor Manila 3rd District Representative Joel Chua said Saturday the panel is betting everything on Article II alone, because it's easier to understand for the public.
“Dito po sa’aming naging desisyon ito po ay pinagaralan namin at sa tingin namin ang article na ito ang pinakamadaling maunawaan ng ating mga kababayan,” he added.
Article II refers to the alleged undeclared and unexplained wealth of the Vice President.

“Mas minarapat namin na mag-focus na lang sa isang article which is ‘yung Article II —‘yung unexplained wealth. Ito po ‘yung huling article na amin pong piniresenta ang mga testigo,” Chua said at a news forum in Quezon City.
Echoing House lead prosecutor Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville Luistro, the lawmaker said, “All-in, itaya na po dito [Article II].”

The prosecution dropped Article I on confidential funds, Article III on bribery, and Article IV on assassination plot, grave threats and inciting to sedition against Duterte after a week of testimonies from the Anti-Money Laundering Council, bank and insurance firm officials, as well as lawyer and accountant Alexander Cabrera ultimately concluding that the Vice President and her husband accumulated unexplained wealth worth P817 million at the least and P1.5 billion at the most.
'Legal strategy'

Chua explained that dropping the three articles of impeachment was part of the House prosecution’s “legal strategy” as they have seen that the defense is planning to prolong the impeachment until next year.
“Kaya minarapat [namin] na mag focus na lamang sa isang article,” he said.
The House prosecutor said that their team is expecting the impeachment process to wrap up “by end of November or at least, at the latest, first week of December.”

However, defense lead counsel Sheila Sison said the prosecution’s decision to drop three of the four Articles of Impeachment against Duterte would not affect the defense panel’s presentation of its own evidence.

“We respect the decision of the prosecution. However, whether this will affect how the defense plans to proceed with its presentation of evidence is something that we must make clear: It will not,” Sison said.

“Because the prosecution cannot make decisions for the respondent and the defense. In other words, the prosecution cannot be allowed to have the benefit of its accusations without bearing the burden of having those accusations tested,” she added.
The House of Representatives impeached Duterte last May 2026 on allegations of culpable violation of the Constitution, graft and corruption, betrayal of public trust, bribery, and other high crimes.
The Senate impeachment court began the trial on July 6. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in Gaza
articles.summary:
Families have been scattered, fathers separated from their children, and couples unable to reunite and marry

Wijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leave Gaza in November 2023 with her eight…

blocks.text: Wijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leave Gaza in November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment, while her injured husband, Hatem, remained behind.

Wijdan and her family were living in the Nuseirat refugee camp when the Gaza war began with the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Ten days later, on 17 October that year, an Israeli strike hit the al-Muhandseen tower, near their home, injuring Wijdan and every member of her family.

“We were sitting together, just about to start lunch when the bombing happened,” Wijdan recalled. “The ceiling collapsed over our heads. Everything went dark. I couldn’t see anything. I just started screaming the names of my sons and daughters.”

Her daughter Nour, 15, suffered the most serious injuries, including a fractured skull and bleeding in the brain. Five-year-old Amna suffered severe burns to her chest. The family was initially separated after the strike.
Nour spent about 33 days in intensive care, with Wijdan by her side. Amna and Aysel, three and a half, were at a different hospital for 15 days.

blocks.caption: Aysel, who incurred severe burns in the bombing, holds up a photograph of her father. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian

blocks.text: On 30 November 2023, Wijdan travelled with Nour to a hospital in Egypt for treatment. For months, the family remained scattered across Egypt, receiving medical treatment and staying with other relatives.
“I felt completely helpless,” Wijdan said. “There was a fire in my heart because I was away from my husband and my family was scattered.”

Eventually, Wijdan managed to bring her children together in an apartment in Egypt. Three years on, however, she is still separated from her husband, who remains in Gaza. “I have become both the mother and the father to my children,” she said. “The responsibility is exhausting me, and I am constantly worried about my husband.”

Hatem suffered a serious leg injury that limits his mobility and is now displaced in a tent in Nuseirat. Even speaking to him is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection. “When he manages to get online, he calls me and the children. He tells me, ‘I am counting the days until I can see you again.’ I can see the tears in his eyes,” Wijdan says.

blocks.caption: Speaking to Hatem is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection, Wijdan says.  Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian

blocks.text: Wijdan has no regular source of income and relies on donations. Hatem stopped receiving a salary 10 months ago and his injury prevents him from working.

In Egypt, life is difficult for Wijdan and her family. She says she cannot afford transportation to send five of her children to school. “I see my children’s future slipping away in front of me, and there is nothing I can do.”
Nour still requires medical treatment, but Wijdan often cannot afford her medication. She sometimes considers returning to Gaza to be with Hatem, but fears exposing her children to further suffering.

“I dream of getting my children the treatment they need, and I hope we can reunite with my husband as soon as possible so he can also receive treatment,” Wijdan said. “I cannot carry all of this alone. Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war.”

blocks.caption: ‘Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war,’ says Wijdan Abu Matar. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian

blocks.text: Since the war began with Hamas’s attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry. Earlier this year an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continues to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
Sami Abu Tabaq, a 29-year-old Palestinian photojournalist, was forced to leave the Gaza Strip in April 2024, leaving behind his family and his fiancee, Ola.
“Loneliness kills me every day,” he said. “Life away from the woman I love and my family is incredibly hard. I’m desperately waiting for the day God brings us together again.”

Sami became engaged to Ola five months before the war began. They had met by chance when he chose her family’s home as a location for a photoshoot. Before the war, they saw each other constantly. They went to the sea, had dinner at restaurants in Gaza, and spent months preparing the house where they planned to live after their wedding, which was scheduled for November 2023.

Sami and his family fled their home in Tal al-Zaatar, Jabaliya, early on in the war. Their home was badly damaged and later destroyed, along with the house Sami and Ola had been planning to move into once they got married.
When his sister decided to flee south with her children, Sami accompanied her but he could not reach Ola to say goodbye.

The separation became unbearable. Days, sometimes weeks, passed without Sami knowing whether Ola was alive. Once, he saw reports that an entire residential block near her home in Gaza City had been bombed. “I almost lost my mind. I had never felt so helpless,” he said. Unable to return north, he asked his brother to check on her. Eventually, his brother confirmed that she and her family were alive.

Sami continued working as a photojournalist from southern Gaza. Four journalists who had shared his tent were later killed, including Hamza al-Dahdouh, a son of the Al Jazeera journalist Wael al-Dahdouh.

As Israel threatened a ground invasion of Rafah in 2024, Ola began urging Sami to leave Gaza, fearing he would be killed. Sami paid a company coordinating exits at the time for both of them to cross into Egypt. But Ola could not reach southern Gaza to travel through Rafah. “She told me, ‘You go, and I’ll follow you,’” Sami said. “And here we are, still waiting, nearly two and a half years later.” They still have not managed to get married.

By his second day in Egypt, Sami was overwhelmed by guilt. “The overthinking kills me,” he said. “I felt ashamed to turn on the lights or eat proper food while my fiancee and my family were struggling to find the most basic things.”

In Egypt, his life has become dominated by loneliness and sleeplessness. “There is safety in Egypt and there are beautiful places, but I stay home. Happiness has no meaning without her. I cannot enjoy anything while she is not here,” he said.

blocks.caption: Sami Abu Tabaq sits alone in his apartment in Cairo, while his fiancee, Ola, remains in Gaza. Images of Gaza are shown on the television. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The Guardian

blocks.text: Despite the war, Ola completed her bachelor’s degree in nursing at the Islamic University of Gaza. She has also endured enormous loss: her cousin, the journalist Ayat Khadoura, was killed, along with about 50 other members of her extended family.

From Egypt, Sami tries to create moments of happiness for her. For her latest birthday, he contacted her brother in Gaza and secretly arranged a cake, gift and flowers. “When she woke up and saw everything, she was so happy. I love her reaction when she’s happy.” The only problem was the flowers. “They were artificial,” he said. “I wasn’t happy with them, but natural flowers can’t get into Gaza because Israel does not allow them in.”
Sami says he has tried every possible way to get Ola out, without success. She is now applying for scholarships abroad, hoping education might provide a route to evacuation and, eventually, to him.

Sami recently travelled to Mecca for Umrah, where one prayer remained constantly on his mind. “I prayed, ‘God, please bring us together soon,’” he said. “But one thing I know for sure: I will wait for her for the rest of my life, until God brings us together.”

articles.title: Senator-judges should consider NBI findings in Sara Duterte impeachment trial, says Chua
articles.summary: House prosecutor Manila 3rd District Representative Joel Chua on Saturday said senator-judges should consider the findings of the National Bureau of Investigation regarding the properties being…

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 2:58pm

House prosecutor Manila 3rd District Representative Joel Chua on Saturday said senator-judges should consider the findings of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) regarding the properties being linked to Vice President Sara Duterte in the impeachment trial of the second highest official in the government.

At a news forum in Quezon City, Chua said that although the alleged properties of the Vice President were not highlighted in the trial, senator-judges should look into it as he believes “baka may misdeclaration dito (maybe there is misdeclaration here).”

NBI Director Melvin Matibag earlier alleged that Duterte declared two properties in Catigan, Davao City. The acquisition cost was P890,000, but the assessed value was actually P40 million to P60 million. The improvements to the property were also not declared

“It should be looked into because if the declared cost was about P800,000 and was declared for agricultural use but there is a mansion, two swimming pools, and a helipad… senator-judges should also consider these because these are in the SALN (Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth) of the Vice President,” Chua said.

Other properties allegedly linked to the Duterte are Davao restaurant Prime Bistro, named under her husband lawyer Manases Carpio with an acquisition cost declared at P10 million but the assessed value was P82,000. The restaurant has a building that cost around P4.5 million, with the land value being P9.5 million, yet the declared acquisition cost was only P10 million.

Duterte’s SALN also listed a property in Don Bosco, Parañaque. The property’s market value on her SALN was P240,000, yet the acquisition cost was P2.2 million and the building was P461,760 but when assessed, it was P14,400,000.

There was also property listed in Aundanao, whose acquisition was P9 million, yet the real assessment was P19.5 million. Matibag said that there were also several undeclared improvements to the property.
Duterte on Tuesday denied ownership of the properties being investigated by the NBI that were supposedly linked to her and her family.
In a statement, the Vice President raised concern about the move of the NBI to associate the properties to her, calling it a kind of “public deception.”
Duterte on Friday also called Matibag as a "nobody" amid the agency's investigation into the properties linked to her and her family.
Matibag however said Duterte’s remark that he is a “nobody” is "true" if the basis is having mansions and receiving profit from Chinese state-owned companies.
The House of Representatives impeached Duterte last May 2026 on allegations of culpable violation of the Constitution, graft and corruption, betrayal of public trust, bribery, and other high crimes.
The Senate impeachment court began the trial on July 6.

The House prosecution team on Tuesday dropped three out of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Duterte, saying its case will stand on Article II alone on alleged unexplained wealth due to non-full declaration of assets and non-divestment of business.

In particular, the prosecution dropped Article I on confidential funds, Article III on bribery, and Article IV on assassination plot, grave threats and inciting to sedition against the President after a week of testimonies from the Anti-Money Laundering Council, bank and insurance firm officials, as well as lawyer and accountant Alexander Cabrera ultimately concluding that the Vice President and her husband accumulated unexplained wealth worth P817 million at the least and P1.5 billion at the most. —KG, GMA News

The wildfires have continued to worsen due to the intense Santa Ana winds, low humidity and unseasonably high temperatures.
According to forecasters, wind gusts of up to 50-70 miles (80-110 kilometers) per hour were recorded in the mountains, with coastal and valley areas seeing gusts between 35 and 55 miles per hour.
Authorities have turned off the electricity supply to reduce the risk of electrical sparks that the heavy wind gusts could carry, leaving thousands of people in the state without power.

articles.title: As Asia grays, can an aging Philippines avoid its neighbors’ fate?
articles.summary: As the share of older Filipinos grows and fewer babies are born, the urgency to prepare rises

blocks.text: LAST OF 2 PARTS

Maria Esperanza Carmen Liamco, 68, once worked overseas on Bahrain’s national ID system and helped found the Philippine School Bahrain. In 1997, after 14 years abroad, she returned to the Philippines to care for her sick mother.

Back home, she went on to work in several government offices over 13 years, eight of which as a contractual. But when she retired at 65 (the mandated government retirement age) in 2023, she did not receive any pension.

The Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) requires at least 15 years of service for a consistent annual pension, and otherwise provides a flat payout — a sum that, for Liamco, has nearly run dry.
After retiring, she returned to work as a board secretary of the school in Bahrain, which supports her. She has savings, and the family owns their Quezon City home, so rent isn’t a worry.
But she has concerns about what the unexpected costs of aging could mean for her — for one, medical treatment that could be expensive can wipe out whatever funds she has.

Liamco is one of 7.4 million Filipinos aged 65 or older, a group set to grow as Filipino women have fewer children than at any point on record. This shift, experts said, is moving the country toward a new demographic reality: an aging society.
Growing old before growing rich

The Philippines, long defined by its large share of young people, is at the start of that transition. The United Nations (UN) considers a country an "aging society" once 7% of its population are 65 or older.
The question is not whether the Philippines will age: it's what the country does with the time it has left before it does.

"The Philippines reached a [fertility rate] of 1.7 at a gross national income per capita of only [P280,450] in 2024, well below the income levels at which most aging societies began their transition," Jose Ramon Albert, a senior research fellow at the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS), said. "This is the risk of growing old before growing rich."
The country’s fertility rate is below the 2.1 total fertility rate needed to keep a population stable, known as "replacement level."

Far from where the Philippines is now, Japan’s gross national income per capita was P1 million when it became an aging society in 1970, while South Korea’s was about P1.4 million in 2000, adjusted for inflation.

The effect of a fertility rate below replacement level takes time to show up. The Philippines still added about 3.7 million people between 2020 and 2024, because a large generation of women is still in their childbearing years. That window is closing.
Shrinking workforce

In the decades ahead, fewer births mean fewer young workers. As more people retire or leave work than young people enter it, and as people live longer, fewer workers are left to support the nation’s economy. That also puts pressure on older Filipinos to keep working, many with no choice.

"The most urgent thing people are usually worried about with aging populations is the workforce shrinking," said Dr. Marie Ng, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore's Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, who studies demographic and health trends across Asia.
"With the workforce shrinking, you also don't have enough of the financial foundation to support the aging needs," she added.
Japan, South Korea trends

Japan's working-age population (people 15 to 64) peaked at about 87 million in 1995 and has since fallen to about 73.5 million. Roughly three in 10 Japanese are now 65 or older, the highest share of any country with a population over 100,000.

The overall population has shrunk for 17 consecutive years. Tokyo has spent more than three decades trying to reverse the trend, including a pledge of about ¥3.5 trillion a year (roughly P1.6 trillion) since 2024. Its fertility rate still fell to a record 1.14 in 2025. Adult diapers now outsell ones for babies, and the country has over 9 million vacant homes.
South Korea is on a similar path. In 2024, its working-age population fell below 70% of the total population for the first time.

After spending an estimated P17.5 trillion over 18 years to boost births, South Korea still has gaps in emergency care and too few neonatal doctors for its already small number of newborns. Its fertility rate is 0.80, among the lowest in the world.
The money in both nations has gone into a wide range of measures. Many are aimed at births, such as cash for new parents, better-paid parental leave, and housing help for young families.
Pronatal incentives, or efforts to encourage an increase in the births of children, "are not shooting up the fertility rate at all," said Ng.
That does not make them worthless. They matter for children's well-being and women's workforce participation, she said, even if they cannot necessarily reverse a decline in population growth.
Even with deep pockets, Japan and South Korea have seen limited results. What does that mean for countries with less money?
“The current systems in Asia, in general, are not quite ready in terms of the influx of aging populations,” said Ng.

The pattern isn’t limited to rich countries. Thailand became an aging society in 2004 with a gross national income per capita of P281,184, according to UN and World Bank data. In 2025, just 416,514 babies were born there, the fewest since 1950, and deaths outnumbered births by more than 143,000.

Vietnam is not far behind. It entered its aging transition in 2015 and is projected to become an aged society by the mid-2030s, according to the World Bank, when 14% of its population will be 65 or older.

Across Asia, a 2024 Asian Development Bank report found, 40% of people over 60 have no pension, and about 60% don’t get regular health checks. Among workers 65 and older, 94% are in the informal sector.

Many Filipinos are no different: workers who are contractuals or in informal jobs have no pension and little savings. As they age, many will have to lean on a stretched public health system and on their children. But there will be fewer children to lean on.
Labor exporter
The Philippines is one of the world's largest exporters of labor too.

At least 10.8 million Filipinos live abroad, and an estimated 2.1 million are overseas workers. Their remittances prop up many households as well as the country’s economy. Albert argued that this also complicates the country's aging timeline in a way none of its neighbors face.

"Aging here will unfold alongside a large diaspora, which cushions household incomes through remittances," he said, "but also means that some of the working-age population supporting our elderly will be abroad, and that our care workers are in demand overseas precisely when we will need them at home."
It is an irony hard to miss. Many Filipino healthcare workers and caregivers look after other countries' older people abroad.
Meanwhile, Filipino children with parents working overseas are cared for by grandparents. When those grandparents need care themselves, who will be there?
Building for what's coming
"Aging is going to be inevitable," Ng said. “And we do expect from data that people will live longer. The question is how to keep people alive, healthy, and productive?"
In the Philippines, the question of meeting the moment comes down to being able to retrofit existing systems for its seniors.
As Liamco thinks about the future, she said the Philippines needs more long-term solutions for supporting its seniors.
“Dole-out programs like bundles of food or funds are good, but we need more proactive efforts and opportunities, especially for seniors who are in more labor jobs who have less support,” she said.

The CPD released the Philippine Population and Development Plan of Action (PPD-POA) for 2023-2028, which includes a portion dedicated to fostering a healthy and productive workforce as the population ages. The National Commission of Senior Citizens (NCSC) has a plan for the same period, Philippine Plan of Action for Senior Citizens 2023-2028.
Some of their provisions include improving health infrastructure, creating long-term insurance policies, and increasing anti-poverty and social programs for seniors.

Scattered data is a hurdle for planning, the office of NCSC Commissioner Gloria-Jumamil Mercado said in a written response to Rappler. Information on seniors is spread across agencies such as the PSA, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), GSIS, and SSS.

“Although the DSWD/PSA has an existing Community-Based Monitoring System (CBMS)/Census, its limitation is timely and accurate record-keeping because it is only updated every three years, causing severe data latency,” said the office.

A proposed Philippine Ageing Data Observatory at the NCSC could bring that information into one database, with dashboards, more timely data and real-time analytics down to the local level, according to documents shared with Rappler. The proposal, sponsored by Commissioner Camilo G. Gudmalin, is still subject to deliberation by the Commission en banc.
Albert argued the Philippines still has the advantage of time. Its working-age population is still rising, even as the number of births decreases and people age.
His prescription: raise the productivity of the country's smaller, incoming generations and broaden pension coverage to informal workers and overseas Filipinos.

He also suggested extending healthy working lives through preventive care and building long-term care infrastructure, an effort that presents a serious challenge, given existing basic gaps in healthcare across the country.
"The demographic future of the Philippines is already visible in the 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey," Albert said.

"Whether we become a development success story depends on whether we treat the next 20 years as the window in which to invest in children and build for aging, rather than as a reprieve." – with reports from Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com
*$1= P62.74 as of October 5, 2026.

articles.title: Oregon school shooting: Police praise 'heroism' of those who intervened to stop more killing
articles.summary: US police have praised the actions of three people who cut short a deadly shooting at a school in the state of Oregon. Three children and a teacher were killed in the attack, carried out by a former…

image.caption: The shooting occurred at the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, OregonImage: Joe Kline/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police in the northwestern US state of Oregon have identified a teenage gunman who shot dead four people at a school as a former special needs student there, while praising people who stepped in to stop more killings.

Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 lost their lives in Thursday's rampage, along with a 25-year-old female teacher, before the shooter was shot dead by a father of two pupils at the school, located in the town of Bend.
Another young child and a teacher were also injured in the attack.
Who intervened to prevent more deaths in Oregon?
A man in a vehicle outside the school who was shot at and missed by the 16-year-old gunman was the first to alert police to the danger.
Before they arrived, however, a female teacher tackled the shooter after he had already killed the victims with a pump-action 12-gauge shotgun in the school's special needs classroom.

While the two wrestled with each other, a man identified by family as Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old father of two girls at the school, rushed in with his legally held weapon and shot the gunman dead.
"He heard shooting and saw a teacher involved in a physical altercation with the suspect ... and fired his weapon, striking the suspect multiple times," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters.

"When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. The teacher who is willing to stand and fight for her children ... incredible. That is true heroism, and we don't see that a lot in society," he said.

blocks.caption: The shooting has shocked the Bend communityImage: ABC affiliate KOHD/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Praise from Trump as gun control debate revived
Giamanco's mother told the local branch of Fox News that she was "very proud" and that her son was "an absolute hero."
US President Donald Trump also hailed Giamanco's actions.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he told reporters.
The shooting in Bend has triggered the usual responses from both sides in the everlasting debate about gun control laws in the US.
The National Rifle Association (NRA), one of the main and most powerful opponents of tighter laws on the possession of weapons by civilians, hailed the actions of the armed bystander.
"Yesterday's terrible act of violence in Oregon serves as another reminder of the importance of a law-abiding armed citizenry," the NRA said in a post on X.

Gun control advocates, however, once more condemned the relative ease with which firearms can be procured in the US, which they see as the main factor in the country's high rate of gun-related deaths compared with most other developed countries.
"America's gun violence crisis is killing our babies. Enough is enough," gun-control group GIFFORDS said.
According to an analysis by the education information portal Education Week, there have been 26 shootings at US schools so far this year that have resulted in injuries or deaths.
More than 360 mass shootings have been recorded across the country this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive.
It defines mass shootings as incidents in which at least four people are shot, excluding the shooter.

articles.title: Chemical spill may have triggered MV June Aster fire — BFP
articles.summary: The Bureau of Fire Protection is investigating how calcium hypochlorite and asphalt allegedly spilled and mixed aboard passenger and cargo vessel MV June Aster, possibly triggering a fire that killed…

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 2:01pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) is investigating how calcium hypochlorite and asphalt allegedly spilled and mixed aboard passenger and cargo vessel MV June Aster, possibly triggering a fire that killed 77 people off Coron, Palawan, on September 9.

Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) Officer-in-Charge (OIC) Fire Chief Superintendent Wilberto Rico Neil Ang Kwan Tiu said that the chemicals were stored near the vessel's engine exhaust, where heat may have contributed to the ignition.
“It's a corrosive agent na pagka nag-mix po siya sa asphalt can be possibly na mag-ignite,” Tiu said during a press briefing on Friday, October 16.
(It is a corrosive agent that could possibly ignite when mixed with asphalt.)

Calcium hypochlorite is a chemical commonly used to disinfect swimming pool water and kill bacteria. It is a strong oxidizing agent that can intensify combustion and pose fire hazards when it comes into contact with incompatible materials.
Asphalt, meanwhile, is a petroleum-derived material commonly used in road construction and waterproofing. It is combustible, particularly when heated.

The BFP is investigating whether rough seas caused the cargo to collapse, spilling calcium hypochlorite onto the asphalt near the vessel's engine exhaust outlet, where high temperatures may have contributed to ignition.

“Then while the vessel experienced Subasco—'yun pong rough sea condition—na-tumba po 'yung mga cargo and that comes the mixture of the calcium hypochlorite and the asphalt. Dun po nag-umpisa,” Tiu said.
(Then, while the vessel was experiencing rough sea conditions, the cargo toppled over, causing the calcium hypochlorite and asphalt to mix. That was where it all started.)

The BFP presented an artificial intelligence-assisted re-enactment of the incident, using photographs of the vessel and generated visuals to illustrate how the fire may have spread from the rear portion of the cargo deck toward the passengers' sleeping area.
The agency's reconstruction indicated that the chemicals were stored at the rearmost portion of the cargo deck, directly in front of the engine room's hot air exhaust outlet.
Tiu also cited a problem with the vessel's ventilation system, which may have allowed heat to build up in the cargo area.
Engine trouble delayed voyage

The BFP said MV June Aster's voyage was originally scheduled for September 3 but was delayed by four days. The vessel's operator, Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc., cited bad weather and low tide conditions, although investigators also received information that the vessel had been experiencing engine problems.
Despite the delay, cargo continued to be loaded onto the vessel, including hardware items, drums of cooking oil, asphalt and calcium hypochlorite.
According to the BFP's reconstruction, the vessel departed Baseco Port in Manila at around midnight on September 8, bound for Coron.

During the voyage, rough seas caused some cargo to shift and collapse. The BFP said a reported cargo-lashing failure occurred at the forward portion of the cargo deck, but no crew member inspected the cargo at the rear portion.
The vessel also encountered engine performance problems and underwent repairs to its engine fuel lines, delaying its arrival by around two hours and 45 minutes.

At around 5 p.m. on September 9, about 50 minutes before the fire broke out, the captain allegedly instructed the chief engineer to increase the engine's revolutions per minute to raise the vessel's speed to nine knots and recover lost time.
The BFP said the prolonged voyage and reported increase in engine speed may have raised exhaust temperatures, affecting the conditions inside the cargo deck.
Asked whether the captain had confirmed the sequence of events, Tiu said investigators obtained accounts from survivors and crew members.

“Yes, our Directorate for Investigation and Intelligence, we created a task force MV Aster. They proceeded to the area and they are able to get the narrative coming from the survivors as well as 'yung mga crew ng barko. So this narrative is really the result of the investigation,” he said.

(Yes, our Directorate for Investigation and Intelligence created a task force, MV Aster. They proceeded to the area and obtained accounts from the survivors as well as the ship’s crew. So, this account is really the result of the investigation.)
77 dead, eight still missing
The fire broke out at around 6:30 p.m. on September 9 while MV June Aster was sailing in waters about 1.2 nautical miles northeast of Barangay Marcilla in Coron, Palawan.
Of the 128 people on board, comprising 111 passengers and 17 crew members, 77 were confirmed dead and eight remained missing, according to the BFP.
Tiu said 63 of the fatalities had been identified by the Scene of the Crime Operatives. He also reported 43 injured people.

The BFP's reconstruction said 43 survivors were rescued from the sea by passing fishing boats about two hours after the fire broke out. Rescue efforts were later supported by the Philippine Coast Guard, BFP personnel, Coron municipal disaster risk reduction and management personnel, and volunteers.
The survivors were brought to the Port of Turda for medical assessment and first aid. Some sustained burn injuries.
Tiu said toxic smoke from the fire may have contributed to the high number of fatalities, as passengers could have been asleep in their bunks when the incident occurred.

articles.title: Fort Chipewyan leaders criticize Elections Alberta over advance voting delays for referendum
articles.summary: Indigenous leaders in Fort Chipewyan, Alta., are accusing Elections Alberta of being poorly prepared to run advance voting polls in the isolated northern hamlet for this month’s provincial referendum.

image.caption: A voter arrives to cast their referendum vote at an advance polling station in Calgary, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton

Indigenous leaders in Fort Chipewyan, Alta., are accusing Elections Alberta of being poorly prepared to run advance voting polls in the isolated northern hamlet for this month’s provincial referendum.
Last-minute staffing shortages forced Elections Alberta to delay advance voting in northern hamlet

At a virtual news conference on Friday, First Nations and Métis leaders in the region said people who arrived at the community’s municipal office to vote early on Thursday morning instead found the doors locked. Elections Alberta told CBC News there were not enough staff available to run the voting station that morning.

The regional Indigenous leaders who spoke said some voters who were left unable to cast their ballots on Thursday had already made travel arrangements for work and medical appointments. Fort Chipewyan is more than 230 kilometres north of Fort McMurray. It can be reached only by boats, planes or by driving on a seasonal winter road.
“This referendum is everything to us,” said Mikisew Cree First Nation Chief Melody Lepine. “Our treaty, our relationship with the Crown, we are defending with everything that we have.
“We’re completely appalled by what happened yesterday when [members] were turned away after we’ve been extending so much resources and support for them to go and vote.”
Chief Melody Lepine of the Mikisew Cree First Nation at the First Nation's office in downtown Fort McMurray on September 11, 2026. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)

Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation Chief Allan Adam said local leaders were told Wednesday evening that Thursday’s advance polls would be cancelled. Advance voting for Friday was cancelled as well. Early voting will still go ahead on Saturday, which is the last day Albertans can vote early in the referendum. Referendum day is on Monday. Adam said he only learned on Thursday that early voting would not resume until Saturday.
Chief Allan Adam of the Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation. (Avery Zingel/CBC)
Ruby Ladouceur, president of the Fort Chipewyan Métis Nation, said the information about early voting being suspended until Saturday was provided to her membership by Adam and not Elections Alberta.
“Notify us directly,” she said. “Notify us early. Work with us so our citizens are informed and able to vote.”
Ladouceur said she believes what happened sends “a clear message that Indigenous people can be informed last, included later or considered secondary. I reject these kinds of notions.”
'This was unfortunate'

A statement from Elections Alberta to CBC News acknowledged the disruption. The agency said there were not enough staff at the polling station, and the staff who were available were not yet trained to process identification requirements.

Elections Alberta said the reason advance voting was suspended until Saturday was so the returning officer could spend Friday training local workers. Voting hours for referendum day on Monday remain unchanged.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: “This was unfortunate, however, without training, the elector experience would have caused confusion and led to many questions on how to receive identification and mark electors from the voting record,” the statement said, noting that working with Indigenous communities to facilitate voting is a “priority.”
Grand Chief has 'serious concerns'
Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi said the confusion highlights the logistical challenges many isolated Indigenous and rural communities can face around election time.

Out of 24 Treaty 8 First Nations in Alberta, Mercredi said only five have advance polling locations. He attended Friday’s virtual news conference from the side of a rural road, saying he was spending seven hours driving so he could cast his ballot early.

“What happened in Fort Chip raises serious concerns across Treaty 8 territory,” said Mercredi. “We understand the importance of making sure that our people see what’s on the table, and making sure that they’re protecting themselves and protecting our people.”
Adam said the early voting problem had never happened during any previous federal, provincial, municipal or First Nation election in his area.
“This is Alberta. You call for a referendum and yet you cannot deliver to host a referendum in our community,” said Adam.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Vincent McDermott covers Fort McMurray and the Wood Buffalo region for CBC News. He was previously the editor of Fort McMurray Today, where he was part of a team that won a National Newspaper Award for coverage of the 2016 Horse River Wildfire. He is also a former contributor to the official magazine of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada. He can be reached at vincent.mcdermott@cbc.ca

articles.title: Chinese Embassy tells lawmakers to 'stop bluffing' amid persona non grata talks
articles.summary: The Chinese Embassy has released a statement amid talks of possibly declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata after his comments perceived by some lawmakers as "threats" against the…

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 1:15pm

The Chinese Embassy has released a statement amid talks of possibly declaring Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata after his comments were perceived by some lawmakers as "threats" against the Philippines.
"Some senators and house representatives are talking about declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata. Is this threat or coercion?" the Chinese Embassy said in a social media post.
"But anyway, just do it. Otherwise, STOP BLUFFING," it added.

The challenge stemmed from Ambassador's statement wherein he said that China would "easily win" if tensions escalated in the West Philippine Sea (WPS). Philippine officials and government agencies have slammed what seemed to be an apparent "threat."
The Chinese Embassy, meanwhile, also targeted Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for the WPS Commodore Jay Tarriela in a series of posts.
The Chinese Embassy took a screenshot of a translated Facebook post from Tarriela dated October 17, saying that it was the Philippines that threatened Jing.

“This is a threat. Jay Tarriela admitted it. Key point: You don't like being threatened. Even when there is no threat, you still create one—but you absolutely love threatening others, including Chinese workers, teachers, fishermen and diplomats,” the Chinese Embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Saturday morning.
But Tarriela was quick to correct this post from the embassy.
“Lost in translation, or just consistently lying, Ambassador Jing Quan? Chinongaling!” Tarriela fired back.

Tarriela’s original post was a response to the Chinese Embassy’s challenge of declaring Quan persona non grata. It originally read as follows: “Ganito kayabang ang dayuhang Ambassador habang nasa loob ng sarili nating bansa. Matapos tayong pagbantaan, siya pa ngayon ang nagmamalaki at hinahamon pa ang isang buong sangay ng ating pamahalaan, ang Lehislatura.”
(This is how boastful the foreign Ambassador is while inside our own country. After threatening us, he is the one being prideful and challenging an entire branch of government, the Legislature.)
Apart from various lawmakers, both the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Department of National Defense have already slammed Jing's statement, with the former calling it a thinly veiled threat.

With China continuing to claim most of the West Philippine Sea for itself, tensions between Manila and Beijing have escalated. Confrontations between Chinese and Filipino vessels in the West Philippine Sea have become a regular occurrence.
Despite the Philippines winning its case for the West Philippine Sea in the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2016, China has continuously disregarded the ruling. --VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Why every audience vote matters in PETA’s ‘Gen G’ play
articles.summary: The choose-your-own-adventure format of ‘Gen G’ forces the audience to stay fully immersed in the story, with the active, live-voting feature directly dictating the fate of the characters

blocks.text: The show begins with the Joker asking the audience to help guide the story toward a satisfying ending. Most of the crowd belongs to the younger generation, or the digital natives widely known as “Gen Z.”
“Gen G began by listening to young people talk about how they make these choices,” said Ian Segarra, director of the interactive theater show Gen G: GG na ‘To!

“Through our conversations with them, what emerged is that choosing is rarely simple. Our decisions are shaped by our families, friends, fears, responsibilities, circumstances, and the systems we live in. What seems like the wrong choice from the outside may feel like the only choice available to us.”

Organized by the Philippine Educational Theater Association (PETA) and Move to Change Foundation, Inc. (M2C), Gen G: GG na ‘To allows viewers, particularly the younger audience, to make choices as they watch the play.

Inspired by what Filipinos commonly say, “Kabataan ang pag-asa ng bayan (The youth is the nation’s hope),” the story features the characters Dex, Achi, Chloe, and Sid, all fighting for survival amid rising floodwaters in Balangay Gen Zones.
“At the heart of Gen G is the image of the Balangay — a vessel built to carry people together. It becomes a symbol of community and of the systems we inherit and build together,” Segarra said.
“We may not have created the world we are given, but we are constantly participating in how it is maintained, shaped, and transformed.”
Perhaps more than entertainment, Gen G is a live exercise in democracy. The show relies on real-time choices from the crowd, which, Segarra noted, resulted in unpredictable choices during the play.
This, he shared, also provided the production team with fresh insights.
“There are surprising answers. Merong mga hindi namin ine-expect na makikita nila, na nakita nila (We see things we didn’t expect them to catch),” said Segarra.
“It’s surprising and sometimes it’s also enlightening. Na parang, ‘Ah okay, ganito pala talaga…ganito mag-isip ang mga kabataan ngayon (Ah okay, so this is how today’s youth actually think).”

This choose-your-own-adventure setup forces the audience to stay fully immersed in the story, with the active, live-voting feature directly dictating the fate of Dex, Achi, Chloe, and Sid as they navigate the rising waters.
Since the cast must adapt to the audience’s decisions, the story flow changes with every single performance.

“I thought that theater is very powerful in evoking the emotions or evoking the capacity and potential of the youth. Hence, we considered to mount this play with PETA,” said Liza Abaya, founder of Move to Change Foundation, Inc.
The cast, all Gen Zs themselves, makes the play even more relatable to the young target audience.

On stage, they portray characters with clashing personalities and conflicting ideas — forcing the audience to carefully weigh options during crucial decision-making moments. Ultimately, the characters have to make choices to achieve their common goal: saving their Balangay.

“In our practice, we cannot prescribe it. We will always pick it up from the audience,” said PETA president Melvin Lee. “If they will bring up a specific issue, the audience has to resolve it and come up with their own stand about a specific issue. Us artists, we cannot prescribe it for the audience.”
Zoe Damag, the cast member who plays the Joker, emphasized how this interactive approach empowers both the actors and the students.

“When students perform and engage, they come alive and realize their true capabilities. You are forced to research and deeply understand your reality, because you cannot portray a character — or make a choice — with half-baked knowledge,” Damag said in Filipino.
Despite the different choices within the story, the casts come in well-prepared to execute different scenarios every show, having rehearsed all possibilities.
“​That’s why it’s difficult at times, challenging at times, but it’s beautiful also because you get to understand how the young people also react to what is [in front of them],” Damag said.
Gen G will continue to tour schools and universities until December 2026.
As the play respects the young audience’s real-time decisions, it also allows them to realize the weight of their choices.
“What if the future of our community depended on the choices we make today?” EO Masilungan, M2C’s executive director, asked.
“​Young people saw something that mattered, and they decided to do something about it. And that is change-making.” – Rappler.com
Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

articles.title: Trend Intel: Chinese microdramas have Filipinos in a chokehold – are you watching?
articles.summary: What drives Filipinos’ consumption of these bite-sized and often emotionally exaggerated shows?

items: Chinese microdramas, known as duanju, have gained popularity in the Philippines, particularly with the success of 'The Heiress Who Won with Brains' and the involvement of actress Zhang Yingfei.
These microdramas, designed for mobile viewing and typically lasting 60 to 90 seconds, have evolved into a billion-dollar industry, with significant revenue growth expected in the coming years.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Hey trendsetters,
Remember when Linda Walker sprinted from our screens to our shores?

The Heiress Who Won with Brains, the vertical Chinese drama following a 17-year-old girl who used her academic excellence to prove herself to her toxic family, took social media by storm, with the actress behind the protagonist, Zhang Yingfei, even making a visit to the Philippines in June. (Yingfei was invited by the Filipino Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Inc., which tapped her to promote education.)

blocks.caption: Trend Intel: Chinese microdramas have Filipinos in a chokehold – are you watching?

blocks.text: This is just one facet of the rise of Chinese microdramas in the Philippines. Referred to as duanju in Mandarin, these are designed for mobile-first viewing, typically running from 60 to 90 seconds per episode. The rapid and serialized content often feeds viewers with over-the-top plots and multiple cliffhangers for instant dopamine hits, making the case for its pay-per-episode system.

Originally emerging on Douyin (the TikTok-equivalent app in China) in 2018, Chinese microdramas have now evolved into a billion-dollar industry worldwide, with revenue outside China poised to increase from $2.7 billion to $3.6 billion this year, then growing to $9.5 billion come 2031, according to Media Partners Asia.

Even brands are joining in the hype. This includes Valorant, a video game by American developers at RIOT, as seen with their fresh collaboration with Old Goat (老山羊): A four-part series called The Dragon King Returns — Brimstone’s Revenge! It’s tension-filled and a little bit outlandish, following the usual narrative DNA that works.

blocks.caption: Trend Intel: Chinese microdramas have Filipinos in a chokehold – are you watching?

blocks.text: Even Shopee, a non-streaming platform, is riding the wave through their Shopee Video Dramas hub, where Chinese microdramas are free to stream. In the app, users can earn Shopee Coins through watching episodes.

blocks.caption: A preview of the Shopee Video Dramas lineup

blocks.text: The local appeal

Gathering data and scanning social media platforms from September 2025 to September 2026, The Nerve discovered that in the case of Pinoy viewership, familiarity breeds… fixation. Chinese microdramas quickly provide teleserye emotions.

blocks.caption: Source: The Nerve

blocks.text: “The stories start off from humiliation to revelation and payoff within a short mobile session. Familiar melodrama makes the compressed format easy to enter,” wrote The Nerve. “Most of these stories start with a major injustice, pivot when a major secret comes to light, and end with payback, personal validation, or true love.”
Tagalog dubbing and less time commitment also contribute to their appeal.

blocks.caption: Source: The Nerve

blocks.text: A form of livelihood

In June, Vera Files reported that Filipino women in provinces are turning the “attention economy” into profit, thanks to streaming and livestreaming apps. This includes Melolo, a Singapore-based platform where users can “earn ‘coins’ by watching series, completing daily missions, and inviting friends using referral codes.”
Chinese microdramas reward viewers emotionally and financially.

In The Nerve’s study, the checkpoints for earning include new-user bonuses and rewards for each time one finishes an episode. Referral codes and cash-out claims become promotional materials, pulling in more viewers. And even if there are cases when the rewards start to decrease after the initial incentives, viewers stay because they’re entertained by the dramas.

blocks.caption: Source: The Nerve

blocks.text: In his column “The Vantage Point,” Val A. Villanueva analyzed how the format orchestrates different elements to make us addicted.

“The architects of the microdrama discovered something more potent: ordinary viewers do not always hunger for a two-hour movie. Frequently, our resolve dissolves before 90 seconds of unrestrained melodrama, an outrageous premise, and an unanswered question,” he said. “And the very moment our curiosity is piqued to discover what happens next, the price of finding out has already been calculated.”
Shaping consumption
The rise of Chinese microdramas has also influenced how studios in the Philippines create their online shows, but they still keep the stories within our entertainment palette.

blocks.caption: Source: The Nerve

blocks.text: In late 2025, Viva launched VMB (Viva Movie Box), or what they call “the first Filipino microdrama app.” Meanwhile, iWant has aggressively expanded its roster of original microdramas with vertical shows like Runaway Love, Shadow CEO, The Heiress Deception, and I Am Your Daughter, with the last three having a similar overarching theme of pulling off fake identities and satisfying revenge.
The AI takeover

But as far as identity goes, the Chinese microdrama industry is hounded by concerns regarding the sudden massive use of AI to produce shows — a move caused by the need for cost efficiency and faster turnaround, as the behemoth of an entertainment market continues to expand, but is affecting copyright, livelihood, and other factors.

A South China Morning Post report said that China’s broadcasting regulator has pushed for greater support for live-action dramas. This follows the government’s aim to maintain quality and protect rights despite AI domination. The National Radio and Television Administration’s Wang Xiaolang revealed that among the 430,000 microdramas released in China during the first eight months of the year, AI dramas accounted for 90% of them.
For a format that tinkers with very human elements, the use of AI to maintain the rise is pretty ironic.
Entertainment (and emotional resonance) as a soft power
While these microdramas are becoming a new Chinese soft power, it might not be the first time that their form of entertainment got people happily addicted.

Ultimately, this culture boom teaches us that it may not be rocket science to strike a chord with people’s emotions, whether it’s through a shareable meme or a confrontation-filled one-minute episode. It can sometimes just take a simple vertical format, as long as you know how to integrate your way into people’s lives.
Until the next scroll!
Jelou Galang
Culture Desk Content Producer

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Pope Leo was hospitalized in Rome’s Gemelli hospital late morning on October 13, ahead of surgery to remove a small growth on one of his lungs. The 71-year-old pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations.

The surgery to remove a small growth discovered during a recent routine health check lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications, according to Leo’s lead surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, and personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone.

Blood tests and a chest X-ray carried out on October 14, showed normal post-operative results, the Vatican said, adding that the pontiff had undergone respiratory physiotherapy. Pope Leo‘s recovery from surgery is progressing as expected and he has begun walking in his hospital room and eating normally.

Meanwhile, on October 13, the prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte withdrew all but one of the articles of impeachment to expedite the proceedings. Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro stated that focusing on one article allows for a more efficient trial, while the defense team expressed concerns about due process and the potential for a mistrial.

The court accepted the withdrawal of the other charges, which prevents the prosecution from reviving those cases during the current Congress, allowing the defense to concentrate on the remaining unexplained wealth allegation.
