articles.title: Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama
articles.summary: Empty lecture halls, burning buildings and demands for change: Albanian students are spearheading a protest movement that has become the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama in years.

image.caption: Student protests in the Albanian capital, Tirana, turned violent on TuesdayImage: Hameraldi Agolli/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The luxury high-rises transforming Tirana's skyline are meant to project the image of a modern European capital. But at the foot of one of these buildings, Samanta, a 22-year-old master's student in economics, is in tears.
She removes the mask she had been wearing to protect herself from tear gas.

"How could I ever afford an apartment in one of these towers on a salary of €540 [$608]?" she shouts, as she stands facing a line of police officers. "I share the rent with people I don't even know because my family has emigrated. We're exhausted."
University lecture halls in Tirana stand empty as students boycott classes and take to the streets, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in power since 2013.
Escalation after months of protests

Albanians have been protesting since late May as part of a broader anti-government movement known as the "Flamingo Revolution," which began in response to a multimillion-euro tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, in the protected coastal area of Zvernec.

blocks.caption: Protesters destroyed an ATM during clashes with police during an anti-government protest by students on ThursdayImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: The movement has, however, since grown into a broader challenge to Rama's government.

Over the past three days, the student demonstrations have erupted into violent clashes. Bins, businesses, buildings and banks have been set ablaze, with some completely burning out. Tear gas has filled the air.

A total of 152 people have been arrested and 324 are under investigation over the three days of protests. Injuries have been reported among both protesters and police officers, with the police saying 71 officers have been injured in the clashes.

The students are angry about conditions at universities, the cost of higher education and poor employment prospects after graduation. But above all, they want the government to step down and say they are not willing to negotiate any of their other demands with the prime minister.
"You didn't listen to us for four months while we protested peacefully. Now you'll listen as the city burns," said Samanta.
Rama breaks his silence
During the first two days of the student protests, the prime minister remained silent.

Then, at 8:03 a.m. on Thursday, Rama appeared in a video message recorded inside the fire-damaged College of Europe building, just meters from his office on Tirana's main street, the Boulevard of the Martyrs of the Nation.

blocks.caption: A total of 152 people have been arrested over the past three days, with injuries reported among both protesters and police officersImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: "These are the hands of an opposition that, hiding behind masked people, wants to drag Albania back to a place it will never return to," he declared.
Later that day, Rama addressed the protesters' central demand — his resignation. In comments to Reuters, he ruled out stepping down, saying governments are changed in elections.
The following day, he also accused "foreign hands" of seeking to prevent Albania from joining the European Union.
The unrest comes at a critical moment for Albania's bid to join the European Union. Brussels has called for calm and restraint, urging all sides to avoid further escalation and engage in dialogue.
Sali Berisha, the 82-year-old leader of the opposition Democratic Party and a former prime minister, rejected Rama's accusations that the opposition was behind the violence.

"We have no idea whether it's Greece, Iran, Serbia or someone else," he told a press conference, mocking Rama's claims of foreign interference. "The Democratic Party fully supports this protest and will stand by it until the end. Resign and leave immediately!"
Students against the political establishment
For Rigels Xhemollari of the Albanian civil society organization Qendresa Qytetare (Civic Resistance), the student revolt is the culmination of months of peaceful protests.

"The main reason is the prime minister's failure to respond during four months of protests and his mockery of the demonstrators. Other reasons include the economic situation, corruption cases and successive scandals," he told DW, referring to a number of corruption investigations involving senior government officials.
But the anger is not directed at Rama alone. Protesters have also voiced their frustration with Albania's political opposition.

blocks.caption: The students are demanding that the government step down and say they are not willing to negotiate with the prime minister, Edi RamaImage: Brunilda Kazani/DW

blocks.text: "We want the political class of the past 35 years to go. We want a new Albania with new leaders," Skerdi Topalli, a 20-year-old journalism student, told DW.
What could come after the protests?
For political analyst Mark Marku, dean of the Faculty of History and Philology at the University of Tirana, the protests mark a turning point.
"This is the reaction of a generation. In a society that was not responding, they woke people up and made us think about change," he told DW.
But Marku warns that even Rama's resignation and fresh elections would not necessarily bring new political leadership.
"Challenging the government is not an end in itself. A protest must produce a result," he said. "There must be a platform, a political alternative. You cannot vote for a protest."
Xhemollari, meanwhile, sees Rama's resignation as the only way to end the revolt.
"The protest has just one political demand, and it requires a political solution: the prime minister's resignation," he told DW.

Xhemollari says that Albania's president should bring political parties together to form a caretaker government led by a non-partisan prime minister, paving the way for local and parliamentary elections in May 2027.

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank
articles.summary:
Settlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and beat photographer Heidi Levine as part of yearly attacks to disrupt harvest

Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank…

blocks.text: Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer.

Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in towns across the West Bank on Friday. At least six people were injured in the town of Abu Falah near Ramallah, the Palestinian Red Crescent Society said.

At least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives in Abu Falah, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.

blocks.caption: Teargas fired by Israeli forces. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”

Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.

“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.

blocks.caption: Levine speaking to journalists in hospital after the attack. Photograph: Ali Sawafta/Reuters

blocks.text: There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.
Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but this year’s harvest has seen an uptick in violence as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.
At least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 others have been injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.

Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C – an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

blocks.caption: Palestinians and activists collecting olives after the attack on Friday. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.

The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026, for the purpose of preventing settler violence.

The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.
Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers had razed trees.

Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.

blocks.caption: Israeli soldiers move towards a Palestinian man lying wounded on the road after they shot him during the settler attack. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop settler violence.

Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.
Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.
Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.
Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.
A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

articles.title: At summit, EU leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
articles.summary: President Zelenskyy has received words of encouragement from EU leaders, who pledged support for Ukraine's self-defense against Russia. This comes as winter approaches and the US seems to be…

image.caption: Zelenskyy thanked European leaders for their support in Brussels, saying Ukraine wants to end the war on its country but needs to survive the winterImage: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended the final day of an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where leaders from across the bloc pledged continued support for the Ukrainian leader and his country in a turbulent week.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa both took the fore in calling on allies to continue their support of Kyiv as it faces increased Russian attacks and detrimental US foreign policy decisions.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
What did EU leaders say about the bloc's support for Ukraine?

"This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine," said Costa as he stood next to the Ukrainian president. "This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."
"One ​thing is absolutely clear," pledged von der Leyen, "we will ​not lift any sanctions unless Russia ⁠stops ​this ​war."

The EU leaders' remarks come just one week after Ukraine and its European allies were blindsided by US President Donald Trump's unilateral decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports and purchase diesel from the Kremlin after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

On Wednesday, a US official said Washington was also considering easing sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet — unflagged tankers that turn off transponders to transport and transfer illicit oil while circumventing international export sanctions.

After undermining years of Western sanctions against Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, Trump is now seeking to increase pressure on Ukraine — calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader and blasting Kyiv's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure as a "disgrace."
Diesel deal between Trump, Putin angers Ukraine
Trump seeks to deflect blame for high energy prices onto Ukraine

Upon arrival at Friday's Brussels summit, Zelenskyy said, "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that ​they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter."
"The winter package is not only energy, ​it's also air defense and funding," he added.
During his speech at the summit, Zelenskyy asked European Union leaders to provide an additional €70 billion ($79 billion) in funding to Kyiv next year to help it continue fighting Russia.

"The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion euros more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support," the Ukrainian president said.

When asked after his meeting with EU leaders if Trump was scapegoating him for troubles in the US, Zelensky gave a knowing smile and stayed mum. "This is my answer," the Ukrainian president said, as journalists broke into laughter at a press conference in Brussels.

Trump last week justified his calls for Zelenskyy to be removed from office by claiming the Ukrainian leader did not want to stop the war — which Russia launched on February 24, 2022 — as well as attempting to divert anger over high global fuel prices away from his own war in Iran, which triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent global oil and gas prices through the roof.

"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher," Trump told far-right US media outlet Newsmax on Thursday. Asked about Ukraine resuming attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, Trump said, "Well, I think that's a disgrace."

Earlier this week, Kyiv reported restrictions on its use of Elon Musk's Starshield system, Starlink's military-grade satellite service which Ukraine relies on for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territories and interceptor drones.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Zelenskyy hails 'very good' meeting with Hungary PM
The Ukrainian president also praised his first bilateral meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar on the sidelines of the summit.

"We had a very good meeting," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels. He added that he and Magyar had discussed "many things, including relations, the economy, and logistics — all of which are important to our two countries."
Zelenskyy also said that he "won't mind" visiting Budapest.
After meeting, Magyar announced that Budapest and Kyiv had agreed to put their relations on a new footing.

"I ​assured the Ukrainian president of my full solidarity over the inhuman Russian aggression against his ​country," Magyar wrote in a Facebook post. He also said that Hungary was ready to assist Ukraine by all possible diplomatic means to reach a ceasefire and lasting peace.
The meeting occurred just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest's long-standing concerns regarding the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine.

articles.title: The EU wants an AI revolution. But on whose terms?
articles.summary: As the US and China race ahead, the European Union seeks to boost its economy with AI. Can it compete while protecting workers, safety and the climate?

image.caption: Microsoft's vice chair and president, Brad Smith, addresses delegatesImage: Paul Faith/AFP

blocks.text: Step-dancers spun across the circular stage in the middle of a dark hall, entrancing an audience of policymakers and tech bosses. Not simply another bureaucratic conference, the International AI Summit, hosted in Dublin this week, aspired to something more spectacular — a grand announcement that Europe is ready for its artificial intelligence (AI) revolution.

Among the more than 1,500 expected guests were Google DeepMind co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis and Microsoft president Brad Smith, in addition to high-ranking European Union and Irish officials. The event was a key part of Ireland's term as president of the EU Council, but a lack of critical voices to counterbalance the AI enthusiasm on display has drawn accusations of tech boosterism.
The summit was "almost like a party political broadcast on behalf of AI," Barry O'Sullivan, an AI professor at University College Cork, told DW.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister of Ireland Micheal Martin and Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Niamh Smyth were also present at the summitImage: Cillian Sherlock/PA/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: AI to help Europe's competitiveness
The overarching theme was how to use AI to get Europe's sluggish economy moving, boost innovation and catch up with the US and China.

On panels packed with senior executives, the potential benefits were made clear: detecting early signs of cancer, improving warnings of extreme weather, and optimising power distribution to save energy. Turning those promises into reliable services, however, still requires testing and validation.

Ireland's interest in these issues doesn't come purely from goodwill towards its fellow EU member states. The country hosts the European operations of several of the world's largest technology companies, and relies heavily on the taxation of multinational firms. Foreign-owned multinationals paid €28.8 billion in corporation tax in 2025, accounting for 87% of the total, excluding exceptional Apple tax proceeds. That includes pharmaceuticals and other sectors, not just technology.

This means Dublin has a clear interest in shaping European rules while keeping investors on board. But Europe's financial firepower remains far behind America's: Private AI investment reached $286 billion (about €253 billion) in the US in 2025, compared with $21 billion (€18.6 billion) in Europe, according to Stanford University's AI Index.

But does Europe even need to compete on the same terms? O'Sullivan thinks it should focus on its own strengths, including industrial robotics and specialised applications: "We have a unique kind of AI opportunity in Europe, and that's what we should back."

Using foreign models could help European businesses move faster. But it also leaves them dependent on suppliers elsewhere, which can change prices, restrict access and decide which capabilities to release.

blocks.caption: Michael McGrath speaks to reporters at the AI Summit in Dublin, where he underlines the EU's approach between control and innovationImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: EU rules under pressure
EU representatives at the summit were quick to underline that rules were now in place to reap AI's benefits while mitigating its risks.

Michael McGrath, the Irish commissioner responsible for democracy, justice, the rule of law and consumer protection, spoke of a balance between AI's potential and the "appropriate guardrails" required to ensure trust.

The AI Act bans certain practices and imposes stronger requirements on sensitive uses. Its Omnibus amendments, in force since July 2026, aim to simplify compliance, though have als delyed some safeguards. Rules covering areas including employment and education now apply from December 2027; those for AI embedded in regulated products from August 2028.
The Commission has said that companies need time to adjust to new standards and guidance. Critics, however, believe protections being delayed under pressure to compete.
For O'Sullivan, regulation and innovation are not contradictory. "The idea that you can't have regulation and innovation is just a nonsense," he said, pointing to pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

blocks.caption: Paul Murphy from 'People over Profits' sees major drawbacks to AI developmentImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: Demonstrations outside the venue

For protesters outside, assurances made by politicians and tech firms ring hollow. Paul Murphy, an Irish lawmaker from the socialist People Before Profit party, argued that even though Europe's regulations are strong than those in the US, the bar remains low. With the latest amendments, he sees a move towards deregulation.
"Big tech is setting the pace and everybody's expected to just get on board," he told DW.
Instead, he wants civil society, trade unions and politicians to discuss how the technology should develop and how limited resources like water and electricity should be used.

Inside, union representative Fionnuala Ní Bhrógáin, one of the few critical voices on stage, questioned who would benefit from higher productivity. Optimization, she said, can put higher pressure on workers.

Murphy, too, fears an increased pressure to work faster, with less autonomy and more supervision. Whether an hour saved on emails becomes time to think, or leads to more assignments, depends on employers' decisions and workers' bargaining power.
O'Sullivan, on the other hand, said that AI removing mundane tasks gives employees "more time to think, and to be more creative in their jobs."

blocks.caption: Google was one of the main tech representatives at the AI SummitImage: Paul Faith/AFP

blocks.text: A heavy environmental toll

In Ireland, the question of resources is particularly pressing. Data centres used 23% of the country's metered electricity in 2025. That includes cloud storage and other services, not just AI. Murphy argued that their expansion raises household bills and undermines climate goals.
Renewable energy could help meet demand. But additional clean electricity must also replace fossil fuels, while housing and other industries need grid capacity too.
"The sustainability of AI is a huge problem," O'Sullivan agreed, calling for the sector to reduce its overall energy footprint.

blocks.caption: Participants were able to try out AI's newest features, like cyber-cycling through major world cities on a bike.Image: Paul Faith/AFP

blocks.text: The future of AI

Back inside the hall, even industry leaders acknowledged the need for boundaries. Hassabis, the chief scientist of Alphabet, called recent AI hacking incidents "early warning shots" and advocated international oversight. Microsoft president Smith said: "We need law. We need regulation."

Their warnings follow concrete failures. During cybersecurity evaluations in July, OpenAI models bypassed isolation controls, hacked the infrastructure surrounding the test, broke containment, and attacked a real company, Hugging Face, which hosts AI models and datasets. Had similar behavior occurred inside a hospital, power grid, or other critical system, the results could have been much worse. Anthropic separately disclosed unintended actions by its AI on real websites, including a ​false homicide tip to the Philadelphia police, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive.

Speakers on and off the stage agreed: The incidents show just how difficult it can be to keep increasingly autonomous systems under control. Developers' assurances alone cannot guarantee safety. Nor can regulation eliminate every risk. But for O'Sullivan and Murphy, it remains essential.

Europe wants to shape AI without compromising on the benefits its promises.This balancing act is a difficult one, involving choices about investment, resources and the distribution of gains. Even a spectacular opening performance cannot dance around those questions.

articles.title: Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
articles.summary: Tesla CEO Elon Musk showcased the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.

blocks.text: A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas.
"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," the car firm's CEO Elon Musk said as he presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.
Musk said an audience was needed to prove the car "is not AI", before showing a demonstration of the Roadster driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air, and landing using air jets.
But there are several reasons we're unlikely to see a flying car on our roads anytime soon, as the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman explains.

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest
articles.summary: Israeli settlers were seen attacking Palestinian farmers and setting fire to olive trees in the West Bank.

blocks.text: The BBC has witnessed Israeli settlers attack Palestinians and set fire to olive trees in the occupied West Bank.

About a dozen settlers dressed in black charged down a hill near an outpost – illegal under international law - to a field where Palestinians and activists were harvesting olives. They torched about a dozen trees and hurled stones from slingshots.
Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was at the scene, was taken to hospital where she told reporters she "got jumped" and described being kicked on the ground.

The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year. It says this year levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high.
The BBC's Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.

articles.title: Italy cuts air traffic in half amid data transmission issue
articles.summary: Citing problems with the data transmission network, Italian authorities have drastically reduced the volume of flights in their airspace. The ENAV authority ruled out malicious activity and said…

image.caption: Air traffic was reduced at hubs across Italy, including Milan Bergamo Airport [FILE: March 10, 2026]Image: Tiziano Manzoni/LaPresse/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Air travelers across Italy faced delays and cancellations on Friday because of a problem with the country's air traffic control systems.

The ENAV air traffic control authority ruled out foul play such as a cyberattack, and said it was forced to introduce temporary restrictions of the volume of flights after identifying a data transmission problem.
Major aiports in cities like Rome and Milan warned of likely disruptions and advised passengers to check with their airlines.
What did authorities say about the problem?
ENAV said it first identified the issue overnight. It was forced to restrict the volume of flights at around 6 a.m. (0400 GMT/UTC) as the number of scheduled services increased.
"We would like to inform you that this morning we guaranteed the greatest possible number of departures, including intercontinental flights," ENAV said.
Shorter-distance services were more likely to be interrupted.

"Despite the anomalies encountered on the data transmission network, we are deploying all avaialable resources to minimize disruption and restore full operations as soon as possible," ENAV said. "We confirm an operational capacity of 50% of total air traffic, ensuring maximum safety at all times, which remains the Company's top priority."
ENAV said it had ruled out the possibility of the disturbance being caused by "malicious acts."

Rome airports operator ADR warned passengers that "flight delays and cancellations may occur" and advised passengers to contact their airline if uncertain. Milan airports company SEA issued a similar notice.

articles.title: Germany, France agree on deal to support Europe's struggling car industry
articles.summary: The two countries said the agreement aimed to safeguard Europe's automotive industry, encouraging development and research. Car makers in Europe have so far struggled to compete with Chinese electric…

image.caption: German car maker Volkswagen has been struggling in recent years, with cost-cutting measures prompting job cuts [FILE: Jul 9, 2026]Image: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany and Francen have reached a deal to protect Europe's automotive industry, the countries said in a statement Friday.
The plan aims to cut CO2 emissions and support the development and construction of electric cars in Europe, the statement added.

"Our shared ambition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe," the countries said.
The pact also includes incentives for investment, research and production.
Europe's automotive industry faces tough competition from China
European car makers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market, resulting in cost-cutting measures.
Premier of the state of Lower Saxony Olaf Lies hailed the agreement as a "strong signal" in support of Europe's car industry that protects jobs in the sector.
Lower Saxony is where German automotive giant Volkswagen's headquarters are located, in the city of Wolfsburg. Lies is also part of VW's supervisory board.
Germany's auto industry faces a deep structural crisis due to intense pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), higher production costs and other challenges.
As Europe's biggest carmaker by volume, VW has the heaviest exposure to overcapacity in its German plants, high fixed costs and its reliance on China.
Can Volkswagen stage an automotive comeback?

articles.title: Flash floods destroy villages in central Nepal
articles.summary:
Landslide blocks river and triggers downstream flooding, while summer temperatures persist in Portugal

Flash floods have swept through Nepal’s central Gorkha district after a pre-dawn…
articles.byline: Matt Andrews and Ed Walton for MetDesk

blocks.text: Flash floods have swept through Nepal’s central Gorkha district after a pre-dawn landslide on 11 October blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, triggering severe downstream flooding. Two villages in the worst-affected Chumanubri rural municipality were reportedly destroyed, with homes, roads and bridges washed away. Part of a hydropower station was also damaged.

After river levels surged from 2 metres to nearly 8.5 metres within hours, the national disaster risk reduction and management authority reported that 204 homes were damaged, and more than 650 people had been affected. More than 100 foreign trekkers were stranded in the popular hiking region. The floods come just two months after catastrophic flooding and landslides devastated parts of the country on the border with Tibet, leaving thousands dead or missing.

An exceptionally deep area of low pressure barrelled towards Iceland this week. The central pressure was measured at 931mb on 14 October. The pressure plummeted by 49mb in 24 hours, meeting the thresholds for explosive cyclogenesis, or a weather bomb. The system brought sustained winds of 55–60mph to the southern shores of the island before moving north-east through the North Atlantic towards Norway.

However, Iceland was spared the strongest winds as the track of the storm meant they remained out at sea. The system also affected areas beyond Iceland: a 108mph gust was recorded at Bealach Na Bà, in the Scottish Highlands, in association with a trailing 1,000-mile cold front that stretched from Norway to the mid-Atlantic.

Summer-like conditions have extended even further into meteorological autumn in Portugal. After temperatures of 40C at the end of September, on 14 October a maximum of 35.6C was recorded in the southern town of Mora, representing a climatological anomaly of more than 10C.

The heat was not localised, with numerous stations recording temperatures well into the mid-30s celsius. The latest forecasts show that the high pressure and unseasonably warm upper air temperatures will remain in place for the next few days. Looking further ahead, however, temperatures are expected to slowly return towards the average around the middle of next week.

articles.title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
articles.summary:
Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance

A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the…

blocks.text: A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.

While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.
The negatives were found more than a decade ago by the archivist Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.

blocks.caption: One of 47 images released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand of Gardner Island, now Nikumaroro. Photograph: RNZAF/RNZAF Official

blocks.text: Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.

What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, and filled with false leads.

A leading theory is that the aviator who broke several records, including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.

blocks.caption: Amelia Earhart standing in front of the Lockheed Electra in which she disappeared in July 1937.  Photograph: Alamy

blocks.text: This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll had been visited dozens of times.

In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said “severe weather” had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.

“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.

“We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience,” said Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute. “This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”
The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.

articles.title: ‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screen
articles.summary:
As violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’

A woman opens a 300‑year‑old…

blocks.text: A woman opens a 300‑year‑old box, unleashing a violent spirit – it is the spirit of colonialism and oppression roaring back to life. It is a pivotal scene in Sky’s supernatural series Possession and symbolises a wider shift in Jamaica’s film industry, where directors are increasingly using the landscape to tell Jamaican stories – including those that confront enslavement, trauma and historical memory.

The series is about a biracial British lawyer who travels to Jamaica to investigate a multimillion-pound inheritance dispute, only to uncover a dark, vengeful spirit tied to the plantation’s brutal colonial past.

For the Jamaican director, Storm Saulter, ensuring that the trauma and enduring legacy of enslavement and colonisation were powerfully represented was critical. Caribbean countries are increasingly arguing that centuries of enslavement have left the region at a lasting disadvantage – fuelling renewed calls for reparations.

Dr Lisa Tomlinson, a lecturer in film studies at the University of the West Indies, says the themes in Jamaican films are changing. “They’re now very much connected and reflective of Jamaican stories – stories that were previously taboo or avoided.”

blocks.caption: Mbatha-Raw plays a lawyer who travels from Bristol to Jamaica to handle an inheritance claim over a former slave plantation. Photograph: Des Willie

blocks.text: While Jamaican films are not always explicitly about reparations, she argues that many are engaging with the legacies of enslavement through cultural memory. “Reparation is not just a political act,” she says. “It’s also culture. These African‑derived spiritualities, the historical knowledge – when they come through creative expression, what they do is give us authority to tell our own stories.”

This, she says, is a form of “cultural reparation”, a reclaiming of narratives devalued or suppressed under colonialism, and a way of educating audiences about the past in ways that academics or politicians struggle to do. “The arts play a critical role in how we are educated in public awareness around reparation,” she says.

Jacqueline Jackson, Jamaica’s film commissioner, sees the shift too. She says productions such as Possession and Delroy Lindo’s Jabari’s People – shot entirely in Jamaica – reflect growing confidence and ambition among Jamaican creatives. “We are well established as a destination for international productions,” she says. “But what we want to see more of is local production and international collaboration that enables us to tell our own stories.”

blocks.caption: Delroy Lindo’s directorial debut Jabari’s People (he is pictured here in Spike Lee’s Da 5 Bloods) is shot entirely in Jamaica.  Photograph: Netflix

blocks.text: Both productions, she notes, worked closely with Jamaican talent to ensure authenticity and demonstrate what is possible when international financing and distribution unite with Jamaican creativity. “They show the growing interest in Jamaican stories and their potential for global audiences,” she says.

Tomlinson believes diaspora film-makers are playing a particularly important role in this shift. Unlike foreign productions that often use Jamaica as an exotic backdrop, diaspora directors are “moving away from the tourist‑gaze depictions” and are “capturing Jamaican everyday life”.

Saulter sees his series as part of a broader political awakening. “The mask has slipped … We’ve been told it’s one thing, and that thing is proven to be false. So there’s a seeking of what is true,” he says.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Storm Saulter, Possession’s director, aims to ‘open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret’.  Photograph: Bertie Watson

blocks.text: He says the box‑opening scene is not simply a plot device, but a metaphor for something larger: the resurfacing of long‑suppressed histories and the growing willingness among Caribbean creatives to confront the legacies of enslavement, inherited trauma and colonial violence through film.
“Literally, we’re going to open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret,” Saulter said. “It’s the spirit of colonial enslavement and oppression coming roaring back.”

That “spirit”, he explains, is embodied in a character who has lived through centuries of brutality – “a witness to history” – whose presence forces the protagonists to reckon with the past they have inherited.
Saulter’s interest in the subject is rooted in his upbringing. “I grew up in the countryside,” he says. “The Obia man, the church … nine nights … I’ve lived through all of those things.”

His experiences inspired him to tell stories that educate and have “real societal political impact”, while remaining thrilling, intriguing and entertaining. That approach, he argues, allows film-makers to tackle difficult histories. “As opposed to doing something that was like talking heads … we’re bringing you on a journey,” he says.
For Dr L’Antoinette Stines, a Yoruba priestess and cultural expert who advised on Possession, the series’ engagement with Afro‑spiritualist traditions is part of a longer history of resistance.

blocks.caption: Sheldon East plays Cudjoe East, the son of a British man who grew up at the Hope Hill plantation in Jamaica. Photograph: Des Willie/©Sky UK Ltd

blocks.text: “Black people have been fighting and using the arts for a very long time. It’s just that there is greater attention on it today,” she says. For decades she has choreographed similar work, she says, and stresses the importance of honouring the academics, poets and creatives who paved the way for today’s boom in authentic Jamaican storytelling.

She praises Saulter’s insistence on authenticity and creating a series that feels both contemporary and deeply rooted, exploring inherited trauma, ancestral memory and the unfinished business of colonialism.

articles.title: Who was Eva Mamlok? Berlin square renamed after Jewish anti-fascist resistance fighter
articles.summary: She started taking action against Hitler as a teenager and never stopped until her death in a concentration camp. Berlin's Blücherplatz is now being renamed after her.

image.caption: The only known remaining photo of resistance fighter Eva MamlokImage: Familienarchiv Siemsen

blocks.text: In the history of German resistance to Nazism, some names have become symbols: Sophie Scholl, Claus von Stauffenberg, Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Georg Elser.
Yet many others have remained largely forgotten.
Among them is Eva Mamlok, a young Jewish woman from Berlin whose acts of defiance began in her teenage years and continued until her murder in a Nazi concentration camp.
Now more people will get to know her story as Berlin renames Blücherplatz, a square in the district of Kreuzberg, Eva-Mamlok-Platz on October 16.

"Eva Mamlok was a very remarkable person. As a young Jewish woman from Berlin, her spirit of resistance was particularly striking," says cultural researcher Alexandra Weltz-Rombach, who has worked extensively with the historians' network "Gruppe Eva Mamlok."
'Down with Hitler'

Eva Mamlok was born on May 6, 1918, into a Jewish family in Berlin. They ran a wholesale wine business, and the family belonged to the vibrant Jewish middle class that formed an important part of Berlin's social and economic life during the Weimar Republic.

But Eva came of age just as Germany was descending into dictatorship. When Hitler became chancellor in 1933, she was only 14 years old. She was also a member of the Socialist Workers' Youth (SAJ). Following the suppression of the left-wing political youth organization later that year, she became active in the underground resistance.

According to testimony from Inge Berner (1922-2012), the sole survivor of Mamlok's later resistance group, Eva climbed onto the roof of a department store on Blücherplatz as a teenager and painted the slogan "Down with Hitler."
"She was caught doing that, though she wasn't arrested at that particular moment — that didn't happen until a year later," notes Weltz-Rombach.

blocks.caption: Known as the Tietz department store, the building onto which Mamlok wrote her slogan was renamed Hertie after its 'Aryanization' by the NazisImage: Public Domain

blocks.text: Arrested for honoring socialist icons Luxemburg and Liebknecht

Eva Mamlok first appeared in official records in November 1934, after she was arrested for taking part in commemorations for socialist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht at Berlin's Friedrichsfelde Cemetery.

Authorities determined that the 16-year-old held "hostile views toward the state" and placed her in "protective custody until further notice" — a euphemism the regime used to justify imprisonment without trial. She was sent to the women's concentration camp at Moringen in Lower Saxony, where she remained until May 1935.
After her release, she continued her anti-Nazi activities despite the increasing danger, facing persecution both as a political dissident and as a Jew.

In these underground circles, she met Pieter Siemsen (1914–2004), and they remained a couple until he emigrated to Argentina in 1937. The only known surviving photograph of Eva comes from his personal archive.

She had a daughter, Tana, in 1939. The father's identity is unknown, however. The child was placed in a Jewish orphanage in Berlin and deported in 1942 to the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp, where she was murdered.

Meanwhile, because she was Jewish, Eva Mamlok was forced to perform compulsory labor at the Berlin firm F. Butzke Schrauben-Industrie in 1940. There she met other women who shared her opposition to Nazism.

Together they formed what later became known as the "Eva Mamlok Group," an informal resistance network of Jewish and non-Jewish women. They distributed anti-Nazi leaflets and wrote slogans critical of Hitler.

They also shared banned books. "They were books that are today part of Germany's educational canon," from Thomas Mann to Lion Feuchtwanger, notes Weltz-Rombach. She adds that the fact that the Berlin Central and Regional Library (ZLB), Germany's largest public library, stands on the new Eva-Mamlok-Platz is a fitting symbol of this act of resistance and the importance of books.
Mamlok and others in her group were arrested for distributing this forbidden literature. On January 13, 1942, she was deported from Berlin to the Riga Ghetto in occupied Latvia.

According to Inge Berner's testimony, Mamlok remained active in the resistance there too. For example, she arranged for a contact still in Berlin to send her a cake with a miniature camera hidden inside it to document persecution in the ghetto.
In October 1944, she was sent to the Stutthof Nazi concentration camp, where she died in December of that year.
Replacing old symbols of Franco-German hostility

Blücherplatz was named after the Prussian field marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, whose most renowned achievement was leading his army against Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.
Several places, including streets and parks, have been named after him in Germany.

"There is no shortage of Blücher memorial sites," says Weltz-Rombach. "And perhaps it's also time to put an end to this old Franco-German enmity — which is, of course, inherent in the name Blücher, given its Prussian tradition — and to establish, in its place, a different form of remembrance," she adds.
The square also happens to be the site of the Carnival of Cultures, a multicultural street festival and parade held every year to celebrate Berlin's global diversity.
Role models for a new generation

Having first heard about Mamlok when a Stolperstein commemorating her was laid in 2011, Weltz-Rombach has been researching her biography for the past few years. The Berlin-based filmmaker, producer and curator has also been sharing the resistance fighter's story through various projects, including an exhibition in 2024 and a podcast series with young Berliners.
Since Eva Mamlok was only a teenager herself when she became politically active, the workshop participants can easily relate to her fate.

These teenagers learn about Mamlok's experiences at the actual locations where she was active, helping them imagine what it would be like to be arrested and imprisoned for six months without trial for doing things that normally wouldn't be considered crimes — such as simply expressing an opinion publicly or laying flowers at a commemorative event, explains Weltz-Rombach.
"Above all, she is, of course, a role model — an example of how one would like to act oneself, and how courageous one would like to be."

Women's "resistance was often of a more everyday nature, rather than planting bombs," notes Weltz-Rombach. Their stories offer examples of "forms of resistance that have only recently received more attention." She mentions, for example, a 2024 exhibition and the launch of a database dedicated to female resistance fighters.

Even though many of the eyewitnesses have now died, Weltz-Rombach believes there are still many more of these stories that deserve to be brought into the spotlight: "There are definitely many names we do not know, that are waiting to be further researched."

articles.title: Greens leader denies knowledge of ‘secret dossier’ on how to handle Jordon Steele-John misconduct allegations
articles.summary:
David Shoebridge says 47-page document not ‘made by, used by, or seen by’ his office as matter referred to parliamentary standards commission

  • Get our

blocks.text: Greens leader David Shoebridge has denied knowledge of the existence of an alleged crisis management document on how to deal with allegations against Jordon Steele-John being made public.

The Nine newspapers reported on Friday afternoon the existence of a “secret dossier”, first drafted in 2016, which contained misconduct allegations against the Western Australian Greens senator and how to suppress their media coverage.
Guardian Australia has not independently confirmed the document’s contents.
In a statement responding to claims that the federal leader’s office had access to the 47-page document, Shoebridge said it was not “made by, used by, or seen by the leader’s office”.
“The office is committed to having the matters comprehensively investigated with a fair, independent and timely process,” he said.
“Everyone deserves a safe workplace, and all complaints should be considered in a fair and robust process.”

Steele-John confirmed he would leave the party room on Thursday after some details of historical complaints about inappropriate comments made to women ranging between 2017 and 2025 were publicly aired in the media.

The 32-year-old senator rejected the claims and said he had referred them to the Western Australian Greens for a “fair, independent process” that “upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved”.
“I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not,” Steele-John said in a statement.

Shoebridge told ABC on Friday morning he referred the complaints outlined in a letter to the parliamentary workplace support service, which he said was “unable to deal with it because of the circumstances and nature of the allegation”.

The PWSS’s chief executive, Leonie McGregor, said the office had not been given the letter but had provided Shoebridge’s office with options, including referring the complaints to the independent parliamentary standards commission.
Guardian Australia understands Shoebridge has now referred the matter to the IPSC.
The WA Greens confirmed on Thursday they would “seek legal advice on how best to establish an independent inquiry” into the matters raised.

A statement from the co-conveners, Giz Watson and Simone Collins, and state director, Dean Smith, said: “Our party is built on the contributions of members, volunteers, staff and supporters, and every one of them deserves to feel safe and respected when they take part in our work. Maintaining that safety is a responsibility we hold seriously.”
Shoebridge confirmed Steele-John would not return to parliament until the independent investigations had been completed.
“It’s my understanding that leave means leave,” he told ABC.

“I have responsibility for the party room and the Greens’ functions, and I have some capacity to direct in relation to the party room. But Senator Steele-John has indicated to me that he’s on leave, and that leave means leave.”

articles.title: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case not ‘prioritised’ due to high workload, inquest hears
articles.summary:
Eight-year-old Queensland girl died in 2022 after being denied insulin by her religious parents

  • Get our breaking…

blocks.text: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case was not “prioritised” or worked intensively because the staff member assigned to her case was “very busy”, a coroner has heard.

The Queensland coroner’s court also heard the case worker may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of Struhs’ “upper class home”, putting cases believed to involve a more immediate risk ahead of Elizabeth’s.

The eight-year-old died on 7 January 2022 of diabetic ketoacidosis, after her father, Jason Struhs, stopped providing insulin to treat her type 1 diabetes at their home in Toowoomba, Queensland. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.

Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard is holding an inquest into Elizabeth’s death. She has previously heard the eight-year-old came to the attention of child safety after a 2019 incident where she presented to hospital in a coma.
Child safety ended its involvement with the family after just 17 weeks of what was supposed to be an intensive intervention, assessing her as “safe”.

But the single child safety officer assigned to Elizabeth’s case told the court on Friday her approach wasn’t intensive and she didn’t make weekly check-ins during that period, despite departmental guidelines.

The department chose to release her back into Jason’s sole care over the objections of specialist doctors who treated Elizabeth in Brisbane, subject to a voluntary intervention with parental agreement (IPA).
The coroner heard just a single child safety officer was assigned to the case, and would often conduct home visits alone.
The officer gave evidence on Friday.

“Ideally I wanted to visit with the family at least once a week, in accordance with our IPAT (intervention with parental agreement team) guidelines,” according to her statement, presented to the court.

“During my management of the IPA for the Struhs family, I recall that I was not always available to conduct home visits with the family. I recall this being a very busy time for the CSSC (child safety service centre) and I also recall being regularly out of the office travelling to visit other families.
“I note that one of the home visits to the Struhs family was conducted by a student who was working in the team at the time.”
She said Elizabeth’s case wasn’t treated as a complex case, which it should have been due to the intervention.

But at the time, she had a “big caseload” – approximately 25-28 children in 15 families on the same intervention– she said. The coroner has previously heard that the Toowoomba region was among the busiest in the state for child safety.

Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris said most of them were experiencing significant domestic violence, drug use, sexual abuse and it was not often that she was required to work with “upper class families” like the Struhs.
The case worker agreed that she may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of the Struhs home.
“I believe that we may have prioritised other cases at the time for children who were presenting at more immediate risk,” she told the court.
after newsletter promotion
She also told the court that she may have had a bias because her own child had nearly died of type 1 diabetes at age 6. She had asked not to be assigned to the case, she said.

Several witnesses have previously told the coroner they expected the intervention to last months or a year, but the case worker said they were supposed to not last longer than three months, because they were an intensive approach.
On Friday, Kirkegaard asked another child safety witness whether they felt “organisational pressure to get a matter like this finalised quickly”.
“Absolutely,” the witness said, adding an IPA could be intrusive and potentially harmful to a child if dragged out.
“I don’t believe it impacted our decision making,” she said.
On 13 November 2019, a more senior child safety officer assessed Elizabeth as “safe” and the intervention was ended.
The case worker told the coroner on Friday that she hadn’t appreciated the danger of Elizabeth’s mother’s church group, which was considered a source of support for the family.
All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including Elizabeth’s parents, Kerrie and Jason, and the group leader, Brendan Stevens.
In her statement she said Jason had agreed to continue to treat his daughter against his wife’s beliefs and that she had “faith” that should Kerrie stand in the way he would leave her.
None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
articles.summary:
Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia

Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla…
articles.byline: Stefano Valentino in Sulawesi and Ajit Niranjan

blocks.text: Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.

Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.

Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.
Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.

“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”

blocks.caption: Wadimula: ‘Destroying [the forest] means destroying our own life.’ Photograph: Stefano Valentino

blocks.text: Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.

Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.

In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.

blocks.caption: Morowali industrial park on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary. Photograph: Stefano Valentino

blocks.text: Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.

The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.

The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.

Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year.

The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.

Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm TreeMap suggests.

blocks.caption: A track cut through forest in the Hengjaya concession. Photograph: Stefano Valentino

blocks.text: Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.

SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.

The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo, Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.

Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits.
Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain.

Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.”
Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.”

Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.”

Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.”

Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.”
General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.”

Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.”

Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.”
CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment.
This investigation was supported by Journalismfund Europe and The Pulitzer Center. Lorenzo Di Stasi and James Jackson contributed reporting.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
articles.summary:
Rights group says Youssef al-Manasif was tortured and first met his lawyer five years after arrest for non-violent crimes

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending…

blocks.text: A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.
The charity Reprieve says Manasif was tortured and coerced into signing a false confession and only met his state-appointed lawyer for the first time in 2022 – five years after his arrest.
Manasif’s death sentence has now reportedly been upheld by the Saudi supreme court, which was likely to be his last hope of avoiding execution.

His family have not spoken in public about the case and could face harassment or arrest if they do so. “There is nothing they can do now but wait,” said Duaa Dhainy, a consultant for Reprieve and the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights.

Saudi Arabia has seen what activists describe as a “horrifying” surge in executions under the rule of the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. Last year saw a record 356 people put to death in the country. Most of those executed are foreigners convicted of minor and non-violent drug crimes.
At least 17 people, who were children at the time of their alleged offences, have been executed in Saudi Arabia since 2015, according to Reprieve.
Saudi Arabia issued a royal decree abolishing the death penalty for children in 2020, stating that individuals would not be sentenced to death for crimes committed when they were minors.

However, it has since upheld the death penalty in a number of cases involving child defendants. In April, it executed Ali al-Subaiti, along with his uncle, Mustafa al-Subaiti, for non-lethal “terrorist” offences committed when he was 12 years old.
after newsletter promotion

The UN’s independent human rights experts have previously expressed concerns about Manasif’s case. It said Saudi Arabia should immediately halt planned executions of people convicted of offences allegedly committed when they were under 18.

“They are using execution as a tool to show how powerful they are and how they can threaten anyone who does not follow their rules,” Dhainy said of the Saudi regime. “We think he should be treated as a minor and not sentenced to death as his charges relate to when he was under 18.”
Human Rights Watch said executing Manasif for a non-violent crime committed as a minor would be “an unconscionable new low”.

articles.title: 'It's really hard to believe' - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded
articles.summary: Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed after a 16-year-old suspect opened fire in the city of Bend, local police say.

blocks.text: Four victims, including a teacher and three children aged 5, 8 and 11, were killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon, local police say.

A 16-year-old suspect forced his way into the school by firing at locked doors. He was also killed in the shooting by an armed member of the community who followed the suspect inside the school, police said at a press conference.
Two additional victims, a 7-year-old and another teacher, were hurt and transported to hospital in critical condition.

articles.title: Carney to speak at pro-Confederation rally in Edmonton

blocks.text: Edmonton·
Prime Minister Mark Carney will speak at Edmonton's Expo Centre on Friday night to urge Albertans to vote to stay in Canada in a provincial referendum.
Prime minister set to deliver remarks in support of Canadian unity ahead of referendum
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 16, 2026 3:14 PM EDT | Last Updated: 7 minutes ago
Mark Carney attends rally ahead of Alberta referendum
Earlier in the day, Carney spoke at a pro-unit event in Red Deer.
Alberta and Canada don't agree on everything, but they're on the same page when it comes to staying in Confederation, Premier Danielle Smith told a crowd in Red Deer Friday.
"We often disagree quite publicly on several things," she said. "But today we can all agree that on Question 10, we are voting for Option 1 to remain in Canada."

Albertans are set to get to polls on Monday for a 10-question referendum. On Question 10, Albertans will choose either Option 1, to remain in Canada, or Option 2, to begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation.
Smith joined Prime Minister Mark Carney at a brewery in Red Deer, as he passed through on his way from Thursday's Forever Canadian rally in Calgary and the one set to take place in Edmonton Friday.

items: 'Vote like Canada depends on it,' Carney says at Calgary rally ahead of Alberta referendum

blocks.text: "This is now a time, a moment in Canadian history, where we are going to be able to work side by side," Smith said. "I feel for the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together."

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: Carney said Alberta's trust in the federal government has been tested, but their interests are now aligned.
"As a country, we are co-operating again," he said. "Canada is working again. We are coming together. "
Premier says Alberta and Canada 'walking together' for first time in a long time

Both leaders urged Albertans to vote and listed examples of what their recent co-operation has achieved, including the announcement of the Pacific Link pipeline and agreements on water, housing and defence.
There are more shared wins to come, Smith said, noting the Supreme Court of Canada agreed Thursday to hear an appeal of the federal ban on single-use plastics.

While Carney and Smith agree on a united Canada, Smith wants Albertans to vote "yes" on nine referendum questions that would give the province more control over immigration and a mandate to pursue constitutional changes to wrest power from Ottawa.
Prime Minister Mark Carney attends a national unity rally in Red Deer alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)
Carney, meanwhile, has urged Albertans to say “no to the nine.”
Smith said Friday she will work to change his mind.
Near the end of his brief comments, Carney held up a pair of red, knitted mittens, calling them a symbol.
They were made in Red Deer with a pattern by an Ontario designer and yarn from New Brunswick. He cited the mittens as an example of the “threads that link us as a country.”
“What we're facing on Monday is, in part, a reflection of that.”

Both leaders called out notable politicians in the crowd, including former Alberta premier Ed Stelmach and former MP Monte Solberg from Stephen Harper's cabinet. Matt Jeneroux, the MP for Edmonton Riverbend, was also there.

items: MP Matt Jeneroux leaves Conservatives to join Liberals, citing 'national unity crisis'

blocks.text: A number of current and former municipal leaders also attended the event, like Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas, former Edmonton mayor Amarjeet Sohi, Sylvan Lake Mayor Megan Hanson, Airdrie Mayor Heather Spearman and Red Deer Mayor Cindy Jefferies.
"I don't think Red Deer's seen this kind of attention for some time," Jefferies said.

She added that when she attended a Liberal caucus retreat a month ago, she told federal politicians at the time that she has noticed them paying more attention to Alberta recently and that she doesn't want that to stop when the referendum is over.
Prime Minister Mark Carney is seen at a national unity rally at a brewery in Red Deer, Alta., on Oct. 16, 2026. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC News)
Jefferies had co-signed a statement with Edmonton Centre MP Eleanor Olszewski last month calling for Albertans to vote for Option 1 on Question 10.

"I hesitated to take a position on it," she told CBC News. "But listening to businesses in the community, many of them were having concerns around recruiting and retention of staff because of the uncertainty created in our province with respect to this referendum and the discussion that's going on.
"I want stability."

While the brewery was filled with people who support Alberta staying in Canada, some people could be seen across the road waving an "Alberta strong" flag and one person told CBC News they support the idea of an independent Alberta.

Red Deer resident Kelsie Petersen said she came because she "never had a chance to see a prime minister before." She said she will vote for Option 2 on Question 10 because even though she "wants a better deal for Alberta," she would rather not separate.

Pro-remain supporters gather outside of Red Hart Brewing in Red Deer, Alta., on Friday, Oct. 16. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith spoke inside the brewery, making a pitch for unity before the Alberta referendum on Monday. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC)

Carney is scheduled to speak later Friday at a Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton, while Smith is headed to Calgary to speak at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference. Earlier Friday, Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre made his pitch for unity at the same conference.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kerry Powell is an editor on the CBC Edmonton digital news desk. She has been telling Edmonton stories for more than three decades, with stints at the Edmonton Journal and Global Edmonton, where she was the managing editor.

articles.title: Watch: What does Starlink have to do with the Ukraine-Russia war?
articles.summary: Ukraine's president has told Elon Musk that any restriction on the Starlink's system cost lives.
